﴿Ta-Sin.﴾

It has been established that the preponderant view is that these letters are an allusive challenge (ta'rid) to the inimitability (i'jaz) of the Qur'an, and that it is composed of the same letters as their speech. What has been said about the various interpretations (mahamil) that many commentators have attempted for such letters has also been mentioned.

On the basis that these letters are abbreviated (muqtadabah) from the Names of Allah the Exalted, what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas may be said about the letters of this surah: that "Ta-Sin" is abbreviated from the ta' of His Name al-Latif (the Subtle), and from the sin of His Name al-Sami' (the All-Hearing). The intended meaning is an oath by these two Names, i.e., "By al-Latif and al-Sami', these are the verses of the clear Qur'an."

* * *

﴿These are the verses of the Qur'an and a clear Book.﴾

The discussion of it is like the discussion of the opening of Surah al-Shu'ara'. This verse of this surah differs from the preceding one in three things: by mentioning the name "the Qur'an," by coordinating (atf) "and a Book" with "the Qur'an," and by indefinitely stating "Book" (kitab).

As for mentioning the name "the Qur'an," it is because it is a proper name (alam) for the Book revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ), for i'jaz and guidance. This proper name is synonymous with "the Book" when defined by the definite article of prior reference (lam al-'ahd), which has become a proper name by predominance (bi'l-ghalabah) for the Qur'an. However, the name "the Qur'an" is more inclusive in definiteness, because it is a transferred proper noun (alam manqul). As for "Book," it is a proper name by predominance. Thus the intended meaning of his saying "﴿and a clear Book﴾" is also the Qur'an. There is no basis for interpreting it as the Preserved Tablet, in order to escape the problem of coordinating a thing with itself, because escaping that is achieved by the fact that the coordination of one of two attributes with the other is common in speech. Since each of "the Qur'an" and "﴿a clear Book﴾" carries an aspect of description, the first by its derivation from recitation (qira'ah), and the second by its description as "clear" (mubin), the coordination of one of them with the other returns to the coordination of attributes with one another. The second was not introduced as a substitution (badal) because coordination (atf) is more closely tied to the independence of both coordinated items as intended in the speech, unlike substitution.

A parallel to this verse is the verse of Surah al-Hijr: ﴿These are the verses of the Book and a clear Qur'an﴾ [al-Hijr: 1]. In that verse, "Qur'an" has the sense of an appositive (atf al-bayan) to "the Book," but it is a coordination for the purpose of combining the two by the annexation of "verses" to both.

[Page 218]

The reason the Qur'an is mentioned first in this verse, with "a clear Book" coordinated after it, contrary to what occurs at the opening of Surah al-Hijr, is that the context here is one of exalting the Qur'an and its believing followers. Therefore it is described as ﴿a guidance and good tidings for the believers﴾ [al-Naml: 2], meaning that they are upon guidance in the present and are given good tidings of a good outcome. Thus what was more important here regarding the revelation comprising these verses was to invoke it by its proper name derived from the source of recitation, because recitation suits the state of those who believe in it and accept its verses, for they study them. For this reason the definite article was introduced to evoke the origin, reminding that it is recited and studied. Then "a clear Book" was coordinated after it, so that the exaltation of it would combine both of its designations and complete the indication, by definiteness, of the meaning of perfection within its category of readable things, and by indefiniteness, of the meaning of its magnification among books, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿confirming what is before it of the Book and a guardian over it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48].

As for what occurs at the beginning of Surah al-Hijr, it is a context of causing regret to the disbelievers because of their turning away from Islam, so it was fitting that it begin with the name "Book," derived from writing (kitabah), rather than "the Qur'an," because they are far removed from its recitation, yet it is written, and a proof against them remaining throughout time. The detailed explanation of this was given earlier at the beginning of Surah al-Hijr. For this reason, here the mention of "a clear Book" is followed by the state ﴿a guidance and good tidings for the believers﴾ [al-Naml: 2].

"Mubin" (clear) is an active participle (ism fa'il), either from abana, intransitive, in the sense of "to be clear" (bana), because describing it as clear and evident has a share of exalting it that is not present in describing it as one that explains and clarifies. Thus "mubin" conveys two meanings: first, that the evidences of its truthfulness, its inimitability, and its guidance are manifest to every reflecting person; and second, that it is one that guides and details.

﴿Guidance and good tidings for the believers﴾ ﴿who establish the prayer, pay the zakat, and who are certain of the Hereafter﴾.

(﴿Guidance and good tidings﴾) are two circumstantial qualifiers (ḥāl, a word describing the state of the subject or object at the time of the action) of "Book" (kitāb), after it has been described as "clear" (mubīn).

The circumstantial qualifier was rendered as a verbal noun (maṣdar) for emphasis, given the strength of the Book's causing guidance and conveying good tidings to the believers. The meaning is: guidance for the believers and good tidings are both produced by it and continue through its verses.

[p. 219]

"Good tidings" (bushrā) is a noun for giving glad tidings (tabshīr). Describing the Book as guidance and good tidings is in the manner of a rational metaphor (majāz ʿaqlī, a figure in which an action is attributed to something other than its true agent), since the true guide and bearer of glad tidings is God or the Messenger, by means of the Book. The element that governs the circumstantial qualifier is the sense of "I point to" (ushīru) contained in the demonstrative (ism al-ishārah), as in His saying ﴿And this is my husband, an old man﴾ [Hud: 72]. What this involves has already been discussed in the commentary on Surah Ibrahim.

﴿For the believers﴾ is governed by ﴿guidance and good tidings﴾, because the believers are those who benefited from its guidance, as in His saying ﴿guidance for the God-conscious﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2].

The description of the believers by the relative clause (ṣilah) serves to distinguish them from others, since they were then known by establishing the prayer and giving charity to the poor and the needy. Do you not see that God identified the disbelievers by His saying ﴿And woe to the polytheists﴾ [Fussilat: 6] ﴿who do not pay the zakat﴾ [Fussilat: 7]? Moreover, the relative clause contains an indication of the reason why the report about them is framed as their being upon guidance from their Lord and being successful.

Zakat means charity, because it purifies the soul or purifies the wealth, that is, it increases it in blessing. The term zakat here means charity in general, or obligatory charity that was incumbent upon the Muslims, which is the mutual support of some of them for others, as indicated by His saying in describing the polytheists: ﴿Nay, but you do not honour the orphan﴾ [al-Fajr: 17] ﴿nor do you urge one another to feed the needy﴾ [al-Fajr: 18]. As for the zakat fixed by the prescribed minimum amounts (nuṣub) and quantities due on the wealth of the rich, it was enjoined after the Hijrah (the Prophet's migration to Madinah), so it is not intended here, since this surah is Meccan (Makkī, revealed in Mecca).

The clause ﴿and they are certain of the Hereafter﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the relative clause, and is not part of it. For this reason its style differs from the style of the relative clause: it is a nominal sentence, given emphasis to its content, because it motivates the doing of good deeds. Also, the second pronoun "they" (hum) may be regarded as a separating pronoun (ḍamīr faṣl) indicating restriction (qaṣr, exclusive limitation), meaning: none is certain of the Hereafter except these people.

The restriction is relative (qaṣr iḍāfī), in comparison with their neighbours among the polytheists. Otherwise, the People of the Book are certain of the Hereafter, but their condition is not what is intended for the addressees from both groups. The fronting of "of the Hereafter" (bil-ākhirah) is for the sake of preserving the rhyme (rāʿāyah ʿalā al-fāṣilah, the verse-ending) and for emphasis on it.

﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter – We have made their deeds appealing to them, so they wander blindly.﴾

Inevitably, the fact that the Clear Book is a guidance and glad tidings for those who have certainty about the Hereafter raises a question in the mind of the listener about the condition of their opposites, those who do not have certainty about the Hereafter: why do they not be guided by the guidance of this Book, which has reached a great degree of clarity and manifestness? Therefore it is fitting for the context to inform about what turned these opposites away from belief in the Hereafter life, and so this explanatory resumption (al-isti'naf al-bayani) occurs to explain the reason for their continuing in their misguidance. That is because Allah knows the corruption of their intentions, so He deprived them of success (tawfiq) and did not turn toward them a care that would pull them out of the snare of Satan, for a wisdom known to Allah from the state in which their souls were molded. Thus this resumption, with its consequences, occurs as an interjection (i'tiraD) between the reports of praising the Qur'an with what preceded and praising it through the one to whom it was revealed, with His saying: ﴿And indeed you are receiving the Qur'an﴾ [al-Naml: 6].

The emphasis of the report with the emphatic particle (harf al-tawkid) is for the sake of giving it importance, because the cause of the division of people in receiving guidance, between one who hastens, one who lags behind, and one who insists on persisting in misguidance, is something that is confusing to people. The bringing of the subject as a relative pronoun (mawsul) indicates that the relative clause is the cause of the predicate.

The "adornment" of those deeds for them: their conceiving of them in their souls as beautiful. Attributing the adornment to Allah Most High returns to the matter of creation (al-takwin), meaning: their souls and minds were created receptive to being affected by and accepting what they see of the evils of beliefs and deeds to which they have become accustomed. So the attribution of "deeds" to the pronoun of those who do not believe in the Hereafter requires that those deeds are the apparent and hidden acts of polytheism; because of their familiarity with them and their rigidity in them, they have become unable to accept the guidance of this Book whose verses have come to them.

The verse has indicated a very subtle meaning: that the variation among people in accepting good is in proportion to the firmness of the opposite of good in their souls and the attachment of their natural disposition (fitrah) to it. This is due to what has befallen the soundness of the natural disposition on which Allah created people, of deterioration toward corruption, as indicated by His saying the Most High (﴿Certainly We created man in the best of stature﴾ [al-Tin: 4] ﴿Then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ [al-Tin: 5] ﴿Except those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ [al-Tin: 6]) and the verse. So the swift acceptance of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, of faith in the Prophet ﷺ is a sign that Allah created him with a soul and intellect free from attachment to evil, longing for good, until when it appeared to them, they accepted it.

Page 221

This is the meaning of the saying of Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari: "Abu Bakr never ceased to be under the eye of good pleasure from the Most Merciful."

The making of the relative clause a present-tense verb indicates that the ruling is tied to the continuation of non-belief, and the making of the predicate a past-tense verb in His saying (﴿zayyanna﴾, "We have made appealing") indicates that this adornment is a ruling that was established and settled earlier. It suffices that it is among the effects of creation according to what has befallen souls of stages.

So the attribution of the adornment of the deeds of the polytheists to Allah in this verse and elsewhere, like His saying: ﴿Thus We made appealing to every nation their deeds﴾ [al-An'am: 108] in Surah al-An'am, does not contradict attributing it to Satan in His later saying ﴿And Satan made their deeds appealing to them and barred them from the way﴾ [al-Naml: 24]; for the whisperings of Satan find in the souls of those people a lush pasture and a soil that does not dry up. So Allah Most High adorns for them because of the development of the constitution of their souls, from the effect of weakness of the soundness of their natural dispositions, and Satan adorns for them through whispering that finds acceptance in their souls, as He said, relating about him: ﴿He said, "By Your might, I will surely mislead them all, / Except among them Your chosen servants."﴾ [Sad: 82–83] And He said: ﴿Indeed, My servants – you have over them no authority, except those who follow you of the deviators﴾ [al-Hijr: 42]. This has already passed in His saying: ﴿Allah has sealed over their hearts﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7] and the verse, in Surah al-Baqarah.

Based on the adornment of their deeds for them, they are in a firmly established blindness (amah), by expressing the report about them with this in a nominal sentence. The form of the present tense indicates that the blindness is renewed and continuous in them, meaning: they do not return to guidance, because they consider themselves to be upon the right course.

Al-'Amah (ʿamah): going astray from the path without guidance. It has been mentioned in His saying: ﴿And He extends them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15] in Surah al-Baqarah. Its verb follows the patterns of mana' and fariha.

So the pronoun (hum) refers to ﴿those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ with regard to this description, not to their persons.

Know that this continuation varies in its extent: among it is the most severe, which lasts with its bearer until death, and among it is less than that. All of that is according to the degree to which disbelief is made appealing in their souls, pure adornment or mixed with some reflection on its corruptions. Those are levels that none encompasses except He who knows the treachery of eyes and what the breasts conceal.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 5:

﴿Those are the ones for whom is the evil of the punishment, and in the Hereafter they are the greatest losers.﴾

He intended by the demonstrative (ism al-ishara, the demonstrative pronoun) to increase their distinction, exposing the wretchedness of their condition. In such a context the demonstrative also draws attention to the fact that what the predicate reports about them arises from what preceded the demonstrative, as in (﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]) in Surat al-Baqarah.

He reinforced what he had indicated with the demonstrative by following it with the relative pronoun (ism al-mawsul) and its clause (silah), because of what this implies about the basis on which the predicate is built.

The lam of specification (lam al-ikhtisas) is used to indicate that, in this their present state, the evil of the punishment has been prepared for them. The apparent meaning is that it refers to the punishment of this world, namely the punishment of the sword and the humiliation of defeat on the day of Badr and after it, by the indication of the conjunction with ﴿and in the Hereafter they are the greatest losers﴾.

Thus the verse indicates two requitals. The first is a requital in this world, reckoned as due to them, which they deserve because of their disbelief. So long as they remain disbelievers, they are prepared to fall into that punishment when its appointed time comes while they are still in unbelief.

The second is a requital in the Hereafter, which befalls whoever arrives in the Hereafter while still a disbeliever. This arrival is called al-muwafah (the state of meeting God in the same condition in which one died) according to al-Ash'ari.

Because the first punishment is capable of being averted by faith just before it descends upon them, the lam of specification is used with it, indicating that it has been prepared in a particular way. As for the essential requital of the Hereafter, there is no escape from it for them if they come on the Day of Resurrection in their disbelief.

The pronouns in His saying (lahum) and His saying (﴿and they in the Hereafter, they are﴾) refer back to (﴿those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Naml: 4]), taking into account the descriptive label that the relative clause conveys. Therefore the pronoun does not indicate specific individuals, but rather those characterized by the content of the relative clause. Whoever is freed from this error and returns to faith is absolved of this ruling.

The predicate concerning their loss is expressed in a nominal sentence (jumla ismiyya) and is joined to a separating pronoun (damir al-fasl), to indicate the permanence of the content of the sentence and that its content is restricted to them, as was mentioned earlier in His saying: (﴿And in the Hereafter they are certain﴾ [al-Naml: 3]).

The predicate came as an elative noun (ism al-tafdil), to indicate that they are unique in loss, and that the loss of others does not resemble theirs. This is because loss in the Hereafter varies in degree and duration, and the greatest of it in both respects is the loss of the polytheists.

[Page 223]

This is an atf (conjunction) on the sentence "﴿These are the verses of the Qur'an﴾ [al-Naml: 1]". It is a shift from praising the Qur'an to praising the one to whom it was revealed. The Qur'an's verses indicate that it is a clear Book, which is a sign that it comes from God. Then, it is a sign of the truthfulness of the one to whom it was revealed, since it informed him of the news of the earlier prophets and nations, which neither he nor his people knew before the Qur'an. Only a few of the People of the Book, the specialists among them, knew some of this, and most of what they knew had been distorted. Furthermore, this serves as an introduction (tamhid) to the stories mentioned after it.

"Tulaqqa" is the present tense of laqqahu, in the passive voice (mabni lil-majhul), meaning: he made it meet (laqiyan), i.e., he caused it to be encountered. Al-luqiyy and al-liqa' mean one of two things reaching another, either intentionally or by chance. Al-talqiyah means making a thing meet another, as in God's words: ﴿And He gave them radiance and joy﴾ [al-Insan: 11]. Here it is a metaphor for the revelation of the Qur'an to the Prophet (ﷺ), described as a process of being met, as if Gabriel (Jibril) strove to bring the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Qur'an together.

The verb was built in the passive without naming its agent because it is known that the agent is God or Gabriel, and the meaning is the same either way. The emphasis is then directed at the disbelievers who are listening, by way of allusion (ta'ridh).

The insertion (iqham) of the word "ladun" between "min" and "hakim" is a signal of how strongly the Qur'an is attributed to the side of God, may He be exalted. The original meaning of "ladun" is indicating a place, like "'inda" (with/at). Then its use spread to refer to what is among the special qualities of the thing it is attached to, as an honour to that thing. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿and taught him knowledge from Us﴾ [al-Kahf: 65].

Al-Hakim is one who is strong in wisdom, and al-'Alim is one who has vast knowledge. The indefinite form (tankir) in "hakim" and "'alim" signals the magnification of this All-Wise, All-Knowing (One), as if it were said: "from a Wise One: what a Wise One! And a Knowing One: what a Knowing One!"

In these two noble attributes there is a fitting connection both to the conjoined sentence and to the introduction it prepares for. What is in the Qur'an is evidence of the wisdom and knowledge of the One who revealed it. What is mentioned here of stories, and what is drawn from them of lessons, examples and admonition, are traces of the wisdom and knowledge of the All-Wise, All-Knowing. The same applies to what this contains of strengthening the heart of the Messenger (ﷺ).

[Page 225]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 7:

﴿When Moses said to his family, "I have perceived a fire. I will bring you from it some news, or bring you a burning brand that you may warm yourselves."﴾

Al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH), al-Zamakhshari and others said: (إذْ) (idh, "when") is governed by an implied verb whose estimate is: "Remember" (اذْكُرْ, udhkur). That is, (إذْ) is detached from the sense of a time-adverb and is used in the general sense of "time," and it is in the accusative as an object: "Remember the story of the time when Moses said to his family." This follows the pattern of ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I will make upon the earth a successor"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30].

Thus the sentence is an independent new statement (istinaf ibtida'i). The fitting relevance of its placement is to show the parallel between the Prophet (ﷺ) receiving the Qur'an and Moses (peace be upon him) receiving the speech of God when he was called: ﴿O Moses, indeed I am Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [al-Naml: 9].

This is part of the fine transition (al-takhallus, a graceful shift) to mentioning the stories of these prophets immediately after praising the Qur'an and affirming that it comes from One who is All-Wise and All-Knowing. The meaning is: God relates to you from the news of the messengers what contains a lesson for you and for your people, and what strengthens your heart.

In this there is a shift to another kind of inimitability (i'jaz, the miraculous inimitability of the Qur'an), namely the reporting of unseen matters (al-mughayyabat). This is what we counted as the fourth aspect of the aspects of the Qur'an's inimitability in the tenth of the introductions (al-muqaddimat).

The clause (﴿Moses said to his family﴾) up to its end serves as a preface to the clause ﴿So when he came to it, he was called: "Blessed is whoever is in the fire"﴾ [al-Naml: 8], etc. The time of Moses' saying this statement to his family was the time of his setting out, in preparation for the revelation coming to him. So this story is an example which God gave for the condition of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with his people. It began with what preceded it of Moses' mission and circumstances, as an embedding (idmaj, weaving) of the story into the admonition.

Al-ahl (the family) here means his wife, and no one was with him except his wife and two young sons. The one addressed in the speech was his wife, and the wife is referred to by "family" as a euphemism. In a hadith: "By God, I know nothing about my family except good."

The fire appeared only to Moses and not to others of his family, because it was not an ordinary fire. Rather, it was one of the lights of the realm of the malakut (the unseen dominion of God), which God manifested to Moses, so no one else could see it. This is supported by his emphasizing the report with (إنَّ, inna, "indeed"), which points to the fact that his wife doubted the appearance of a fire, because she had not seen it.

(al-iynas) is perceiving and feeling something hidden, so it can apply to visible things and to sounds, as al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

"She perceived a sound, and the hunter startled her in the afternoon, when evening had drawn near."

The meaning of (al-khabar, "news") here is news of the place from which the fire shines. Perhaps he thought there was a house there, and hoped that they would be hosted there with its people that night. However, the people of the fire were not a household that would host them, since they were men of strength who would bring from them a live coal of fire, so that he could light a fire for his family from the wood along the road, to warm themselves by it.

(al-shihab) is a blazing coal, and (al-qabas) is an ember or a flaming torch taken from a fire, i.e., its burning is taken from another fire, to light wood or a wick or something else with it.

The majority of readers (al-Jumhur) read (شِهابٍ, shihabin) as a genitive construction with (قَبَسٍ, qabasin), an idafa of the general to the specific, like "a ring of iron" (khatam hadid). ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub and Khalaf read (شِهابٍ) with tanwin (nunation), so that (قَبَسٍ) is then either an apposition (badal) to (شِهابٍ) or a qualifier (na't) of it. This was discussed at the beginning of surah Ta-Ha.

(al-istilaʾ, "warming oneself") is a form of the verb (اصْطَلى, istalā), a derived form (iftiʿal) from (al-salyu), which is roasting by fire. The form (iftiʿal) indicates that it is an attempt at roasting, so it came to mean warming oneself by the heat of the fire.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 8–11 (part 1 of 2):

Page 226

﴿So when he came to it, he was called: "Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it. And glory be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ ﴿"O Musa, indeed it is I, Allah, the Mighty, the Wise."﴾ ﴿"And throw down your staff." So when he saw it moving as if it were a snake, he turned back retreating and did not return. "O Musa, do not fear. Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence. Except one who wrongs and then substitutes good after evil; indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful."﴾

The pronoun in (jā'ahā, "came to it") is feminine, in keeping with what preceded regarding calling the light "fire" according to what appeared to Musa. This story has already been mentioned in Surat Ta-Ha, so here we should address what these verses uniquely contain of vocabulary and constructions. Following the name of Majesty with the description (Lord of the worlds) carries the sense of causation for the exaltation above the affairs of created things, because He is Lord of the worlds, so His affair does not resemble their affairs.

The pronoun in (innahū, "indeed it") is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), and the clause (anā Allāh al-'Azīz al-Ḥakīm, "It is I, Allah, the Mighty, the Wise") is the predicate of the pronoun of the matter. Presenting this before what will be communicated to him of the command serves to produce steadiness of heart in Musa, so that he knows that the prophethood has been bestowed upon him, since the revelation has been cast to him, and so that he knows that he will be exposed to harm and to gathering against him. This is a metonymy for his becoming a messenger, and that Allah supports and assists him against every strong one; and so that he knows that what he witnessed of the fire, and what he received of revelation, and what he will witness of the staff turning into a snake, is not strange in the scope of the wisdom of Allah Most High. These are three metonymies, and therefore

He followed this with His saying: ﴿And throw down your staff﴾. The meaning: And We said: throw down your staff.

Perhaps the intention of conveying the intensity of his turning away when he saw his staff moving is what calls for emphasizing the verb (wallā) with His saying: ﴿retreating and did not return﴾, so reflect.

His saying: ﴿O Musa, do not fear﴾ is the quoted speech of a deleted verb, that is, We said to him. The prohibition against fear is used to prohibit the continuation of fear, because his fear had already occurred. The fear that occurred to Musa (peace be upon him) was the fear of awe at the staff's turning into a serpent, not the fear of sin. So the meaning: the messengers do not cower in My presence, because I protect them.

And ﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾ is a justification for the prohibition against fear and a confirmation of what his prohibition implies, namely the absence of its cause. This is a metonymy for honoring him with the rank of messengership, since it is given as the reason that the messengers do not fear in the presence of Allah Most High.

The sense of (ladayya, "in My presence") is in My presence, that is, at the time of receiving My message. The literal sense of (ladayya, "with Me") is impossible for Allah, since its literal sense is place.

Since the turning of the staff into a serpent occurred at the time of the revelation, it was following what preceded it of revelation, and this is a teaching to Musa (peace be upon him) to adopt the character of the messengers in steadiness of heart. There is no lowering of Musa's (peace be upon him) rank below the ranks of other messengers in the prohibition; rather it proceeds according to the manner of: "someone like you does not hesitate." The intended meaning is the prohibition against the fear that occurred to him from the staff turning into a serpent, and against every fear he might feel, as in His saying: ﴿Strike for them a dry path through the sea, not fearing being overtaken, nor being afraid﴾ [Ta-Ha: 77].

The exception in His saying: (﴿except one who wrongs﴾) apparently is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil). Ibn 'Atiyyah attributed this to Muqatil and Ibn Jurayj, so that ﴿one who wrongs and then substitutes good after evil﴾ is an exception from the generality of fear, the action of which falls within the scope of negation; so it includes fear in the sense of dread and the fear that is fear of punishment for sin. That is: except a messenger who wronged, that is, there issued from him an injustice, that is, a sin before his selection for messengership, that is, there proceeded from him transgression by doing what his like would not do according to the commonly known laws of humankind that are established as just, by committing what contradicts what is established among the upright as just (before the messenger is bound by a law). So he fears that Allah will take him to account for it and requite him for committing it. This is like the plot of Joseph's brothers against their brother, and Musa's transgression against the Egyptian by killing him without knowing who was in the right in that matter. So the one who wronged and then substituted good after evil, that is, turned in repentance from his act and set his condition right, Allah forgives him.

The purpose of this exception in this manner is to calm Musa's heart and to give him good news that Allah has forgiven what he had committed in excess, and that He accepted his repentance for what he said on the day of the transgression: ﴿This is from the work of Satan; indeed, he is an enemy, a clear misleader﴾ [al-Qasas: 15], ﴿He said: My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾ [al-Qasas: 16]. So this reassurance to Musa was poured into the mold of generality, generalizing the benefit.

The soundness of the structure of the speech in this meaning requires postulating a deleted statement indicated by the consequence in His saying (﴿then indeed I am Forgiving and Merciful﴾). The estimate: except one who wronged before the sending and repented of his wrong, so he feared My punishment, and so he does not fear, because I am Forgiving of him and Accepting of his repentance, because I am Forgiving and Merciful. The speech was arranged with a wondrous brevity required by the situation of hastening joy, and was woven in the manner of symbolic reminder, since the addressees know this, as if He were saying: I did not neglect your repentance on the day you transgressed and your saying: ﴿This is from the work of Satan; indeed, he is an enemy, a clear misleader﴾ [al-Qasas: 15], ﴿He said: My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾ [al-Qasas: 16], and your resolve to be upright on the day you said: ﴿My Lord, for that with which You have favored me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾ [al-Qasas: 17].

For this reason, the exception was restricted to the specific case of one who substituted good after evil, since it is inconceivable that a messenger would persist in wrongdoing.

Among the most subtle allusions is the use of the verb (ẓalama, "wronged"), to allude to Musa's saying on the day he committed the transgression: (﴿My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself﴾ [al-Naml: 44]). For this reason it became determined that the intended referent of ﴿one who wronged and then substituted good after evil﴾ is Musa himself.

Al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and al-Zamakhshari said, and the speech of al-Dahhak also went in this direction: the exception is disconnected (munqati'), and the exception particle carries the sense of (istidrak, "a corrective contrast"). So the speech is a digression to draw attention to the fact that whoever among the people wronged and substituted good after evil is forgiven. On this view, (man, "whoever") applies to any individual who wronged, and the intent is not the transgressions of some messengers. This interpretation was prompted by the fact that messengership is incompatible with having previously wronged oneself. What led them to this is that it is a requirement of a connected exception that the negation of the excepted ruling be affirmed, namely that he is forgiven, so there is no disagreement about this. And it is understood from it that if he wronged and did not substitute good after evil, he fears the punishment of the Hereafter.

As for al-Zamakhshari, he went beyond what al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj took, and made the referent of (man zalama, "whoever wronged") a messenger who wronged. What prompted him to consider the exception disconnected is one of the two considerations that prompted al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, namely that the ruling affirmed for the excepted party is not the contradiction of the ruling of the party from which it is excepted; therefore he made the referent of (man zalama) a messenger among the messengers who wronged by the minor sins that proceeded from him, so as to include Musa, who is one of them.

It has become established from the two possibilities concerning the meaning of the exception that the messengers in the presence of Allah (that is, at the time

...the performance of the duties of the message). He does not fear anything among created beings, because Allah, exalted is He, has guaranteed their safety. Nor do they fear sins, because Allah has guaranteed them protection from sin (ʿiṣmah). Nor do they fear punishment for sins, because they do not come near them. As for others, if one wrongs himself and then replaces bad with good after evil, he is safe from what he fears of the punishment for sins, because he has made up for his wrong by repentance (tawbah). If one wrongs himself and does not repent, he fears the punishment for the sin. If he does not wrong himself, then there is no fear for him. These are the meanings indicated by the exception (istithnāʾ, the exception clause) in both of its possibilities, and this is brevity (ījāz).

In the Tafsir of Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, it is reported that Abū Jaʿfar recited (ألا مَن ظَلَمَ) with a fatḥah on the hamzah of (ألا) and a light lām, so that it is the particle of alerting (ḥarf tanbīh). The attribution of this reading to Abū Jaʿfar is not known in the books of the science of Qur'anic readings (ʿilm al-qirāʾāt) that we have seen. Perhaps it is a weak narration from Abū Jaʿfar.

The verb (بَدَّلَ) requires two things: something taken and something given. The verb takes the two objects at times directly, as in His saying in Sūrat al-Furqān: ﴿Those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds﴾ [al-Furqān: 70]. At other times it takes the object taken directly and the object given with the preposition bāʾ, by implicit meaning (tadmīn) of the sense of ʿāwaḍa (to exchange), as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not substitute the bad with the good﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 2], that is, do not take the bad of wealth and waste its good. When both objects are mentioned in the accusative, the taken and the given are determined by context. Otherwise, the noun in the bāʾ-phrase is the thing given. If only one object is mentioned, it is the thing taken, as in the saying of Imruʾ al-Qays:

"I was given a bleeding wound after health, so how strange are favors that turned into miseries."

Likewise is His saying here: ﴿then replaces good after evil﴾, meaning he took good in place of evil. The word (baʿda, after) indicates that what it is attached to is what was established and then passed away, and something else replaced it. The same applies to what conveys the meaning of (baʿda), as in His saying: ﴿Then We substituted good in place of evil﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 95]. Here, the good state is the one taken, placed in the position of the evil state.

Since the turning of the staff into a serpent occurred at the time of the revelation, it was following what preceded it of revelation, and this is a teaching to Musa (peace be upon him) to adopt the character of the messengers in steadiness of heart. There is no lowering of Musa's (peace be upon him) rank below the ranks of other messengers in the prohibition; rather it proceeds according to the manner of: "someone like you does not hesitate." The intended meaning is the prohibition against the fear that occurred to him from the staff turning into a serpent, and against every fear he might feel, as in His saying: ﴿Strike for them a dry path through the sea, not fearing being overtaken, nor being afraid﴾ [Ta-Ha: 77].

The exception in His saying: (﴿except one who wrongs﴾) apparently is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil). Ibn 'Atiyyah attributed this to Muqatil and Ibn Jurayj, so that ﴿one who wrongs and then substitutes good after evil﴾ is an exception from the generality of fear, the action of which falls within the scope of negation; so it includes fear in the sense of dread and the fear that is fear of punishment for sin. That is: except a messenger who wronged, that is, there issued from him an injustice, that is, a sin before his selection for messengership, that is, there proceeded from him transgression by doing what his like would not do according to the commonly known laws of humankind that are established as just, by committing what contradicts what is established among the upright as just (before the messenger is bound by a law). So he fears that Allah will take him to account for it and requite him for committing it. This is like the plot of Joseph's brothers against their brother, and Musa's transgression against the Egyptian by killing him without knowing who was in the right in that matter. So the one who wronged and then substituted good after evil, that is, turned in repentance from his act and set his condition right, Allah forgives him.

The purpose of this exception in this manner is to calm Musa's heart and to give him good news that Allah has forgiven what he had committed in excess, and that He accepted his repentance for what he said on the day of the transgression: ﴿This is from the work of Satan; indeed, he is an enemy, a clear misleader﴾ [al-Qasas: 15], ﴿He said: My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾ [al-Qasas: 16]. So this reassurance to Musa was poured into the mold of generality, generalizing the benefit.

The soundness of the structure of the speech in this meaning requires postulating a deleted statement indicated by the consequence in His saying (﴿then indeed I am Forgiving and Merciful﴾). The estimate: except one who wronged before the sending and repented of his wrong, so he feared My punishment, and so he does not fear, because I am Forgiving of him and Accepting of his repentance, because I am Forgiving and Merciful. The speech was arranged with a wondrous brevity required by the situation of hastening joy, and was woven in the manner of symbolic reminder, since the addressees know this, as if He were saying: I did not neglect your repentance on the day you transgressed and your saying: ﴿This is from the work of Satan; indeed, he is an enemy, a clear misleader﴾ [al-Qasas: 15], ﴿He said: My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾ [al-Qasas: 16], and your resolve to be upright on the day you said: ﴿My Lord, for that with which You have favored me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾ [al-Qasas: 17].

For this reason, the exception was restricted to the specific case of one who substituted good after evil, since it is inconceivable that a messenger would persist in wrongdoing.

Among the most subtle allusions is the use of the verb (ẓalama, "wronged"), to allude to Musa's saying on the day he committed the transgression: (﴿My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself﴾ [al-Naml: 44]). For this reason it became determined that the intended referent of ﴿one who wronged and then substituted good after evil﴾ is Musa himself.

Al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and al-Zamakhshari said, and the speech of al-Dahhak also went in this direction: the exception is disconnected (munqati'), and the exception particle carries the sense of (istidrak, "a corrective contrast"). So the speech is a digression to draw attention to the fact that whoever among the people wronged and substituted good after evil is forgiven. On this view, (man, "whoever") applies to any individual who wronged, and the intent is not the transgressions of some messengers. This interpretation was prompted by the fact that messengership is incompatible with having previously wronged oneself. What led them to this is that it is a requirement of a connected exception that the negation of the excepted ruling be affirmed, namely that he is forgiven, so there is no disagreement about this. And it is understood from it that if he wronged and did not substitute good after evil, he fears the punishment of the Hereafter.

As for al-Zamakhshari, he went beyond what al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj took, and made the referent of (man zalama, "whoever wronged") a messenger who wronged. What prompted him to consider the exception disconnected is one of the two considerations that prompted al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, namely that the ruling affirmed for the excepted party is not the contradiction of the ruling of the party from which it is excepted; therefore he made the referent of (man zalama) a messenger among the messengers who wronged by the minor sins that proceeded from him, so as to include Musa, who is one of them.

It has become established from the two possibilities concerning the meaning of the exception that the messengers in the presence of Allah (that is, at the time

Page 231

...the performance of the duties of the message). He does not fear anything among created beings, because Allah, exalted is He, has guaranteed their safety. Nor do they fear sins, because Allah has guaranteed them protection from sin (ʿiṣmah). Nor do they fear punishment for sins, because they do not come near them. As for others, if one wrongs himself and then replaces bad with good after evil, he is safe from what he fears of the punishment for sins, because he has made up for his wrong by repentance (tawbah). If one wrongs himself and does not repent, he fears the punishment for the sin. If he does not wrong himself, then there is no fear for him. These are the meanings indicated by the exception (istithnāʾ, the exception clause) in both of its possibilities, and this is brevity (ījāz).

In the Tafsir of Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, it is reported that Abū Jaʿfar recited (ألا مَن ظَلَمَ) with a fatḥah on the hamzah of (ألا) and a light lām, so that it is the particle of alerting (ḥarf tanbīh). The attribution of this reading to Abū Jaʿfar is not known in the books of the science of Qur'anic readings (ʿilm al-qirāʾāt) that we have seen. Perhaps it is a weak narration from Abū Jaʿfar.

The verb (بَدَّلَ) requires two things: something taken and something given. The verb takes the two objects at times directly, as in His saying in Sūrat al-Furqān: ﴿Those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds﴾ [al-Furqān: 70]. At other times it takes the object taken directly and the object given with the preposition bāʾ, by implicit meaning (tadmīn) of the sense of ʿāwaḍa (to exchange), as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not substitute the bad with the good﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 2], that is, do not take the bad of wealth and waste its good. When both objects are mentioned in the accusative, the taken and the given are determined by context. Otherwise, the noun in the bāʾ-phrase is the thing given. If only one object is mentioned, it is the thing taken, as in the saying of Imruʾ al-Qays:

"I was given a bleeding wound after health, so how strange are favors that turned into miseries."

Likewise is His saying here: ﴿then replaces good after evil﴾, meaning he took good in place of evil. The word (baʿda, after) indicates that what it is attached to is what was established and then passed away, and something else replaced it. The same applies to what conveys the meaning of (baʿda), as in His saying: ﴿Then We substituted good in place of evil﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 95]. Here, the good state is the one taken, placed in the position of the evil state.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 12:

﴿And put your hand into your bosom; it will come out white, without harm, among nine signs to Pharaoh and his people. Indeed, they have been a defiantly disobedient people.﴾

It is conjoined to His saying: ﴿And throw down your staff﴾ [al-Naml: 10], and what lies between them is a parenthetical digression. After showing him the sign of the staff turning into a serpent, He showed him another sign, so that his heart would be reassured by the support (ta'yid) [of God]. It has already been stated explicitly in Ta-Ha that He showed him another sign. The purpose of this is that He might hasten to him what would settle his soul concerning the support of God Almighty when he meets Pharaoh.

His saying ﴿among nine signs﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to ﴿it will come out white﴾, meaning: in a state of being one of nine signs. And ﴿to Pharaoh﴾ is a qualifier of ﴿signs﴾, meaning: signs directed to Pharaoh. In this there is an indication, by concise elision, of a omitted statement, namely God's command to Moses that he go to Pharaoh, as explained in Surat al-Shu'ara'.

The signs are: the staff, the hand, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the drought, and the splitting of the sea, which is the greatest of them. Some of them were enumerated in Surat al-A'raf. Al-Fayruzabadi gathered them in a verse that he cited under the root (tis') in the Qamus, and it is:

A staff, drought, a sea, locusts, and lice,
a hand, and blood, after the frogs, a flood.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 13–14:

﴿So when Our signs came to them, clear to see, they said, "This is plain magic."﴾ ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance. So see what was the end of the corrupters.﴾

He abbreviated the rest of the stories and moved on to the lesson in the denial of Pharaoh and his people of the signs, so that the condition of those who denied the signs of Muhammad (ﷺ) might be taken as a lesson. By this abbreviation he intended to fold up the cloth of the narrative, so as to pass from it to the story of Dawud and then the story of Sulayman, which is expanded in this surah. The meaning of the coming of the signs is their occurrence one after another, and they are the eight signs that came before the drowning.

Al-Mubsirah (the manifest, clear) means "evident." It is formed in the pattern of the active participle of sight (ibsar), by way of metonymy in the intellect (al-majaz al-'aqli), whereas what is truly "seeing" (mubsir) is the one who looks at it. It has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿And We gave Thamud the she-camel as a clear sign﴾ [al-Isra': 59] in Surat al-Isra'.

Al-juhud (jahd, denial) is denial by the tongue.

(﴿wa-istayqanatha﴾) means "were certain of them," so the preposition was dropped and the verb was made to govern the object directly, either by extension (tawassu') or by removal of the preposition (naz' al-khafid), meaning: their minds were certain of them. The sin and the ta' (in istayqanat) are for emphasis (lil-mubalaghah). Wrongdoing (zulm) lies in their denial of the Messenger, because they attached to him what was not true, so they wronged him his due right.

Al-'uluw (arrogance) is pride (al-kibr). It is appropriate that the clause ﴿wa-istayqanatha﴾ be a circumstantial clause (hal), so His saying ﴿wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ is an unfolding (nashr) in the order of the folding (laff): the wrongdoing is in their denial of them, and the arrogance is in their being certain of them.

﴿Wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the pronoun in ﴿they denied﴾ [Hud: 59]. What was known of their condition regarding the punishment that befell them was treated as something witnessed by the hearers, so He commanded them to look at it with His saying: ﴿So see what was the end of the corrupters.﴾ The address is to an unspecified audience. It is also permissible that the address be to the Prophet (ﷺ), as consolation for him regarding what befell those who denied the messengers before him, since this contains an allusion threatening the polytheists with a similar end.

The word (kayfa) may be used stripped of the meaning of interrogation, in the accusative as an object (maf'ul bihi). It may also be an interrogative that suspends the verb of looking from acting, and the interrogation in that case is for amazement (lil-ta'ajjub).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 15:

﴿And We certainly gave David and Solomon knowledge. And they said, "Praise be to God, who has favoured us above many of His believing servants."﴾

Just as the story of Moses, his being sent to Pharaoh, contained signs of admonition and an example for those who denied the message of Muhammad (ﷺ), so too in the story of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, what she witnessed of his signs and her belief in him, is an example for the knowledge of the Prophet (ﷺ), and a demonstration of the excellence of the Queen of Sheba, in that her kingdom did not prevent her from acknowledging the signs of Solomon, so she believed in him. In this there is also an example for those among the believers who were guided.

The mention of David first is so that the mention of Solomon can follow from it, since his kingdom was inherited from his father David. Also, in the mention of David there is an example of knowledge being bestowed upon one who was not seeking it. He was not among the people of knowledge of the Book in the days when there were rabbis (aḥbār) and scholars among them. David was a shepherd of his father's (Yassi's, Jesse's) flock in Bethlehem (Bayt Laḥm), and God commanded the Prophet Samuel (Shamwīl) to make David a prophet during the reign of Saul (Ṭālūt, Shā'ūl). So there is nothing strange about the prophethood of Muhammad, the unlettered (ummī, one who could not read or write) among the unlettered, so that the polytheists would know that God gave wisdom and prophethood to Muhammad (ﷺ), and he did not know this before. Rather, among his people there were those who knew this, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿You did not know it, neither you nor your people, before this﴾ [Hud: 49]. Thus this story connects to His saying: ﴿And indeed, you receive the Qur'an from One who is All-Wise, All-Knowing﴾ [al-Naml: 6].

It is permissible for the clause ﴿And We certainly gave David﴾ to be coordinated (ma'ṭūf) upon ﴿When Moses said to his family﴾ [al-Naml: 7], if we take (idh) as an object of a deleted verb "remember" (udhkur).

It is also permissible for the waw to be for resumption (li'l-isti'nāf), so the clause is resumed. The connection of the mention is evident. Moreover, in every story of the stories of the Qur'an there is knowledge, admonition and an example.

Opening the sentence with the particle of oath (lām al-qasam) and the particle of affirmation (ḥarf al-taḥqīq) is to treat the addressees as one who doubts this, because they denied the prophethood of the likes of David and Solomon when they said: ﴿We will never believe in this Qur'an or in what came before it﴾ [Saba: 31].

The indefinite form of "knowledge" ('ilman) is for magnification, because it is knowledge of prophethood and wisdom, like His saying about the companion of Moses: ﴿and We had taught him knowledge from Us﴾ [al-Kahf: 65].

In the verb "We gave" (ātaynā) there is an indication that it is knowledge bestowed from God, because bestowing (īttā') is more specific than "taught" ('allamnāhu). Therefore, the phrase "from Us" is dispensed with here.

The quoting of their words, ﴿Praise be to God, who has favoured us﴾, is a metonymy (kināya) for their being favoured with virtues other than knowledge. Do you not see His saying: ﴿above many of His believing servants﴾, among whom are the people of knowledge and others? It also points out that they were thankful for His blessing.

For this reason, their statement is linked with the conjunction waw rather than fa', because it is not praise merely for thanks for the bestowal of knowledge.

The apparent view is that the quoting of their two statements was in meaning (bi'l-ma'nā), such that each of them said: "Praise be to God who has favoured me," and when the two statements were quoted, the pronoun of the speaker was made plural. It is also possible that each of them thanked God for His gifts and the gifts of his relative, given that the use of the pronoun of the speaker together with others is common, not for the purpose of magnification but to hide the speaker himself as far as possible, out of humility, as Solomon said after this: ﴿We have been taught the speech of birds, and given of everything﴾ [al-Naml: 16].

They made their favouring above "many" of the believers, not above all the believers. Either because they meant by "believing servants" everyone who had this attribute among those who had passed, among whom were Moses and Aaron, and many who were more excellent or equal; or because they were restrained in their expression, not encompassing all who received this favour; or because they meant by "servants" the people of their own era, and so they expressed it as "many of His servants" out of humility before God.

Then, if their statement was spoken aloud, which is the apparent case, it is evidence that it is permissible for a scholar to mention his rank in knowledge for legitimate benefits, which return to warning people against being deceived by one who lacks the qualification, among those making false claims and loud, harmful boasting. This is a ruling derived from the verse, because the law of those before us is law for us. If they said it in private, this argument would not apply.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 27, verse 16:**

﴿And Sulayman inherited from Dawud﴾.

He passed over the report of Dawud's kingship and some of his circumstances up to his death, because the purpose is the story of Sulayman, as we have mentioned just before. Dawud was a king over the Children of Israel, and his kingship lasted forty years. He died at the age of seventy.

Sulayman succeeded him, so he is the heir of his kingship, which continued in his place in governing the community, in the manifestation of wisdom, in the prophethood of the Children of Israel, and in the great reputation he had among them. Thus "inheritance" here is used in its figurative meaning, namely the comparison of noble conditions to property, and the comparison of succession to the transfer of the ownership of wealth. It is evident that the purpose of the verse is not to inform us who received Dawud's wealth after the words: ﴿And We gave knowledge to Dawud and Sulayman, and they said, "Praise be to Allah, who has favoured us over many of His believing servants."﴾ [al-Naml: 15]. So it is established that the inheritance of wealth is not intended, since it is a trivial aim.

Dawud had eleven sons, so the inheritance of his property is not specific to Sulayman, and he was not the eldest. Dawud had installed Sulayman as king over Israel. By this it becomes clear that there is nothing in the verse that can be used as evidence that the property of a prophet is inherited, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "We prophets do not leave inheritance; what we leave behind is charity." Its apparent meaning is that he intended by the pronoun the body of the prophets. It has become common on the tongues of scholars to say: "We, the company of prophets, do not leave inheritance." This wording is not known, but it occurred in the speech of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab with al-'Abbas and 'Ali concerning the charity of the Prophet (ﷺ). 'Umar said: "I beseech you by Allah, do you both know that the Messenger of Allah said: 'We do not leave inheritance; what we leave behind is charity,'" meaning the Messenger of Allah himself. 'A'isha also said the same. If we take the apparent meaning of the verse, this would be a ruling in the law of earlier communities, which is abrogated (naskh) by Islam. If we take the interpretation (ta'wil), then it is clear. The Rightly Guided Caliphs (al-Khulafa' al-Rashidun) and others agreed upon this, in opposition to al-'Abbas and 'Ali, who then returned when 'Umar argued with them. The reason is the blocking of the means (sadd al-dhari'ah, the principle of closing avenues that lead to harm), namely that the thought of wishing for the death of the Prophet should not arise in the mind of some of his heirs.

* * *

﴿And he said, "O people, we have been taught the speech of birds, and we have been given of everything. Indeed, this is evident bounty."﴾

Sulayman said this statement in a great assembly, because the tone of this speech is the tone of his address to a gathering of people present, both the elite of his council and the common folk who were listening. This sentence includes the thanks of Allah the Exalted for what He granted him of knowledge and kingship, so that people might appreciate his worth, know the obligation of obeying him, since Allah had chosen him for this, and had informed him of the intentions of the most distant of animals and the furthest from familiarity with humans, which is the bird. So how much more would he know the intentions of the people among his subjects and soldiers? For drawing up the rules of kingship and its duties is among the aims for the welfare of the kingdom, through the people rallying around their king and the purity of their intentions towards him. To the extent that this is achieved on the part of the people, cooperation in goodness occurs and divine tranquillity descends. When Sulayman acknowledged this bounty to Allah the Exalted, he discharged his duty towards his community, and nothing remained except that the community should discharge its duty towards its king. Likewise, teaching the virtues of prophethood is among the aims of the Shari'ah. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I am the master of the descendants of Adam, and I say it without boasting." That is, he says it for the purpose of informing them of the duty of honouring him, not for the purpose of boasting over people, so that they may know the obligation of obeying him.

The knowledge of the speech of birds was given to Sulayman through revelation (wahy, divine inspiration), in that Allah informed him of what lies in the varied and differing modulations of the whistling or cawing of birds, indicating what is in their perception and will. The benefit of this knowledge is that Allah made it a means through which he could be guided to knowing worldly conditions, which birds perceive before others by the many faculties that He placed in them. Birds have an indication in their communication among their species, in summoning their kinds and in announcing what is around them, which helps in administering his kingdom and governing his community, such as employing the hoopoe to carry news and bring back replies, and similar things.

Beyond all this is the expansion of the breast with wisdom and knowledge of many natures and properties of existing things. The indication of the sounds of birds on what is in their minds: some of it is well known, such as the indication of some of their sounds calling males to their females, and the indication of others of the agitation of fear when a holder grasps them or a predator attacks them. Beyond that are indications that have detail. Every mode of these general indications contains hidden modulations of vocal modes, some of which differ from others, with indications of conditions that make explicit what the general conditions left implicit. These modulations are not discovered by people and are not known except by their Creator. This is close to the indication of the articulation points and qualities of letters in a language, their separation and merging, and the differences in their vowels, which convey meanings that one who knows that language weakly and has not mastered its subtleties cannot grasp, such as hearing "ḍalaltu" and "ẓaliltu" (two different verbs). So Allah the Exalted informed Sulayman by revelation of the varied vocal modulations that are in the whistling of birds, and informed him of the conditions of the souls of birds when they whistle with those modulations. People were perplexed about this, as al-Ma'arri said:

"Has that dove wept, or has it sung
upon the branch of its swaying tree?"

And our friend, the eloquent poet Shaykh 'Abd al-'Aziz al-Mas'udi, said in some verses on this theme:

"Whoever is joyful sees it as singing,
and whoever is sorrowful says it is wailing."

Limiting the statement to the speech of birds is a form of brevity (ijaz), because if he knew the speech of birds, which are the furthest of animals from relying on humans and the swiftest in fleeing from them, he would know, all the more so, the speech of what is more closely mixed with humans. This is indicated by His saying, the Exalted, later on: ﴿So he smiled, laughing at her word﴾ [al-Naml: 19]. This verse indicates that he knew the speech of every kind of animal. This knowledge the Arabs called ʿilm al-hukl, with a non-emphatic ḥāʾ vowelled with a ḍamma and a sukūn on the kāf. Al-Hajjaj, and it is said his son Ru'bah, said:

"If only I had been given the knowledge of al-hukl,
the knowledge of Sulayman, the speech of the ant,"

"or if I had been granted the lifespan of the young ox (hisl),
or the lifespan of Nuh in the age of al-Fitah (a fabled creature),"

"I would have been held captive by old age or by death."

He expressed the sounds of birds with the word "speech" (mantiq), by analogy with human speech, insofar as it is significant to Sulayman of what is in the minds of birds. The reality of speech is a sound comprising letters that indicate meanings.

The pronoun in "we have been taught" and "we have been given" refers to himself, and it is expressed in the form of the plural speaker, either for the purpose of humility, as if a group had been taught and given, and he was not alone, as was mentioned earlier in some possibilities of His saying, the Exalted, just before: ﴿And they said, "Praise be to Allah, who has favoured us over many of His believing servants."﴾ [al-Naml: 15]; or because it is appropriate for displaying the greatness of kingship, and in this there is an awe-inspiring effect on the authority of the ruler in the eyes of the subjects. This may be among the requirements of statecraft in some situations, as Mu'awiyah answered 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, when he met him with an army and pomp in the lands of al-Sham. 'Umar said to Mu'awiyah: "Is it Kisrawi-style, O Mu'awiyah?" Mu'awiyah said: "We are in lands bordering the enemy, and they only fear the like of this." 'Umar said: "A clever deception or a correct judgment; I neither order you nor forbid you." So he left the matter to Mu'awiyah's responsibility and to what he discerned of the methods of governing peoples.

What is meant by ﴿all things﴾ is all of the important things. In ﴿all things﴾ there are two generalities: the generality of "all" (kull) and the generality of the indefinite noun. Both of these here are customary generality. "Kull" is used for abundance, and "shay'" (thing) is used for important things that have a connection with Sulayman's status. It is like His saying, the Exalted, in what He related about the news of the hoopoe: ﴿and she has been given of all things﴾ [al-Naml: 23], meaning many precious things and wealth. In every context it is understood according to what suits the subject spoken of.

The emphasis in ﴿Indeed, this is evident bounty﴾ is by the particle of emphasis and its lam, which in origin is the lam of oath, and by the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl), intended to magnify the blessing, as an expression of gratitude for it with the means of expression that is within one's power.

And "﴿bounty﴾" means excess of good and benefit. And "﴿evident﴾" means apparent and clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 17:

[239]
﴿And his hosts were gathered before Solomon, of the jinn and mankind and the birds, and they were set in battle order﴾.

God granted Solomon a power from the faculties of prophethood (quwa min quwa al-nubuwwah) by which he perceives the states of spirits and immaterial beings, just as he perceives the speech of birds, the signaling of ants, and the like. He keeps those beings in order (yaza'u) by means of it, so they are subjected to him in submission (taskhir), just as some elements are subjected to others in chemistry and electricity. God granted this power to Muhammad (ﷺ) as well, so He turned toward him a group of jinn who listened to the Qur'an and addressed him. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) refrained from exercising this power and ordering it, out of honour for his brother Solomon, who asked God for a kingdom that would not be fitting for anyone after him. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not exercise it even though he was able to do so, because God had dedicated him to what is more important and more elevated, so he obtained by this a virtue like the virtue of Solomon. By his abstention from exercising it, he gave precedence to, and vindicated, the prophetic call of his brother, because the aspect of prophethood in the Messenger of God is stronger than the aspect of kingship, as he said to the man who trembled when he stood before him: "I am not a king nor a tyrant." It has also been related in a hadith: "He was given the choice between being a prophet servant or a prophet king, and he chose to be a prophet servant." Thus the rank of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is the rank of legislation, which is greater than the rank of kingship. Solomon was not a lawgiver, since he was not a messenger, so God granted him a kingdom by which he exercised governance (siyasah). These ranks overlap, some of them included within what is higher than them. So he is not a king, yet he governs the community in the manner of kings, a governance free of the ornament and pomp that kingship demands, as we have explained in the book of critique (al-Naqd) of the work of Shaykh 'Ali 'Abd al-Raziq al-Misri, which he titled Al-Islam wa Usul al-Hukm.

Al-hashr means gathering. The meaning is that his hosts were brought present in his presence, subjected to his command at the time he was [in that state].

Al-junud is the plural of jund, which is a company that has a unified task and is put at someone's disposal. The term jund came to be applied chiefly to a body of people that a king prepares for fighting the enemy and guarding the land.

[240]
His words ﴿of the jinn and mankind and the birds﴾ specify the hosts, which are of three kinds: the kind of jinn, who direct hidden powers and influence spiritual affairs; the kind of mankind, who are the hosts that execute his orders, fight the enemy and guard the realm; and the kind of birds, who complete the army by conveying news, receiving it, and carrying messages to his commanders and governors. He mentioned only the jinn and the birds because of the strangeness of their being among the hosts, and therefore he did not mention horses, though they are part of the army.

Al-wazʿ is restraining from what is not desired, so it includes both command and prohibition, meaning: they are commanded and they obey, and they are forbidden and they desist. Thus God subjected to him all of his subjects.

The fa' (so) is for sequence following the sense of "was gathered," because gathering is only intended for this purpose.

The verse also points out that gathering the hosts and training them is among the duties of kings, so that the soldiers attend to their conditions and needs, become aware of what lacks in them, and remember what they may forget when minds are disturbed in battle and at the call to mobilize.

[p. 241]

﴿Until, when they came upon the valley of the ants, an ant said: "O ants, enter your dwellings, lest Solomon and his soldiers crush you while they do not perceive."﴾ ﴿So he smiled, laughing at her words, and said: "My Lord, inspire me to be grateful for Your blessing with which You have blessed me and my parents, and to do righteous deeds that please You, and admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants."﴾

(Ḥattā) is ibtidā'iyya (an inceptive "until," introducing a new sentence), and the sense of a limit (ghāya) does not leave it. But with the inceptive sense, it is a limit that is not a termination.

(Idhā) is a temporal adverb meaning "when." It requires two verbs after it that resemble the protasis and apodosis of a conditional sentence, because (idhā) carries the meaning of a condition. (Idhā) is governed by the verb of its apodosis. As for its protasis verb, it is a clause in the genitive position after (idhā), since it is a noun modified by a clause. The implied sense is: "until an ant said, when they came upon the valley of the ants."

The "valley of the ants" may be intended as a generic reference, since ants have cracks and passages that are, relative to them, like valleys for humans who dwell in them. It may also refer to a known place famous for ants, which this idafa (construct phrase) came to designate, just as the "Valley of the Beasts" (Wādī al-Sibā') was the name of a known location between Basra and Mecca. It has been said that the "Valley of the Ants" lies in the direction of al-Ṭā'if, and it has been said otherwise. All of this is not apparent from the context of the verse.

The noun (namal) is a collective noun for small insects with six legs that live in cracks in the ground. They vary in size. The singular is (namla), with the feminine unit marker. The word (namla) denotes only one individual of this kind, without indicating masculine or feminine. So His saying "namla" (an ant) means: "one of this kind said."

The attachment of the feminine marker to the verb (qālat) follows the form of the word, because of its resemblance to the feminine ending (tā' marbūṭa). But this is only the marker of singularity. The Arabs do not say "mashā shāt" (a female goat walked) when the walker is a male of the sheep; rather they say "mashat shāt" (the female walked) and "ṭārat ḥamāma" (a dove flew). If that individual were a male, and if the sexes of that kind are distinguished in people's affairs, and they wished to show that it was male, they would say "ṭāra ḥamāma dhakar" (a male dove flew), and they would not say "ṭāra ḥamāma," because that would not make the distinction. Do you not see that it cannot serve as a sign that the agent is female? Consider the words of al-Nābigha:

"What calamity have we suffered from it: a male serpent, sharp in striking misfortunes, a hissing one of the rocks."

Here he used the name "ḥayya" (serpent), which is a generic noun joined with the feminine ending. Then he described it with the description "dhakar" (male). Then he applied the feminine to it in his words "naḍnāḍa" (sharp, vibrating), since it is an adjective of "ḥayya."

Here he described "ḥimār" (donkey), which is a generic noun, with a term specific to its female. Therefore, the attachment of the feminine marker to the verb "qālat" here is only out of regard for the wording, and no purpose depends on distinguishing the female ant from the male. Moreover, the Qur'an's purpose is not connected to such trivia; its aim is the occurrence of this event and the demonstration of Solomon's knowledge, not what lies beyond that of trivial matters.

It is mentioned in al-Kashshāf that Qatāda entered Kufa, and people gathered around him, and he said: "Ask me about whatever you wish." Abu Hanifa was present, and he was a young man. Abu Hanifa said to them: "Ask him about the ant of Solomon: was it male or female?" They asked him, and he was silenced. Abu Hanifa then said: "It was female." He was asked: "How do you know?" He said: "From the Book of Allah, His saying: ﴿A certain ant said﴾. Had it been male, He would have said 'qāla namla' (a male said)." Al-Kashshāf says: "That is because the ant, like the dove and the sheep, applies to both male and female, so they are distinguished by a sign, as in the phrases 'male dove' and 'female dove,' and 'he' and 'she.'" End of quotation. This was a secret between him and his Lord, made as an admonition for him and a call to thank his Lord, so he said: ﴿My Lord, inspire me to be grateful for Your blessing﴾.

"Awza'a" is a derivative of (wazaʿa), which means "to restrain," as mentioned just above. The hamza marks removal: he removed the restraint, meaning the restraint itself. It has been reported: "Blessings are wild; bind them with gratitude, for if they are thanked they stay, and if they are disbelieved they flee."
