Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 20–21:

Page 245
﴿And he inspected the birds and said, "Why do I not see the hoopoe? Or is he among the absent?"﴾ ﴿"I will surely punish him with severe punishment, or slaughter him, or he must bring me a clear authority."﴾

The form tafaqqada (taffa‘ala) indicates effort (takalluf), and takalluf means seeking (talab). The derivation of tafaqqada from fiqd (loss) implies that tafaqqada means "seeking the loss." However, they extended its use to mean seeking knowledge of the cause of the loss, i.e., knowing what the loss has caused in a thing. Thus tafaqqud (inspection) is searching for the loss in order to know thereby that the thing has not diminished. The birds were among the troops, because many birds are suitable for benefit in military affairs: among them is the carrier pigeon, and among them is also the hoopoe, for knowing water; and among them are the falcons and hawks, for the king's hunting and his troops, and for bringing food to the troops from game when the troops settle in deserts or the provisions run out. The birds have their own troops who attend to their affairs. Inspecting the troops is among the marks of kings and commanders, and it is among the aims of mustering and marshaling the troops. The meaning: he inspected the birds among the other things he inspected, and he said to those in charge of the birds: "Why do I not see the hoopoe?"

Among the duties of rulers is inspecting the conditions of the subjects and inspecting the officials and the like, either personally, as 'Umar did in his journey to Syria in the year seventeen AH, or by entrusting it to whomever he delegates; 'Umar appointed Muhammad ibn Maslama al-Ansari to inspect the officials.

The hoopoe (al-hudhud) is a type of bird; it utters a cooing sound, has a foul smell, has a black tuft above its head, has black talons and yellow eyelids, feeds on grains and worms, sees water from a distance, and senses it beneath the earth; when it hovers over a place it is known that there is water there, and this is the reason it was taken into Solomon's troops. Al-Jahiz said: "They claim that it was the one that guided Solomon to the places of water in the deep parts of the earth when he wished to extract something from them."

His saying: ﴿Why do I not see the hoopoe?﴾ is a question about something that occurred to him in the state of not seeing the hoopoe, so "ma" is interrogative. The lam in "li" (to me) is for specification (ikhtisas). The prepositional phrase with the lam is a predicate of the interrogative "ma." The estimate is: what is the matter that is mine?

Page 246
The clause ﴿I do not see the hoopoe﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the first-person pronoun governed by the lam, so the question concerns what happened to him in this state, i.e., about what prevents him from seeing the hoopoe. The speech is addressed to his guards. He means: is the non-seeing of the hoopoe due to my vision not encompassing it, or due to the hoopoe's concealment? The question is genuine, and it is a metaphor (kinayah) for the hoopoe's non-appearance.

"Am" is disjunctive (munqati‘ah), because it comes after the interrogative hamza by which one seeks to specify one of two things. "Am" is never free of an implied sense of interrogation after it, so here it indicates a transition (idrab al-intiqal) from one question to another. The estimate is: rather, was he among the absent?

The author of al-Miftah cited this verse as an example of using the interrogative for wonder (ta‘ajjub), and the example suffices with supposition. Since this statement of Solomon came after his scrutiny of the state of the birds, and it was his assessment that the hoopoe was absent, he said: ﴿I will surely punish him with severe punishment, or slaughter him﴾, because his absence without permission is disobedience that calls for his punishment. That is entrusted to Solomon's judgment regarding the measure he sees as corrective if his reform is hoped for, or as execution if it is not, lest he infect others with corruption so that corruption enters the troops, and his punishment serves as a deterrent to others. Thus Solomon resolved that he would inflict a penalty upon him in recompense for his not being present among the troops. From this is derived the permissibility of punishing a soldier who opposes what has been assigned to him of work or is absent from it.

As for punishing animals, it is only when they exceed their customary conditions. Al-Qarafi said in Tanqih al-Fusul at the end of his chapters: The Shaykh 'Izz al-Din ibn 'Abd al-Salam was asked about killing a harmful cat, whether it is permissible, and he wrote, while I was present: "If its harm departs from the habit of cats and this recurs from it, it is killed." Al-Qarafi said: By the first condition he excluded what is in the nature of the cat, eating meat when left alone; if it eats it, it is not killed because that is its nature, and by the second condition he excluded the case where this occurs from it only rarely, for that does not require its killing. Al-Qarafi said: Abu Hanifa said: If a cat harms and one intends to kill it, it is not tormented or strangled, but slaughtered with a sharp blade, based on his saying ﷺ: "Indeed God has prescribed excellence (ihsan) in all things; so when you kill, kill well."

Page 247
Shaykh Ibn Abi Zayd said in al-Risalah: "There is no harm, God willing, in killing ants when they harm and it is not possible to leave them." So Solomon's saying: ﴿I will surely punish him with severe punishment﴾ is an abrogated law (shari‘ah mansukhah).

As for light chastisement of animals for their training and discipline, such as striking horses to teach them to travel and the like, it is permitted for the benefit of the journey; likewise racing between horses, along with what it entails of exhausting them, for the benefit of riding them in armies.

The particle "aw" indicates one of the things, so his saying ﴿or he must bring me a clear authority﴾ makes it the third of the matters he set as the recompense for his absence, namely that he bring what would avert punishment from himself, an acceptable excuse for his absence.

Sultan means proof (hujjah), and mubin means one who manifests the truth and argues by it. This addition from the Prophet Solomon is a thorough demand from the hoopoe on his own behalf, because the absent one's proof is with him.

He emphasized his resolve to punish him by emphasizing the two clauses ﴿I will surely punish him﴾ and ﴿I will surely slaughter him﴾ with the emphatic lam called the lam of oath, and with the energetic nun, so that the troops would know this; so that if the hoopoe was lost and did not return, this emphasis would serve as a deterrent to the rest of the troops from committing the same act and thus incurring punishment.

As for the emphasis of the clause ﴿or he must bring me a clear authority﴾, it serves to establish that there is no escape for him from punishment except by bringing a proof that justifies his absence; because the context of that clause indicates that its content is the counterpart of the punishment. Since the punishment was emphatic and certain, the exit from it was also required to be emphasized; so that nothing would free him from it except the certain bringing of an evident proof, lest leniency be suspected in presenting the proof. Thus the emphasis of the counterpart is like the emphasis of its counterpart. From this it becomes clear that the first "aw" is for choice (takhyir) and the second "aw" is for division (taqsim). It has been said: the emphasis on the clause "la-ya'tiyanni" was introduced in conformity with the two clauses before it and for predominance (taghlib). Some researchers preferred this, but it is not from verification (tahqiq).

In the mushafs it is written ﴿la adhbahannahu﴾ with a lam, then an alif, followed by an alif, so that it might be taken to mean negation of slaughter; but it is not a negation, because the occurrence of the energetic nun after it indicates that it is an affirmation, since a negated verb is not emphasized with the energetic nun except rarely in their speech; and because the context of the speech and its meaning guard against the possibility of negation; and because the Muslims' reliance in the wording of the Qur'an is on memorization, not on writing, for the mushafs were not written until the Qur'an had been recited for more than twenty years. Things in the orthography of the mushaf may differ from what the later scribes established, because the script in the early period of Islam was not fully vocalized, and the Arabs relied on their memories.

Ibn Kathir read ﴿la-ya'tiyanniya﴾ with two nuns: the first doubled, which is the energetic nun, and the second, the nun of protection (nun al-wiqayah). The rest read with a single doubled nun, dropping the nun of protection because the nuns converge.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verses 22–23 (part 1 of 2):

﴿But he stayed not long, and said: "I have encompassed [knowledge of] what you have not encompassed, and I have come to you from Sheba with certain news. Indeed, I found a woman ruling over them, and she has been given of everything, and she has a great throne. I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah."﴾ [An-Naml: 22–24].

The fa' (ف) indicates the continuation of the narrative, linking one sentence to another. The pronoun in (﴿مَكَثَ﴾ [Al-Isra: 106]) refers to the hoopoe.

Al-muk (المُكْث) means remaining in a place and staying in it for some period of time. Its verb is of the pattern karama and nasara. The majority of readers recited it with the first vowel pattern (i.e., makatha), while 'Asim and Rawh from Ya'qub recited it with the second.

Al-muk is used here to mean slowness, because the hoopoe was not remaining in one place; rather, it was flying and moving about. Therefore, using al-muk to mean slowness is a majaz mursal (a figurative usage in which a more general or related meaning is used for another), since staying necessarily implies a period of time.

﴿غَيْرَ بَعِيدٍ﴾ (ghayra ba'id, "not far") is an adjective modifying an omitted noun of time or place, placed in the accusative as an adverbial complement. That is, it means "he stayed for a period that was not long," or "in a place that was not far." Both meanings imply that he returned to Solomon after a short time.

﴿غَيْرَ بَعِيدٍ﴾ denotes a nearness that is described by the opposite of distance, meaning that it is about to become distant. This is the reason for choosing this expression with ghayr, because ghayr conveys the removal of the assumption that it might be distant; such an assumption arises only when nearness resembles distance.

Distance (al-bu'd) and nearness (al-qurb) are, in their original sense, attributes of place, and they are used figuratively for a small portion of time, by likening a short period of time to a nearby place. This usage became so common that it became equivalent to the literal meaning. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the people of Lot are not far from you﴾ [Hud: 89].

The fa' in (فَقالَ) is conjunctive, coordinating with (﴿مَكَثَ﴾ [Al-Isra: 106]). The speaking was placed immediately after the staying because, when he arrived, the speech proceeded from him, so the sequence is real (ta'qib haqiqi).

If the speech attributed to the hoopoe is taken in its literal sense, which is the speech that people are capable of uttering, then this speech of the hoopoe is not part of the language of birds that Solomon had been taught, because that language is the one that indicates what is in the souls of birds of perceptions, and these are limited, as we have previously explained at the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿We have been taught the speech of birds﴾ [An-Naml: 16]. The hoopoe had no capacity to comprehend what the attributed speech contained, nor to derive the conditions of nations and lands from observing peoples and regions, such that these thoughts would occur to it and such that it would express them with its speech, which Solomon had been taught the meaning of, as we have previously stated. Therefore, this is a revelation to Solomon which Allah carried out upon the tongue of the hoopoe.

As for Solomon's saying: ﴿We will see whether you have told the truth or were among the liars﴾ [An-Naml: 27], it is possible that Solomon feared that this speech which he heard from the hoopoe was words cast by Satan on the side of the hoopoe in order to mislead Solomon and tempt him by searching for an imaginary kingdom, so as to mock him, as one mocks someone who yawns. So Solomon determined to verify the news through an investigation that leaves no doubt about its truth, as a humiliation of Satan.

Now let us turn to what this statement contains. Its beginning with ﴿I have encompassed [knowledge of] what you have not encompassed﴾ is an alert to Solomon that among the creatures of Allah there are kingdoms and kings who approach his kingdom or surpass it in some aspects of royal conditions, which Allah made an example for him, just as He made the knowledge of Khidr an example for Moses, peace be upon him, so that he would not be deceived by the end of his affair reaching what he himself had attained. It also contains an invitation to attentiveness to what will be communicated to him with his whole being, because of the importance of this opening in the discourse. The knowledge of the conditions of kingdoms and nations is among the most important things that righteous rulers concern themselves with, so that they may be prepared for what comes to them unexpectedly from them, and so that it may be one of the motivations for increasing beneficial works for the kingdom, by emulating what is beneficial in the conditions of others, and by withdrawing from what is defective in the conditions of their own kingdom through observing the effects of the like of it in others.

[Page 250]

From the passages of the vizier Ibn al-Khatib al-Andalusi: "The news of the regions is that upon which kings spend their evenings in conversation, and with its marvelous adornments they inscribe its moons, and from it they derive the goodness of conduct and safety from calamities, so they seek help against time through experiences, and they infer the absent from the present." End of quote.

Al-ihata (الإحاطة) is containing something and placing it within the possession of the one who encompasses it. Here it is used figuratively for comprehensive knowledge of the things known, like the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And how can you be patient over that which you do not encompass in knowledge?﴾ [Al-Kahf: 68]. Thus, what is encompassed in (﴿ما لَمْ تُحِطْ بِهِ﴾ [Al-Kahf: 68]) refers to things known which Solomon's knowledge did not encompass.

Saba' (سَبَأٌ) has a hamza at its end and may be pronounced with lightening. It is the name of a man: 'Abshams ibn Yashjub ibn Ya'rub ibn Qahtan. He was given the epithet Saba' because, it is said, he was the first to take captives in his military campaigns. The hamza in it is due to his name changing from a verbal noun to a proper name. He is the progenitor of Jidhm 'Azim, one of the great branches of the Arabs. His descendants were in Yemen, then they dispersed, as will come in Surat Saba'. This name is used here for their lands, because (مِن) is the initial particle of origin, which is generally used for the starting points of places. The name Saba' came to be applied to the tribe descended from the aforementioned Saba', and they belong to the Qahtani branch known as the Musta'ribah Arabs, meaning those who did not grow up in the lands of the Arabs, but migrated from Iraq to the lands of the Arabs. The first migrant among them was Ya'rub, with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the ra', son of Qahtan (in Hebrew, Yaqtan), son of 'Abir, son of Shalikh, son of Arfakhshad (in Hebrew, Arpakhshad), son of Sam, son of Noah. This lineage agrees with what is in the Book of Genesis from Sam to Eber. From Eber, the lineage of the Qahtanis diverges from the lineage of the Hebrews. As for the genealogists of the Arabs, they assign to Eber two sons: one named Qahtan, and the other named Faligh. As for the Book of Genesis, it makes one of them named Yaqtun. There is no doubt that the one called Qahtan among the Arabs is the same, and the other is named Faliğ, with a fa' at its beginning and a jim at its end. Thus some letters of the two names changed due to the difference of the two languages.

When Ya'rub moved, he settled in the southern part of the Arab lands, Yemen, and he settled in a place where he built the city of Dhafar, with a ẓā' pronounced with emphasis and dotted, and a kasra on the ra'. It is the first city in the land of Yemen. His sons spread throughout the southern lands along the sea, which is the land of Hadramawt. Then his son Yashjub, with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the jim, built the city of Sana'a, and he named the land Yemen. Then his son 'Abshams, with the consonant shadda, whose meaning is the light of the sun, succeeded him and became the leader of his people. He was given the epithet Saba', with two fathas and a hamza at its end, and he took independent control of his people. He built the city of Ma'rib, the capital of Saba'. Al-Nabigha al-Ja'di said:

"Among the Saba' who dwell in Ma'rib, when they build beyond its torrent the dam."

The distance between Ma'rib and Sana'a is three easy stages of travel.

Then after Saba' came his son Himyar, who is called al-'Aranjah (meaning "the ancient"). It appears that he made his land Dhafar after the sons of Yashjub had moved from it to Sana'a. There is a proverb: "Whoever triumphs becomes Himyarite," meaning: whoever enters Dhafar must speak in the Himyarite language. This proverb has a story.

Thus the Yemeni or Qahtani lands were divided into three tribes: the Yemenite, the Sabaean, and the Himyarite. Each tribe had its own king, and their clans became independent in locations which they called by the name of mikhlaf (with a kasra on the mim). Each mikhlaf had a chief called qayl, and he was referred to as Dhu such-and-such, by attribution to the name of his mikhlaf, such as Dhu Ru'ayn. The king whom all the qayls follow, and who rules all of Yemen, is called Tubba', because he is followed by many princes.

Saba' alone held the kingdom around the seventeenth century before the Hijrah. Their most famous or first king was al-Hadhhad ibn Shurahbil, who is called al-Yasharrah, with a fatha on the ya', a fatha on the shin with a dot, a fatha on the ra' with a shadda, and a ḥā' without dots at its end. Then after him ruled Bilqis, daughter of Shurahbil, or Sharahil also. She was apparently not married, according to the context of the Qur'an. It is said that she was married to Shadad ibn Zar'ah, and if that is correct, perhaps his reign was not long and he died. The people of Saba' were Sabians who worshipped the sun. The rest of the account of their civilization comes in the commentary on Surat Saba'.

The word (﴿أحَطْتُ﴾) is read with a shadda on the ṭā', because it is the meeting of the ṭā' of the word with the tā' of the speaker, so this tā' was changed into a ṭā' and they were assimilated.

[Page 252]

The bā' in His saying (بِنَبَأٍ) is for accompaniment, because the news was accompanying the hoopoe at the time of its arrival. Naba' is an important report.

Between (بِسَبَأٍ) and (بِنَبَأٍ) there is a double paronomasia (jinas muzdawij, identical in sound and differing in meaning). In it there is also a jinas al-khatt, which is when the form of the two words is the same in writing, but they differ in pronunciation. From this is His saying: ﴿It is He who feeds me and gives me drink﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara: 79], ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara: 80].

Describing it as (﴿يَقِينٍ﴾) is a confirmation that what will be communicated to him is something verified, with no doubt in it, so it was described by the verbal noun for emphasis.

The clause (﴿إنِّي وجَدْتُ امْرَأةً﴾) is an explanation of (نَبَأٍ), so it was not conjoined. Introducing (إنَّ) at the beginning of this clause is for the importance of the report, since it was not customary among the Children of Israel for a woman to be a king.

The verb (﴿تَمْلِكُهُمْ﴾) here is derived from al-mulk, with a damma on the mim, and its verb is like the verb for owning things. The hadith of Heraclius is narrated ("Was there among his forefathers any malak?") with a fatha on the lam, meaning "a king." The two verbs are distinguished by their verbal nouns: the verbal noun of this one is mulk with a damma on the mim, and the other with a kasra. The plural pronoun refers to Saba'.

This woman is meant to be Bilqis, with a kasra on the bā', a sukun on the lam, and a kasra on the qaf, daughter of Sharahil. There is confusion among historians regarding her placement among the kings of Saba' and the specification of her name and her father's name. What is reliably established is that she was a contemporary of Solomon at the beginning of the seventeenth century before the Hijrah, and she was an intelligent woman. It is said that she is the one who built the Dam of Ma'rib. The capital of her kingdom was Ma'rib, a great city in Yemen, between it and Sana'a a distance of three stages of travel. Its mention will come in Surat Saba'. The indefiniteness of (امْرَأةً), which is the first object of (﴿وجَدْتُ﴾), has the status of the subject, so it is like beginning with an indefinite noun when the indefinite is intended to express wonder at its kind, as in the saying: "A cow spoke." This is because the intention is to relate a strange matter in their view, that a woman should be a queen over a people. For this reason he did not say: "I found them ruled by a woman."

Al-iti'a' (الإيتاء) is giving, and it implies that what is given is desired, and it is used for its consequence, which is attainment.

[Page 253]

The meaning of (﴿وأُوتِيَتْ مِن كُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾) is: she attained from every good thing of the affairs of kingship. The generality of "every thing" is a customary generality from two directions, which the context explains, just as the words of Solomon were explained: ﴿and we have been given of everything﴾ [An-Naml: 16]. That is: she was given of the qualities of kings, of their treasures, their numbers, their armies, the prosperity of their kingdom, its adornments, and the like of praiseworthy and good qualities.

The verb (﴿أُوتِيَتْ﴾ [Ta-Ha: 36]) is in the passive because the purpose does not depend on specifying the causes of what she attained; rather, the aim is what she attained, while the means and causes are diverse. Some of it was an inheritance from the kings who preceded her, some of it was earned by her own effort and acquisition, and some of it Allah granted her in the form of intellect and wisdom, and what her land was given of fertility and abundance of water. The Greeks used to call the kingdom of Yemen "Arabia Felix" in Arabic, al-Sa'ida, deriving it from the meaning of yumn (blessing) in Arabic. And Allah the Exalted said: (﴿There was for Sheba in their dwelling a sign: two gardens on the right and on the left. "Eat from the provision of your Lord and be grateful to Him: a good land and a forgiving Lord."﴾ [Saba': 15]). As for the soundness of their intellects, in the hadith: "The people of Yemen have come to you; they are more tender of heart. Faith is Yemeni, and wisdom is Yemeni." So the intended meaning is not specifically what Allah gave her in the origin of her creation, or the creation of her people and her land. Therefore the agent was not determined by custom. And all of it is from Allah.

He singled out her throne from among the most precious of things, since it was a wondrous throne, and Solomon had no throne like it. In the tenth chapter of the First Book of Kings there is what implies that Solomon made his wondrous chair (kursiyy) after the Queen of Sheba visited him. We will point to it when we reach His saying, ﴿Which of you will bring me her throne?﴾ [al-Naml: 38].

Al-'azim (the great) is used here in the sense of greatness of worth and preciousness, and in the sense of magnificence of form and essence. Having highlighted her status, he followed with a lowering of the state of their belief, since they were prostrating, i.e., worshipping the sun. The repetition of the verb "I found her" (wajadtuha) is for emphasis, denouncing their prostrating to the sun. This is from the degradation of the belief-based intellect, so their decline lay in the unseen side of thought, which is where the deficiency of the minds' capacity to grasp realities becomes evident, because it is a domain purely of mental work in which sensory evidence cannot be relied upon. Thus it is no wonder that the minds of many people of sound intellect go astray in it, in matters that are subject to the senses. God the Exalted said concerning the polytheists: ﴿They know an outward appearance of the worldly life, but they are heedless of the Hereafter﴾ [al-Rum: 7]; ﴿Do they not reflect within themselves? God did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth﴾ [al-Rum: 8].

At that time the Arabs of Yemen were sun-worshippers, then the Jewish religion entered among them in the era of Tubba' As'ad, one of the kings of Himyar. Because they were sun-worshippers, they were called 'Abd Shams, as mentioned previously in the name of Saba'.

This statement that was conveyed to Solomon gathered the principles of political geography: the nature of the place, the religions, the character of the state and its wealth. The concern with the news of the kingdom of Saba' arose because that matter was more important for Solomon's kingdom, since it was neighbouring his realm, separated by the Red Sea, so the affairs of this kingdom were more beneficial for his undertaking.

Al-Jumhur read (min Saba') with tanwin (ṣarf). Abu 'Amr and al-Bazzi, from Ibn Kathir, read it without tanwin (ghayr maṣrūf), on the interpretation of a land or a tribe. Qunbul, from Ibn Kathir, read it with the hamza silent (sukūn), considering the pause as a means of treating the connected speech in the manner of pause.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verses 22–23 (part 1 of 2):

﴿But he stayed not long, and said: "I have encompassed [knowledge of] what you have not encompassed, and I have come to you from Sheba with certain news. Indeed, I found a woman ruling over them, and she has been given of everything, and she has a great throne. I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah."﴾ [An-Naml: 22–24].

The fa' (ف) indicates the continuation of the narrative, linking one sentence to another. The pronoun in (﴿مَكَثَ﴾ [Al-Isra: 106]) refers to the hoopoe.

Al-muk (المُكْث) means remaining in a place and staying in it for some period of time. Its verb is of the pattern karama and nasara. The majority of readers recited it with the first vowel pattern (i.e., makatha), while 'Asim and Rawh from Ya'qub recited it with the second.

Al-muk is used here to mean slowness, because the hoopoe was not remaining in one place; rather, it was flying and moving about. Therefore, using al-muk to mean slowness is a majaz mursal (a figurative usage in which a more general or related meaning is used for another), since staying necessarily implies a period of time.

﴿غَيْرَ بَعِيدٍ﴾ (ghayra ba'id, "not far") is an adjective modifying an omitted noun of time or place, placed in the accusative as an adverbial complement. That is, it means "he stayed for a period that was not long," or "in a place that was not far." Both meanings imply that he returned to Solomon after a short time.

﴿غَيْرَ بَعِيدٍ﴾ denotes a nearness that is described by the opposite of distance, meaning that it is about to become distant. This is the reason for choosing this expression with ghayr, because ghayr conveys the removal of the assumption that it might be distant; such an assumption arises only when nearness resembles distance.

Distance (al-bu'd) and nearness (al-qurb) are, in their original sense, attributes of place, and they are used figuratively for a small portion of time, by likening a short period of time to a nearby place. This usage became so common that it became equivalent to the literal meaning. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the people of Lot are not far from you﴾ [Hud: 89].

The fa' in (فَقالَ) is conjunctive, coordinating with (﴿مَكَثَ﴾ [Al-Isra: 106]). The speaking was placed immediately after the staying because, when he arrived, the speech proceeded from him, so the sequence is real (ta'qib haqiqi).

If the speech attributed to the hoopoe is taken in its literal sense, which is the speech that people are capable of uttering, then this speech of the hoopoe is not part of the language of birds that Solomon had been taught, because that language is the one that indicates what is in the souls of birds of perceptions, and these are limited, as we have previously explained at the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿We have been taught the speech of birds﴾ [An-Naml: 16]. The hoopoe had no capacity to comprehend what the attributed speech contained, nor to derive the conditions of nations and lands from observing peoples and regions, such that these thoughts would occur to it and such that it would express them with its speech, which Solomon had been taught the meaning of, as we have previously stated. Therefore, this is a revelation to Solomon which Allah carried out upon the tongue of the hoopoe.

As for Solomon's saying: ﴿We will see whether you have told the truth or were among the liars﴾ [An-Naml: 27], it is possible that Solomon feared that this speech which he heard from the hoopoe was words cast by Satan on the side of the hoopoe in order to mislead Solomon and tempt him by searching for an imaginary kingdom, so as to mock him, as one mocks someone who yawns. So Solomon determined to verify the news through an investigation that leaves no doubt about its truth, as a humiliation of Satan.

Now let us turn to what this statement contains. Its beginning with ﴿I have encompassed [knowledge of] what you have not encompassed﴾ is an alert to Solomon that among the creatures of Allah there are kingdoms and kings who approach his kingdom or surpass it in some aspects of royal conditions, which Allah made an example for him, just as He made the knowledge of Khidr an example for Moses, peace be upon him, so that he would not be deceived by the end of his affair reaching what he himself had attained. It also contains an invitation to attentiveness to what will be communicated to him with his whole being, because of the importance of this opening in the discourse. The knowledge of the conditions of kingdoms and nations is among the most important things that righteous rulers concern themselves with, so that they may be prepared for what comes to them unexpectedly from them, and so that it may be one of the motivations for increasing beneficial works for the kingdom, by emulating what is beneficial in the conditions of others, and by withdrawing from what is defective in the conditions of their own kingdom through observing the effects of the like of it in others.

[Page 250]

From the passages of the vizier Ibn al-Khatib al-Andalusi: "The news of the regions is that upon which kings spend their evenings in conversation, and with its marvelous adornments they inscribe its moons, and from it they derive the goodness of conduct and safety from calamities, so they seek help against time through experiences, and they infer the absent from the present." End of quote.

Al-ihata (الإحاطة) is containing something and placing it within the possession of the one who encompasses it. Here it is used figuratively for comprehensive knowledge of the things known, like the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And how can you be patient over that which you do not encompass in knowledge?﴾ [Al-Kahf: 68]. Thus, what is encompassed in (﴿ما لَمْ تُحِطْ بِهِ﴾ [Al-Kahf: 68]) refers to things known which Solomon's knowledge did not encompass.

Saba' (سَبَأٌ) has a hamza at its end and may be pronounced with lightening. It is the name of a man: 'Abshams ibn Yashjub ibn Ya'rub ibn Qahtan. He was given the epithet Saba' because, it is said, he was the first to take captives in his military campaigns. The hamza in it is due to his name changing from a verbal noun to a proper name. He is the progenitor of Jidhm 'Azim, one of the great branches of the Arabs. His descendants were in Yemen, then they dispersed, as will come in Surat Saba'. This name is used here for their lands, because (مِن) is the initial particle of origin, which is generally used for the starting points of places. The name Saba' came to be applied to the tribe descended from the aforementioned Saba', and they belong to the Qahtani branch known as the Musta'ribah Arabs, meaning those who did not grow up in the lands of the Arabs, but migrated from Iraq to the lands of the Arabs. The first migrant among them was Ya'rub, with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the ra', son of Qahtan (in Hebrew, Yaqtan), son of 'Abir, son of Shalikh, son of Arfakhshad (in Hebrew, Arpakhshad), son of Sam, son of Noah. This lineage agrees with what is in the Book of Genesis from Sam to Eber. From Eber, the lineage of the Qahtanis diverges from the lineage of the Hebrews. As for the genealogists of the Arabs, they assign to Eber two sons: one named Qahtan, and the other named Faligh. As for the Book of Genesis, it makes one of them named Yaqtun. There is no doubt that the one called Qahtan among the Arabs is the same, and the other is named Faliğ, with a fa' at its beginning and a jim at its end. Thus some letters of the two names changed due to the difference of the two languages.

When Ya'rub moved, he settled in the southern part of the Arab lands, Yemen, and he settled in a place where he built the city of Dhafar, with a ẓā' pronounced with emphasis and dotted, and a kasra on the ra'. It is the first city in the land of Yemen. His sons spread throughout the southern lands along the sea, which is the land of Hadramawt. Then his son Yashjub, with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the jim, built the city of Sana'a, and he named the land Yemen. Then his son 'Abshams, with the consonant shadda, whose meaning is the light of the sun, succeeded him and became the leader of his people. He was given the epithet Saba', with two fathas and a hamza at its end, and he took independent control of his people. He built the city of Ma'rib, the capital of Saba'. Al-Nabigha al-Ja'di said:

"Among the Saba' who dwell in Ma'rib, when they build beyond its torrent the dam."

The distance between Ma'rib and Sana'a is three easy stages of travel.

Then after Saba' came his son Himyar, who is called al-'Aranjah (meaning "the ancient"). It appears that he made his land Dhafar after the sons of Yashjub had moved from it to Sana'a. There is a proverb: "Whoever triumphs becomes Himyarite," meaning: whoever enters Dhafar must speak in the Himyarite language. This proverb has a story.

Thus the Yemeni or Qahtani lands were divided into three tribes: the Yemenite, the Sabaean, and the Himyarite. Each tribe had its own king, and their clans became independent in locations which they called by the name of mikhlaf (with a kasra on the mim). Each mikhlaf had a chief called qayl, and he was referred to as Dhu such-and-such, by attribution to the name of his mikhlaf, such as Dhu Ru'ayn. The king whom all the qayls follow, and who rules all of Yemen, is called Tubba', because he is followed by many princes.

Saba' alone held the kingdom around the seventeenth century before the Hijrah. Their most famous or first king was al-Hadhhad ibn Shurahbil, who is called al-Yasharrah, with a fatha on the ya', a fatha on the shin with a dot, a fatha on the ra' with a shadda, and a ḥā' without dots at its end. Then after him ruled Bilqis, daughter of Shurahbil, or Sharahil also. She was apparently not married, according to the context of the Qur'an. It is said that she was married to Shadad ibn Zar'ah, and if that is correct, perhaps his reign was not long and he died. The people of Saba' were Sabians who worshipped the sun. The rest of the account of their civilization comes in the commentary on Surat Saba'.

The word (﴿أحَطْتُ﴾) is read with a shadda on the ṭā', because it is the meeting of the ṭā' of the word with the tā' of the speaker, so this tā' was changed into a ṭā' and they were assimilated.

[Page 252]

The bā' in His saying (بِنَبَأٍ) is for accompaniment, because the news was accompanying the hoopoe at the time of its arrival. Naba' is an important report.

Between (بِسَبَأٍ) and (بِنَبَأٍ) there is a double paronomasia (jinas muzdawij, identical in sound and differing in meaning). In it there is also a jinas al-khatt, which is when the form of the two words is the same in writing, but they differ in pronunciation. From this is His saying: ﴿It is He who feeds me and gives me drink﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara: 79], ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara: 80].

Describing it as (﴿يَقِينٍ﴾) is a confirmation that what will be communicated to him is something verified, with no doubt in it, so it was described by the verbal noun for emphasis.

The clause (﴿إنِّي وجَدْتُ امْرَأةً﴾) is an explanation of (نَبَأٍ), so it was not conjoined. Introducing (إنَّ) at the beginning of this clause is for the importance of the report, since it was not customary among the Children of Israel for a woman to be a king.

The verb (﴿تَمْلِكُهُمْ﴾) here is derived from al-mulk, with a damma on the mim, and its verb is like the verb for owning things. The hadith of Heraclius is narrated ("Was there among his forefathers any malak?") with a fatha on the lam, meaning "a king." The two verbs are distinguished by their verbal nouns: the verbal noun of this one is mulk with a damma on the mim, and the other with a kasra. The plural pronoun refers to Saba'.

This woman is meant to be Bilqis, with a kasra on the bā', a sukun on the lam, and a kasra on the qaf, daughter of Sharahil. There is confusion among historians regarding her placement among the kings of Saba' and the specification of her name and her father's name. What is reliably established is that she was a contemporary of Solomon at the beginning of the seventeenth century before the Hijrah, and she was an intelligent woman. It is said that she is the one who built the Dam of Ma'rib. The capital of her kingdom was Ma'rib, a great city in Yemen, between it and Sana'a a distance of three stages of travel. Its mention will come in Surat Saba'. The indefiniteness of (امْرَأةً), which is the first object of (﴿وجَدْتُ﴾), has the status of the subject, so it is like beginning with an indefinite noun when the indefinite is intended to express wonder at its kind, as in the saying: "A cow spoke." This is because the intention is to relate a strange matter in their view, that a woman should be a queen over a people. For this reason he did not say: "I found them ruled by a woman."

Al-iti'a' (الإيتاء) is giving, and it implies that what is given is desired, and it is used for its consequence, which is attainment.

[Page 253]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verses 24–26:

﴿And Satan made their deeds seem good to them, and averted them from the way, so they are not guided﴾ ﴿—that they should not prostrate to Allah, who brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and the earth, and knows what you conceal and what you reveal﴾ ﴿Allah—there is no deity except Him, Lord of the Great Throne﴾.

It is possible that this is part of the speech conveyed on the tongue of the hoopoe, so the waw is for conjunction (ʿatf). The more apparent view is that it is another statement from the Qur'an, appended to the speech addressed to Sulayman, so the waw is for parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ) between the speech addressed to Sulayman and Sulayman's reply, and the intended purpose is an indirect rebuke (taʿrīḍ) of the polytheists.

As for His saying, ﴿ألّا يَسْجُدُوا﴾ [allā yasjudū], the majority (al-Jumhur) read it with a shaddah on the lām, considering it to be composed in the script of (an) and the negative (lā), written as a single word in consideration of how it is pronounced, with all the meanings intended from it. And yasjudū is a present-tense verb in the subjunctive. A preposition lām of causation (lām al-jarr) is to be understood as connected to ṣaddahum ʿan al-sabīl, meaning: he averted them so that they would not prostrate to Allah, i.e., so they prostrated to the sun.

It is also possible that the verbal noun (maṣdar) formed from ﴿ألّا يَسْجُدُوا﴾ is a substitute (badal al-baʿḍ) for aʿmālahum, with what lies between them being a parenthetical insertion.

It has also been permitted that ألّا [allā] is a single word with the meaning of هلّا [hallā], since its hāʾ is replaced by a hamzah. And parsing yasjudū as composed of the vocative particle yā, used as emphasis for alerting, and the imperative verb of prostration (asjudū), like the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

Ala yā isламī yā dāra Mayy ʿalā al-bilā
However, this does not fit the orthography of the Muṣḥaf, except that it is said it was written thus contrary to analogy. al-Kisa'i read it with a light lām, taking it as ألا [alā], the particle of opening, and it is necessary that yasjudū be composed of the vocative yā and the imperative verb, as previously mentioned, and with it what was previously mentioned. The pause in this case is on ألا.

The adornment of deeds was discussed at the beginning of the surah, at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter—We have made their deeds appear attractive to them, so they wander blindly﴾ [an-Naml: 4]. Its attribution here to Satan is literal. And "the way" (al-sabīl) is a metaphor for the religion by following which one attains deliverance from punishment and reaches the abode of reward.

Al-khabʾ is the verbal noun of khabba'a al-shay' when he concealed it. It is used here in the sense of the passive participle, i.e., "that which is hidden," in the manner of intensification in concealment, as is the case with describing by a verbal noun. The appropriateness of the description by the relative clause in His saying ﴿who brings forth the hidden﴾ to the circumstance of the hoopoe's report is evident, since it involves knowledge of a hidden matter. Bringing forth the khabʾ means making it manifest to people, i.e., giving it, that is, giving what is unknown to them of rain, bringing forth plants, and granting provisions, and this indicates the attribute of power. His saying, ﴿and knows what they conceal and what they reveal﴾ indicates the general attribute of knowledge.

The majority read (yukhfūna… wa yuʿlinūna) with the yāʾ of the third person, while al-Kisa'i and Hafs from ʿAsim read them with the tāʾ of address, which is an iltifat (shift of person).

The coming of the sentence ﴿Allah—there is no deity except Him﴾ after that is a resumptive statement (istiʾnaf) which functions as the conclusion (natījah) of the attributes applied to the Name of Majesty, and it is the intended purpose of this appendage, i.e., there is no divine share for anyone other than Allah.

His saying ﴿Lord of the Great Throne﴾ means: owner of the greatest kingdom, which encompasses the upper worlds, as has been mentioned previously. In this there is an indirect allusion that the greatness of Bilqis's kingdom and the magnificence of her throne were not worthy of deceiving her into turning away from the worship of Allah, Exalted is He, since Allah is the Lord of the greatest kingdom. So the definiteness of "the Throne" serves to indicate the meaning of perfection, and describing it as "the Great" serves to indicate perfect greatness in the embodiment of excellence.

At the end of this verse is a place of prostration of recitation, in order to act upon the implication of His saying, ﴿that they should not prostrate to Allah﴾. And whether ﴿ألّا يَسْجُدُوا﴾ is read with the shaddah on the lām or without it, the meaning according to both readings ultimately is one and the same, namely the denunciation of their prostrating to other than Allah, since Allah is the One deserving of prostration.

It is used here in the sense of the passive participle, i.e., "that which is hidden," in the manner of intensification in concealment, as is the case with describing by a verbal noun. The appropriateness of the description by the relative clause in His saying ﴿who brings forth the hidden﴾ to the circumstance of the hoopoe's report is evident, since it involves knowledge of a hidden matter. Bringing forth the khabʾ means making it manifest to people, i.e., giving it, that is, giving what is unknown to them of rain, bringing forth plants, and granting provisions, and this indicates the attribute of power. His saying, ﴿and knows what they conceal and what they reveal﴾ indicates the general attribute of knowledge.

The majority read (yukhfūna… wa yuʿlinūna) with the yāʾ of the third person, while al-Kisa'i and Hafs from ʿAsim read them with the tāʾ of address, which is an iltifat (shift of person).

His saying ﴿Lord of the Great Throne﴾ means: owner of the greatest kingdom, which encompasses the upper worlds, as has been mentioned previously. In this there is an indirect allusion that the greatness of Bilqis's kingdom and the magnificence of her throne were not worthy of deceiving her into turning away from the worship of Allah, Exalted is He, since Allah is the Lord of the greatest kingdom. So the definiteness of "the Throne" serves to indicate the meaning of perfection, and describing it as "the Great" serves to indicate perfect greatness in the embodiment of excellence.

At the end of this verse is a place of prostration of recitation, in order to act upon the implication of His saying, ﴿that they should not prostrate to Allah﴾. And whether ﴿ألّا يَسْجُدُوا﴾ is read with the shaddah on the lām or without it, the meaning according to both readings ultimately is one and the same, namely the denunciation of their prostrating to other than Allah, since Allah is the One deserving of prostration.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verses 24–26:

﴿And Satan made their deeds seem good to them, and averted them from the way, so they are not guided﴾ ﴿—that they should not prostrate to Allah, who brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and the earth, and knows what you conceal and what you reveal﴾ ﴿Allah—there is no deity except Him, Lord of the Great Throne﴾.

It is possible that this is part of the speech conveyed on the tongue of the hoopoe, so the waw is for conjunction (ʿatf). The more apparent view is that it is another statement from the Qur'an, appended to the speech addressed to Sulayman, so the waw is for parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ) between the speech addressed to Sulayman and Sulayman's reply, and the intended purpose is an indirect rebuke (taʿrīḍ) of the polytheists.

As for His saying, ﴿ألّا يَسْجُدُوا﴾ [allā yasjudū], the majority (al-Jumhur) read it with a shaddah on the lām, considering it to be composed in the script of (an) and the negative (lā), written as a single word in consideration of how it is pronounced, with all the meanings intended from it. And yasjudū is a present-tense verb in the subjunctive. A preposition lām of causation (lām al-jarr) is to be understood as connected to ṣaddahum ʿan al-sabīl, meaning: he averted them so that they would not prostrate to Allah, i.e., so they prostrated to the sun.

It is also possible that the verbal noun (maṣdar) formed from ﴿ألّا يَسْجُدُوا﴾ is a substitute (badal al-baʿḍ) for aʿmālahum, with what lies between them being a parenthetical insertion.

It has also been permitted that ألّا [allā] is a single word with the meaning of هلّا [hallā], since its hāʾ is replaced by a hamzah. And parsing yasjudū as composed of the vocative particle yā, used as emphasis for alerting, and the imperative verb of prostration (asjudū), like the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

Ala yā isламī yā dāra Mayy ʿalā al-bilā
However, this does not fit the orthography of the Muṣḥaf, except that it is said it was written thus contrary to analogy. al-Kisa'i read it with a light lām, taking it as ألا [alā], the particle of opening, and it is necessary that yasjudū be composed of the vocative yā and the imperative verb, as previously mentioned, and with it what was previously mentioned. The pause in this case is on ألا.

The adornment of deeds was discussed at the beginning of the surah, at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter—We have made their deeds appear attractive to them, so they wander blindly﴾ [an-Naml: 4]. Its attribution here to Satan is literal. And "the way" (al-sabīl) is a metaphor for the religion by following which one attains deliverance from punishment and reaches the abode of reward.

He said, "We will see whether you have told the truth or were among the liars."

We have already explained, at His saying ﴿So he said, "I have encompassed [knowledge of] what you have not encompassed"﴾ [an-Naml: 22], the reason for Sulayman's seeking to verify the truth of the hoopoe's report. Here, "al-nazar" (consideration, reflection of the intellect) is the rational examination, namely contemplation. Moreover, the insertion of "kunta" (you were) is more forceful in attributing him to lying than the form "aṣadaqta" (have you told the truth), because the verb "kunta min al-kadhibin" (you were among the liars) indicates firm establishment in the description, that he is characterized by it. The phrase "min al-kadhibin" (among the liars) is stronger in attributing lying to him, by entering him into the category of liars, such that lying becomes his habit. In this there is an indication of clarifying the accusation of lying against him so that he may be freed from punishment, and an indication of rebuke, threat, and instilling fear in him, since his lying is weightier in the eyes of the king, so that the hoopoe would be inclined to let fear outweigh hope. This is more fitting for disciplining one who does such a deed, and for his eagerness to confirm his own truthfulness by delivering the letter that he sends with him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 28:

﴿Go with this letter of mine, deliver it to them, then withdraw from them and see what they return.﴾

The sentence explains the sentence ﴿We shall see whether you have told the truth or were among the liars﴾ [An-Naml: 27], because what will become clear after sending his letter to the Queen of Sheba is this: if a reply to his letter comes from the Queen, it confirms the report of the hoopoe (al-Hudhhud); and if no reply comes from her, it refutes the report of the hoopoe. God inspired Sulayman, by His wisdom, to make a channel of correspondence to connect him with the land of Yemen, in order to bring the kingdom within the sphere of his authority, to benefit by bringing in its goods, and to make it a route of trade with the eastern part of his kingdom. So he wrote to the Queen of Sheba a letter, so that she would come to him and submit to his obedience and reform the religious practice of her people. He also intended that she know that God had cast into the hearts of the contemporary kings awe of his kingdom and a desire to win his favour, because God had strengthened him, even though his kingdom was smaller than the kingdoms of his neighbours, such as the kingdom of Yemen and the kingdom of Egypt. Sulayman's kingdom at that time was bounded by the Jordan, the borders of Egypt and the Mediterranean Sea (Bahr al-Rum). The exchange of letters between kings has always been part of the custom of states and part of the custom of those who call to goodness. The Prophet (ﷺ) wrote to Khosrow and Caesar. The importance of writing has grown greatly in the states of Islam. Al-Hariri said in the twenty-second Maqama: (And the writer is the gatherer of news, the keeper of secrets, his pen is the tongue of the state and the knight of its circuits...) etc.

Carrier pigeons, such as doves and the like, were used for correspondence, and the hoopoe belongs to the family of doves and is capable of being domesticated. His saying: (﴿Go with this letter of mine﴾) implies an omitted statement, namely that Sulayman thought about making contact between his kingdom and the kingdom of Sheba, so he brought a letter and entrusted it to the hoopoe.

The word (ماذا) was discussed earlier, at His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?"﴾ [An-Nahl: 24], in Surat an-Nahl. The verb (انْظُرْ, "see") is suspended from acting by the interrogative.

Al-Ilqa' (casting) is throwing to the ground. It was discussed earlier at His saying: (﴿And cast him into the depths of the well﴾) [Yusuf: 10], in Surat Yusuf. Here it is used either in its literal sense, if it is the nature of the hoopoe to reach the place and drop the letter from its beak, or in its figurative sense, if it enters the place to which it is sent and its companions take the message from its leg, to which the message is tied; in that case the casting is like His saying: ﴿So they cast the word to them, "Indeed, you are liars"﴾ [An-Nahl: 86], in Surat an-Nahl.

The meaning of ar-raj' (return) is the return of a reply to the letter, that is, acceptance or rejection. This is like His later saying: ﴿So see what you command﴾ [An-Naml: 33].

[Page 258]

﴿She said, "O chiefs, indeed there has been delivered to me a noble letter."﴾ ﴿It is from Solomon, and it reads: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate."﴾ ﴿"Do not exalt yourselves against me, and come to me in submission."﴾

Many reports have been omitted, and what lies between the two mentioned reports indicates them, since a sequence of events is implied. The implied sense is: the hoopoe went to Sheba, threw the letter down, and the letter reached the queen while she was in her council seat. She read it and said: ﴿O chiefs﴾, and so on.

The clause "she said" (qalat) is a resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani), because the strangeness of the story of the letter being thrown to her raises the question of what she did when the letter reached her.

Al-mala' means the group of the noble men of the people, who are the people of her council. The apparent meaning of her words ("it has been delivered to me") is that the letter was handed to her without the presence of her council. This was mentioned more than once before: it was the protocol of her court that letters be delivered to her directly.

Al-ilqa' (delivery) was discussed just above.

Describing the letter as "noble" refers to its excellence in its kind, as was explained earlier at the words of the Exalted: ﴿For them is forgiveness and a noble provision﴾ [al-Anfal: 74], in Surat al-Anfal. That is, the sheet was of fine quality, its layout was fine, its form was pleasing, and it had all the elegance that such letters customarily had. Among this is that it was sealed. It has been said: "The nobility of a letter is its seal," so that what is inside it is restricted to the one to whom it is sent, who may reveal it to whomever he wishes and conceal it from whomever he wishes. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "Describing a letter as noble is the utmost description. Do you not see the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 77]? The people of his time describe a letter as 'weighty,' 'precious,' or 'blessed.' If it belongs to a king, they say 'honored,' and they omit 'noble' out of heedlessness, though it is the best of its qualities."

As for the meanings the letter contained, they were not praiseworthy in her view, because she said: ﴿Indeed, when kings enter a town, they ruin it and make the honored people of its folk humiliated﴾ [al-Naml: 34].

Then she related the letter to them when she said: ("﴿It is from Solomon, and it reads﴾") to the end of it. It is possible that it had been translated for her before she went out to her council of consultation. It is also possible that she knew Hebrew. It is also possible that the letter was written in the old South Arabian (Qahtani) Arabic, since the greatness of Solomon's kingdom would not be without scribes knowledgeable in the languages of the peoples neighboring his kingdom. Its being in his own language is more apparent and more suitable to the emblem of kings. The Prophet (ﷺ) wrote to kings in the Arabic language.

As for the speech mentioned in this verse, it is the translation of the letter into classical Arabic, including its subtleties and the particularities of the language in which it was composed.

His saying ﴿It is from Solomon﴾ is part of the queen's speech. She began with it in addressing the people of her council, to awaken their understanding to reflect on its meaning. This is because it is fitting for Solomon not to put anything in his letter before the name of Allah the Exalted, and the knowledge of Solomon's name is taken from his seal, which was outside the letter. For this reason she began with it as well.

The emphasis with (inna) in both places translates what is in their speech in the Sabaean language of expressions indicating their concern with the sender of the letter and with what the letter contained, a concern that in classical Arabic would be conveyed by the emphatic particle that indicates concern in a situation where there is no doubt.

The repetition of the particle (inna) after the conjunction waw is a hint that the conjoined and the conjoined-to differ: the conjoined-to refers to the letter itself, and the conjoined refers to its meaning and what it contained, as you say: "Indeed, so-and-so has a handsome appearance, and indeed he is pure." This is one of the particularities of repeating the governing word after the conjunction, with the conjunction standing in for the governing word. Its parallel is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those of you in authority﴾ [al-Nisa': 59], where "obey" is repeated because the meanings of the two obediences differ: obedience to Allah refers to religious acts, while obedience to the Messenger is meant as obedience in worldly affairs. For this reason, "those in authority among the community" are conjoined to "the Messenger."

His saying ﴿It is from Solomon﴾ is a quotation of her speech. She knew that from the heading of the letter at its top, or from its outward appearance, according to the practice of royal letters in that era among the Children of Israel, like the opening of the letters of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to kings with the phrase "From Muhammad, Messenger of Allah."

[Page 260]

The opening of the letter with the basmala phrase indicates that its equivalent was specific to the letters of the Prophet Solomon. It is required to follow the name of Allah with the two attributes "the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate." This became a custom for opening matters of importance in Islam, which Allah preserved for the Muslims from the remnants of the practice of the prophets after it had been forgotten. It is not known that the Children of Israel opened their books with "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate."

Abu Dawud narrated in the book al-Marasil: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to write '(In your name, O Allah)' as the Quraysh used to write. When this verse was revealed, he began writing '(In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate)'." That is, he began writing the basmala at the start of his letters. As for making it a separator between surahs or a verse of every surah, that is a separate question.

Solomon's letter was brief, because that is more suitable for addressing someone who does not understand the language of the one addressing him. It restricts itself to the intended purpose so that it can be translated and understood. Thus his letter encompassed the intended purpose, which is warning the queen of Sheba against trying to rise above submission to Solomon and obedience to him, as was the custom of the kings neighboring him in Egypt, Tyre, and Iraq.

Thus the coming commanded in His saying ﴿and come to me in submission﴾ is a figurative coming, like the saying: "Follow my path."

"Muslimin" (in submission) is derived from aslama, meaning to take on Islam. The use of the name Islam for the religion indicates that Solomon only called the queen of Sheba and her people to renounce polytheism and to acknowledge Allah's divinity and oneness. He did not call them to follow the law of the Torah, because they were not addressed by it. As for calling them to single out Allah for worship and to acknowledge His oneness in divinity, this is something Allah addressed to all of mankind, and it was widespread among them from the time of Adam, Noah, and Abraham. We have explained this at the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ [al-Baqarah: 132], in Surat al-Baqarah. The Exalted said: ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, not to worship Satan?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 60]. Solomon combined calling her to peace with him and obedience to him, which is an action in the manner of kingship, with calling her people to follow the religion of monotheism, which is an action in the manner of prophethood. This is because the prophet offers guidance to righteousness wherever he is able, as Shu'ayb said: ﴿I only intend reform as much as I am able﴾ [Hud: 88]. This is similar to the saying of Joseph to his two companions in prison: ﴿Are separate lords better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?﴾ [Yusuf: 39], and so on. Even if he was not sent to them, the prophets are commanded in a general way to guide to the truth, and so is Solomon's call here. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "That Allah guides a man through you is better for you than red camels." This is the custom of the laws, because the important goal for them is the reform of souls, not vengeance or love of domination.

The particle (an) in His saying ﴿that you do not exalt yourselves against me﴾ is obscure in its position, because the apparent meaning is that it is among what Solomon's letter contained, since it comes after the basmala, which is the beginning of the letter. This particle can be either (an) the verbal-noun particle that governs the present tense, or the lightened form of the heavy (inna), or the explanatory (an).

As for the meaning of (an) as the verbal-noun particle governing the present tense, it is not clear, because it requires a governing word whose verbal noun formed with it would be governed by it, and there is nothing in the sentence suitable for that, either as a word in absolute terms or in meaning, except by strained interpretation. Ibn Hisham allowed this in Mughni al-Labib in the discussion of (alla), which is a particle of urging, and this was the view of our teacher Muhammad al-Najjar, may Allah have mercy on him: that ﴿that you do not exalt yourselves﴾, and so on, is a predicate of the pronoun in "a letter" in His saying "and it is," so that since the content of the letter is the prohibition of exalting oneself, ﴿that you do not exalt yourselves﴾ is made the letter itself, as the predicate is sometimes given with a verbal noun. This is far-fetched, because it requires separating the parts of the letter with the saying ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾.

As for the meaning of the lightened form of the heavy (inna), it is similarly so, because a verbal noun must substitute for it, and it must be governed by a governing word, and there is nothing in the sentence suitable for that either. A third possibility has also been mentioned for the verse in some copies of Mughni al-Labib in the discussion of (alla), but it is not found in the correct copies of the Mughni or its commentaries, and perhaps it is an addition by some students. Al-Kashshaf limited itself to the explanatory (an), knowing that other than that should not be assumed. It followed this with what was narrated from a copy of Solomon's letter, to show that there is nothing in Solomon's letter corresponding to the particle (an). For this reason, (an) is specifically the explanatory (an) referring to the pronoun in "and it is" which returns to "a letter," as you have known just above. Since it returns to "a letter," it carries the meaning of its referent, and so it is among what has the meaning of speech without its letters, and thus it is correct for (an) to occur after it. So (an) is part of the speech of the queen of Sheba, by which she explained, along with what follows it, the content of "a letter" in her words: ﴿A noble letter has been delivered to me.﴾

And ﴿Do not exalt yourselves against me﴾ would be the first part of Solomon's letter, and it would be a quotation of Bilqis's speech. Al-Kashshaf (in its unveiling commentary, al-Kashf) states: it becomes clear that His saying ﴿It is from Solomon﴾ explains the heading of the letter, and His saying ﴿and it is: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾, and so on, explains the content of the letter. So there is no objection about how He placed ﴿It is from Solomon﴾ before ﴿and it is: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.﴾

My soul has not been at rest with these interpretations of this verse, and it occurs to me that the position of this (an) is a special usage at the opening of speech, on which the speaker relies at the beginning of his speech, and that it is the lightened form of the heavy (inna). In some of the Prophet's (ﷺ) sermons, I have seen the opening with (an) in the second sermon he delivered in Medina in the Sirah of Ibn Ishaq. al-Suhayli mentioned: "an al-hamdu" (that all praise is), vowelled with a damma as an implied pronoun of the matter and the affair. But his speech proceeded on the basis that the hamza of (inna) is kasra with a doubled nun. It appears to me that the hamza is fatha, and that it is a usage of the lightened form of the heavy (an) in the opening of important matters, and that among it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And the last of their call is: that all praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [Yunus: 10].

And ﴿Do not exalt yourselves against me﴾ is a prohibition used in the sense of threat. For this reason the queen of Sheba followed it with her words: ﴿O chiefs, advise me in my affair﴾ [al-Naml: 32].

When this verse was revealed, he began writing '(In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate)'." That is, he began writing the basmala at the start of his letters. As for making it a separator between surahs or a verse of every surah, that is a separate question.

Solomon's letter was brief, because that is more suitable for addressing someone who does not understand the language of the one addressing him. It restricts itself to the intended purpose so that it can be translated and understood. Thus his letter encompassed the intended purpose, which is warning the queen of Sheba against trying to rise above submission to Solomon and obedience to him, as was the custom of the kings neighboring him in Egypt, Tyre, and Iraq.

Thus the coming commanded in His saying ﴿and come to me in submission﴾ is a figurative coming, like the saying: "Follow my path."

The use of the name Islam for the religion indicates that Solomon only called the queen of Sheba and her people to renounce polytheism and to acknowledge Allah's divinity and oneness. He did not call them to follow the law of the Torah, because they were not addressed by it. As for calling them to single out Allah for worship and to acknowledge His oneness in divinity, this is something Allah addressed to all of mankind, and it was widespread among them from the time of Adam, Noah, and Abraham. We have explained this at the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ [al-Baqarah: 132], in Surat al-Baqarah. The Exalted said: ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, not to worship Satan?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 60]. Solomon combined calling her to peace with him and obedience to him, which is an action in the manner of kingship, with calling her people to follow the religion of monotheism, which is an action in the manner of prophethood. This is because the prophet offers guidance to righteousness wherever he is able, as Shu'ayb said: ﴿I only intend reform as much as I am able﴾ [Hud: 88]. This is similar to the saying of Joseph to his two companions in prison: ﴿Are separate lords better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?﴾ [Yusuf: 39], and so on. Even if he was not sent to them, the prophets are commanded in a general way to guide to the truth, and so is Solomon's call here. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "That Allah guides a man through you is better for you than red camels." This is the custom of the laws, because the important goal for them is the reform of souls, not vengeance or love of domination.

The particle (an) in His saying ﴿that you do not exalt yourselves against me﴾ is obscure in its position, because the apparent meaning is that it is among what Solomon's letter contained, since it comes after the basmala, which is the beginning of the letter. This particle can be either (an) the verbal-noun particle that governs the present tense, or the lightened form of the heavy (inna), or the explanatory (an).

As for the meaning of (an) as the verbal-noun particle governing the present tense, it is not clear, because it requires a governing word whose verbal noun formed with it would be governed by it, and there is nothing in the sentence suitable for that, either as a word in absolute terms or in meaning, except by strained interpretation. Ibn Hisham allowed this in Mughni al-Labib in the discussion of (alla), which is a particle of urging, and this was the view of our teacher Muhammad al-Najjar, may Allah have mercy on him: that ﴿that you do not exalt yourselves﴾, and so on, is a predicate of the pronoun in "a letter" in His saying "and it is," so that since the content of the letter is the prohibition of exalting oneself, ﴿that you do not exalt yourselves﴾ is made the letter itself, as the predicate is sometimes given with a verbal noun. This is far-fetched, because it requires separating the parts of the letter with the saying ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾.

As for the meaning of the lightened form of the heavy (inna), it is similarly so, because a verbal noun must substitute for it, and it must be governed by a governing word, and there is nothing in the sentence suitable for that either. A third possibility has also been mentioned for the verse in some copies of Mughni al-Labib in the discussion of (alla), but it is not found in the correct copies of the Mughni or its commentaries, and perhaps it is an addition by some students. Al-Kashshaf limited itself to the explanatory (an), knowing that other than that should not be assumed. It followed this with what was narrated from a copy of Solomon's letter, to show that there is nothing in Solomon's letter corresponding to the particle (an). For this reason, (an) is specifically the explanatory (an) referring to the pronoun in "and it is" which returns to "a letter," as you have known just above. Since it returns to "a letter," it carries the meaning of its referent, and so it is among what has the meaning of speech without its letters, and thus it is correct for (an) to occur after it. So (an) is part of the speech of the queen of Sheba, by which she explained, along with what follows it, the content of "a letter" in her words: ﴿A noble letter has been delivered to me.﴾

And ﴿Do not exalt yourselves against me﴾ would be the first part of Solomon's letter, and it would be a quotation of Bilqis's speech. Al-Kashshaf (in its unveiling commentary, al-Kashf) states: it becomes clear that His saying ﴿It is from Solomon﴾ explains the heading of the letter, and His saying ﴿and it is: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾, and so on, explains the content of the letter. So there is no objection about how He placed ﴿It is from Solomon﴾ before ﴿and it is: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.﴾

My soul has not been at rest with these interpretations of this verse, and it occurs to me that the position of this (an) is a special usage at the opening of speech, on which the speaker relies at the beginning of his speech, and that it is the lightened form of the heavy (inna). In some of the Prophet's (ﷺ) sermons, I have seen the opening with (an) in the second sermon he delivered in Medina in the Sirah of Ibn Ishaq. al-Suhayli mentioned: "an al-hamdu" (that all praise is), vowelled with a damma as an implied pronoun of the matter and the affair. But his speech proceeded on the basis that the hamza of (inna) is kasra with a doubled nun. It appears to me that the hamza is fatha, and that it is a usage of the lightened form of the heavy (an) in the opening of important matters, and that among it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And the last of their call is: that all praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [Yunus: 10].

And ﴿Do not exalt yourselves against me﴾ is a prohibition used in the sense of threat. For this reason the queen of Sheba followed it with her words: ﴿O chiefs, advise me in my affair﴾ [al-Naml: 32].

[Page 258]

﴿She said, "O chiefs, indeed there has been delivered to me a noble letter."﴾ ﴿It is from Solomon, and it reads: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate."﴾ ﴿"Do not exalt yourselves against me, and come to me in submission."﴾

Many reports have been omitted, and what lies between the two mentioned reports indicates them, since a sequence of events is implied. The implied sense is: the hoopoe went to Sheba, threw the letter down, and the letter reached the queen while she was in her council seat. She read it and said: ﴿O chiefs﴾, and so on.

The clause "she said" (qalat) is a resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani), because the strangeness of the story of the letter being thrown to her raises the question of what she did when the letter reached her.

Al-mala' means the group of the noble men of the people, who are the people of her council. The apparent meaning of her words ("it has been delivered to me") is that the letter was handed to her without the presence of her council. This was mentioned more than once before: it was the protocol of her court that letters be delivered to her directly.

Al-ilqa' (delivery) was discussed just above.

Describing the letter as "noble" refers to its excellence in its kind, as was explained earlier at the words of the Exalted: ﴿For them is forgiveness and a noble provision﴾ [al-Anfal: 74], in Surat al-Anfal. That is, the sheet was of fine quality, its layout was fine, its form was pleasing, and it had all the elegance that such letters customarily had. Among this is that it was sealed. It has been said: "The nobility of a letter is its seal," so that what is inside it is restricted to the one to whom it is sent, who may reveal it to whomever he wishes and conceal it from whomever he wishes. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "Describing a letter as noble is the utmost description. Do you not see the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 77]? The people of his time describe a letter as 'weighty,' 'precious,' or 'blessed.' If it belongs to a king, they say 'honored,' and they omit 'noble' out of heedlessness, though it is the best of its qualities."

As for the meanings the letter contained, they were not praiseworthy in her view, because she said: ﴿Indeed, when kings enter a town, they ruin it and make the honored people of its folk humiliated﴾ [al-Naml: 34].

Then she related the letter to them when she said: ("﴿It is from Solomon, and it reads﴾") to the end of it. It is possible that it had been translated for her before she went out to her council of consultation. It is also possible that she knew Hebrew. It is also possible that the letter was written in the old South Arabian (Qahtani) Arabic, since the greatness of Solomon's kingdom would not be without scribes knowledgeable in the languages of the peoples neighboring his kingdom. Its being in his own language is more apparent and more suitable to the emblem of kings. The Prophet (ﷺ) wrote to kings in the Arabic language.

As for the speech mentioned in this verse, it is the translation of the letter into classical Arabic, including its subtleties and the particularities of the language in which it was composed.

His saying ﴿It is from Solomon﴾ is part of the queen's speech. She began with it in addressing the people of her council, to awaken their understanding to reflect on its meaning. This is because it is fitting for Solomon not to put anything in his letter before the name of Allah the Exalted, and the knowledge of Solomon's name is taken from his seal, which was outside the letter. For this reason she began with it as well.

The emphasis with (inna) in both places translates what is in their speech in the Sabaean language of expressions indicating their concern with the sender of the letter and with what the letter contained, a concern that in classical Arabic would be conveyed by the emphatic particle that indicates concern in a situation where there is no doubt.

The repetition of the particle (inna) after the conjunction waw is a hint that the conjoined and the conjoined-to differ: the conjoined-to refers to the letter itself, and the conjoined refers to its meaning and what it contained, as you say: "Indeed, so-and-so has a handsome appearance, and indeed he is pure." This is one of the particularities of repeating the governing word after the conjunction, with the conjunction standing in for the governing word. Its parallel is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those of you in authority﴾ [al-Nisa': 59], where "obey" is repeated because the meanings of the two obediences differ: obedience to Allah refers to religious acts, while obedience to the Messenger is meant as obedience in worldly affairs. For this reason, "those in authority among the community" are conjoined to "the Messenger."

His saying ﴿It is from Solomon﴾ is a quotation of her speech. She knew that from the heading of the letter at its top, or from its outward appearance, according to the practice of royal letters in that era among the Children of Israel, like the opening of the letters of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to kings with the phrase "From Muhammad, Messenger of Allah."
