Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 32:

﴿She said: "O chiefs, advise me in my affair. I would not decide on any matter until you are present with me."﴾

She asked them to state their opinions about what she should do regarding the call of Sulayman. The sentence is a resumptive sentence of the explanatory kind (al-isti'naf al-bayani), like the one before it.

Al-ifta' (giving a fatwa, i.e., giving a ruling) is informing someone of a fatwa (fatwa: a legal or practical resolution of a difficulty that arises). The term was discussed earlier at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The matter about which you two inquire has been decided﴾ [Yusuf: 41], in Surah Yusuf.

Al-amr (the matter) is the important state of affairs. It is attributed to her pronoun because she is the one addressed by the letter of Sulayman, and because she is the one charged with carrying out what must be done in the affairs of the kingdom, and upon her falls the responsibility for error in the policy she follows, which is why the ruler, the caliph, the commander, and the scholar of religion are all called wali al-amr (holder of authority). By these three meanings was interpreted His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those of authority among you﴾ [al-Nisa': 59]. The poet al-Ra'i addressed 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, saying:

"O holder of Allah's authority, we are a people of monotheists (hunafa'), who prostrate morning and evening."

This is the meaning of their words to her: (﴿And the matter is up to you﴾ [al-Naml: 33]).

The attribution of (amri) has made it definite, i.e., in this specific incident.

The meaning of (﴿qati'a amran﴾) is: acting with a deed free of hesitation, by resolving upon what you will answer Sulayman with.

The form (﴿kuntu qati'a﴾) indicates that this was her habit and custom with them. She was thus wise and judicious, one who consulted, not one who risked acting arbitrarily with the interests of her people, nor one who exposed her kingdom to the abysses of the errors of despots.

The word amr in (﴿ma kuntu qati'a amran﴾) is likewise the important matter; that is, she does not decide on important matters except after consulting them.

(Tashhadunni) is the present tense of shahida, used in the sense of "to be present," as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever of you is present in the month﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], i.e., until you are present with me. Shahida transitively governs directly whatever the subject is present at, of place, time, or a concrete entity, and this is an extended usage because of its frequency; the proper usage of the verb would be to govern it with a preposition or to make a adverbial complement depend on it. One says: shahida 'inda fulan, and shahida majlis fulan, and one says: shahida al-Jumu'ah. The verb (tashhadunni) here is used as a metonymy for consultation, because consultation generally requires presence, since no consultation takes place with an absent person.

The nun in (tashhadunni) is the nun of protection (nun al-wiqayah). The ya' of the first person was deleted for lightness, and the kasra of the nun that was introduced to protect the final letter of the verb from being kasra was dropped, and the nun of protection indicates the deleted letter.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read it with the ya' deleted both in continuation and in pause. Ya'qub read it with the ya' affirmed both in continuation and in pause.

In her words (﴿until you are present﴾) there is a metonymy for the meaning: you agree with me in what I decide, that is, what issues from her in decisions regarding rights and policy, either by speech, as occurred in this incident, or by silence and not objecting; for the presence of those counted for consultation at the place of consultation suffices instead of consulting them, since their silence is agreement. For this reason our jurists said: when a judge sits to judge, it is incumbent upon him to judge in the presence of the people of knowledge or after consulting them. 'Uthman used to judge in the presence of the people of knowledge, and 'Umar used to consult them even if they were not present. The jurists said that their silence in their presence is an affirmation of his ruling.

This verse does not provide evidence for the legitimacy of consultation (shura), because it does not narrate a divine law, nor is it presented in the manner of praise; rather it is a narration of what took place among a people not adhering to divine revelation. However, the nature of the Qur'an in what it mentions of narratives is that it mentions the important parts of them for admonition or as an example, as we have stated in the Seventh Introduction. Therefore, the goodness of consultation may be inferred from the context of this verse. The mention of consultation has already occurred in Surah Al 'Imran.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 33:

﴿They said: "We are possessors of strength and possessors of great might, but the command is yours, so see what you will command."﴾

This is a reply in the manner of dialogue (muhawara), which is why it is detached and not joined with a conjunction, as is the way of dialogues. By their saying "We" they meant: we are the body of the kingdom, who are of the people of war. It is thus the report of the notables of the people about the condition of their group and of those to whom their affairs are entrusted. Strength (quwwa): its literal and figurative meanings were discussed earlier at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So take it with strength﴾ [al-A'raf: 145] in Surat al-A'raf. It is applied to the means of strength, as was discussed earlier at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And prepare against them what you can of strength﴾ [al-Anfal: 60] in Surat al-Anfal, that is, the means of capability for fighting and overpowering. Among strength is also the multitude of those capable of fighting and those skilled in its methods.

Might (ba's): severity against the enemy. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿and the patient in adversity and hardship and time of might﴾ [al-Baqara: 177], that is, in the places of fighting, and He said: ﴿Their might among themselves is severe﴾ [al-Hashr: 14]. This reply is an explicit statement that they are prepared for war to defend their kingdom, and an allusion that they inclined toward repelling by force, should he intend to compel them to enter under his obedience, since they understood what his letter contained as leading to this.

Page 265

Yet, while expressing this opinion, they entrusted the matter to the queen, relying on the soundness of her judgment, so that she might look at what she would command them and they would comply. So the object of (you command) and its complement were omitted, because they are evident from the context, and the estimate is: what you command us with; that is, if your opinion is other than war, then command us with it and we will obey you.

The verb (see) is suspended from operating on what follows it, namely the interrogative (what you command), which is (ماذا تَأْمُرِينَ).

The discussion of (what) has already been given at His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?"﴾ [al-Nahl: 24] in Surat al-Nahl.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 27, verses 34–35:**

﴿She said: "Indeed, when kings enter a town, they corrupt it and make the most honourable of its people the most humble. And thus do they do."﴾ ﴿"And indeed, I am going to send them a gift, and will wait to see with what the envoys return."﴾

(She said) is the answer in a dialogue, and therefore it is separated (from what precedes it without a conjunction).

She set forth her opinion, preferring the side of peace over the side of war, and she was wary, by choice, of entering under the authority of Sulayman. This is because the outcome of war carries the possibility that Sulayman would win, and then the kingdom of Saba' would pass to him. And entering under Sulayman's authority means handing the kingdom over to his disposal. In both cases a new king would take control of her city. So, by inferring from the evidence of history and from her knowledge of the natures of kings, she knew that when kings take control of another's kingdom, they tend to overturn its order so that it accords with their own interests, and so that their minds are at ease regarding any uprising of the defeated nation when weakness appears or when they are preoccupied with important events. The first thing they do is to remove those who held power, because danger is expected from them once their rule has been overthrown by the new authority. Then they change the laws and systems by which the state was governed. As for taking the city by force (ʿunwatan), the seizure inevitably involves destruction, captivity and plunder, and that is even greater corruption. Both situations are included in her words: ﴿when they enter a town, they corrupt it and make the most honourable of its people the most humble.﴾

**(Page 266)**

The opening of the clause "Indeed, the kings" with the particle of emphasis (inna) serves to draw attention to the report and to affirm it. Thus her words, "when they enter a town, they corrupt it," are an argument based on the evidence of past history. For this reason (idha) is used here as an adverb referring to the past, by the indication of context, as in the Almighty's saying: ﴿And when they see a trade or a diversion, they rush to it﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 11], and His saying: ﴿Nor (is there blame) upon those who, when they came to you to be provided with mounts, you said, "I cannot find anything to mount you upon," and they turned away﴾ [al-Tawbah: 92].

The clause ﴿And thus do they do﴾ is an argument concerning the future, drawn from the ruling of the past by way of istishab (the principle of presuming continuity). It is like the conclusion of the proof contained in her words, "Indeed, the kings, when they enter a town, corrupt it." The reference to what has been mentioned, namely corruption and the making of the honourable into the humble, means: how then could we surrender ourselves to one who will spare no effort in corrupting our condition?

So she resolved to avoid both war and surrendering by hand, by the method of conciliation and of courting Sulayman through sending him a gift. She had determined upon this, and did not seek the opinion of her counsellors, because they had delegated the opinion to her, and because their silence about what she informed them of counts as agreement and consent.

This statement is an introduction to what she will communicate to them of her resolution, and it includes a justification for what she has decided upon.

The "bi" in "bi-hadiyyatin" (with a gift) is the bi of accompaniment. The object of "mursilah" (sending) is omitted, indicated by the description "mursilah" and by the fact that the consultation concerns what Sulayman's letter contained. The implied meaning is: sending to them a letter and an envoy accompanied by a gift. For the envoy must necessarily be accompanied by a letter in which she replies to Sulayman's letter, since answering a letter is an ancient custom and is one of the practices of Muslims, and it is counted among the rights of one Muslim over another. Its plural, in the standard language, is hadaya. In the dialect of the lower Ma'add, it is different. The original form of hadaya is hidaʾiy, with a hamzah after the alif of the plural and then a yaʾ. This is because fa'ilah is pluralised as fa'ail, with the yaʾ of fa'ilah converted to a hamzah, since it is a letter that occurred in the plural after a letter of madd (prolongation). Then, when they found the damma in the nominative case heavy on the yaʾ, they made the yaʾ quiescent, in accordance with the general pattern, and then converted the quiescent yaʾ into an alif for lightness. So the hamzah came between two alifs, and it became heavy, so they converted it into a yaʾ, because it is fathah and that is lighter. As for the dialect of the lower Ma'add, they say hadawa, converting the hamzah that lies between the two alifs into a waw, because it is a sister of the yaʾ, and both are sisters of the hamzah.

And "nazirah" (waiting, watching) is the active participle from nazara meaning intazara, that is, awaiting expectantly. **Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 27, verses 34–35:**

﴿She said: "Indeed, when kings enter a town, they corrupt it and make the most honourable of its people the most humble. And thus do they do."﴾ ﴿"And indeed, I am going to send them a gift, and will wait to see with what the envoys return."﴾

(She said) is the answer in a dialogue, and therefore it is separated (from what precedes it without a conjunction).

She set forth her opinion, preferring the side of peace over the side of war, and she was wary, by choice, of entering under the authority of Sulayman. This is because the outcome of war carries the possibility that Sulayman would win, and then the kingdom of Saba' would pass to him. And entering under Sulayman's authority means handing the kingdom over to his disposal. In both cases a new king would take control of her city. So, by inferring from the evidence of history and from her knowledge of the natures of kings, she knew that when kings take control of another's kingdom, they tend to overturn its order so that it accords with their own interests, and so that their minds are at ease regarding any uprising of the defeated nation when weakness appears or when they are preoccupied with important events. The first thing they do is to remove those who held power, because danger is expected from them once their rule has been overthrown by the new authority. Then they change the laws and systems by which the state was governed. As for taking the city by force (ʿunwatan), the seizure inevitably involves destruction, captivity and plunder, and that is even greater corruption. Both situations are included in her words: ﴿when they enter a town, they corrupt it and make the most honourable of its people the most humble.﴾

The clause ﴿And thus do they do﴾ is an argument concerning the future, drawn from the ruling of the past by way of istishab (the principle of presuming continuity). It is like the conclusion of the proof contained in her words, "Indeed, the kings, when they enter a town, corrupt it." The reference to what has been mentioned, namely corruption and the making of the honourable into the humble, means: how then could we surrender ourselves to one who will spare no effort in corrupting our condition?

So she resolved to avoid both war and surrendering by hand, by the method of conciliation and of courting Sulayman through sending him a gift. She had determined upon this, and did not seek the opinion of her counsellors, because they had delegated the opinion to her, and because their silence about what she informed them of counts as agreement and consent.

This statement is an introduction to what she will communicate to them of her resolution, and it includes a justification for what she has decided upon.

That is, "when the messenger came" refers to the messenger indicated by her words: ﴿And I am sending a gift to them﴾ [al-Naml: 35]. Sending requires a messenger, and the word "messenger" (rasul) is singular in form but applies to one or to a group, as was explained earlier in the story of Musa in Surat al-Shu'ara'. Also, the gifts of kings are carried by a caravan (rakb), so the subject of "came" (ja'a) may be the familiar caravan that carries the gifts of kings of that rank.

Sulayman refused to accept the gift because the queen sent it after his letter had reached her. Perhaps she remained silent about the content of his letter, which included his words: (﴿And come to me in submission﴾ [al-Naml: 31]). Thus it became clear to him that her purpose in the gift was to turn him away from pursuing what the letter contained. The gift was therefore a bribe (rishwah) to divert him from extending his authority over the kingdom of Saba'.

The address in "Will you supply me with wealth?" (atumiddunani) is directed to the delegation carrying the gift, with the intention that they convey it to the queen, because address to messengers is ultimately aimed at the one who sent them, concerning the matter for which they were sent.

The interrogative is a rebuke (inkari), because the situation of sending a gift and remaining silent about the reply implies an attempt to turn Sulayman away from his demand by offering him wealth. This implies that they supposed him to be in need of such wealth and that he would be satisfied with what was sent to him.

It appears that the gift was gold and wealth.

The majority of readers (al-Jumhur) read "atumiddunani" with two nuns. Hamzah and Khalaf read it with a single shaddah nun, through assimilation (idgham). The fa' (fa') introduces what follows as a consequence of the preceding rebuke. That is: "I rebuke you for your assumption that I would rejoice in what you have sent me, because what God has given me is better than what He has given you." In other words, it is superior to it in the qualities of wealth, in preciousness and abundance.

The presentation of the causal clause (sawq al-ta'lil) indicates that he knew the queen did not know that Sulayman possessed wealth better than what she had. Had he believed she knew this, he would not have needed to introduce the consequence.

This is one of the secrets of the distinction, in eloquent speech, between the waw and the fa' in this sentence. Had he said, "and what God has given me is better than what He has given you," it would have implied that she knew this, because the waw would be the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal).

The particle "bal" (bal) is for the transitional turning away (al-idrab al-intiqali), which is a shift from his rebuke of them for supplying him with wealth to returning that wealth and sending it back to them.

The genitive construction "your gift" (hadiyyatikum) is a figurative (tashbih) construction. It may be an attribution of a thing to what is in the sense of the object: that is, "what you give as gifts." It is also possible that it is a construction resembling attribution to what is in the sense of the object: that is, "what is given as a gift to you." The statement is used as an allusion (kinayah) to returning the gift to the one who sent it.

The meaning of "you rejoice" (tafrahun) may be "you are gladdened," or it may be "you boast." That is, that gift is great in your estimation, not in mine, because God has given me something better than it.

The placement of the subject before the verbal predicate in "You... rejoice" (antum... tafrahun) serves to express restriction (qasr), meaning: it is you (and not I) who rejoice. This is the allusion to returning the gift.

He threatened and warned them that he would send to them an army that they could not withstand in battle. The pronouns of the masculine plural absent in his words "we will surely come to them" (fala-na'tiyannahum) and "we will surely expel them" (wa-lanukhrijannahum) refer to the people, meaning: we will surely expel whoever we expel from among the captives.

His words "﴿We will surely come to them with armies﴾" may mean that he intended to attack their land in person, in which case the ba' (ba') is for accompaniment (musahabah). It may also mean that he intended to send armies to attack them, in which case the ba' is for transitivity (ta'diyah), like the ba' in God's words, ﴿God took away their light﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], meaning: "He removed it." The meaning would then be: "we will surely bring them armies," that is, we will make them come to them.

Al-qibal means capacity (al-taqah). Its original sense is confrontation (al-muqabalah), and it was applied to capacity because one who is able to bear something stands firm to meet it and faces it. If he is not able to bear it, he retreats from meeting it. It is likely that the origin of this usage looks to confrontation in battle.

The ba' in "bi-ha" is causal (sababiyyah), meaning: they had no capacity against it because of its cause. Or the ba' may be for accompaniment, meaning: the capacity to meet it, accompanying it, was absent from them, that is, the power to confront it.

The pronoun in "bi-ha" refers to the armies, and the pronoun in "min-ha" refers to the city, which is Ma'rib. That is, he will expel them as captives and bring them to his city.

The word al-sagir (al-sagir), meaning "humbled," is an active participle from saghura, with the ghayn vowelled with damma, used in the sense of being humiliated, and its verbal noun is al-sagar. The intended meaning is the humiliation of defeat and captivity.

﴿He said: "O chiefs, which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?"﴾ ﴿A powerful one of the jinn said: "I will bring it to you before you rise from your place. And when he saw it placed beside him, he said: "This is from the bounty of my Lord, to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful. This is a fresh resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) introducing part of the story. The report of the return of the messengers and the gift has been omitted. Sulayman knew that the queen of Saba' could not but submit to him and come to him, or it reached him from her that she had resolved to come to his presence, in accordance with his saying: "(And come to me in submission)."

Then it is possible that Sulayman said this after the queen's caravans had settled in the city of Urshalim (Jerusalem) and before she had prepared to enter upon the king. Or it was when the news reached him that she was approaching the city, so he wished to bring her throne before she entered upon him, in order to show her the capability of the people of his realm.

Her throne may have been carried with her in her baggage; she brought it with her so that she might sit upon it, fearing that Sulayman would not prepare a throne for her, for kings have estimations and suspicions against which they guard, fearing humiliation.

His saying "(I will bring it to you)" may be a verb in the present tense from atā (to come), or an active participle from it; the bā' (with) in both possibilities is for transitivity. When Sulayman knew that she would be present before him, he wished to astonish her by bringing her throne, which she prides herself on and considers the rarest thing in the world. So he addressed his chiefs, that there might become apparent from them the extent of their knowledge and strength. The bā' in "(bi-'arshihā)" is like the bā' in His saying: "(﴿So We will surely bring to them hosts﴾ [An-Naml: 37])," and it admits both possibilities.

The clause "(He said: O chiefs)" is a fresh beginning, resuming a part of the story. The clause "(He said: a powerful one)" stands in the position of a response within a dialogue, so it is separated in the manner of dialogues, as has been mentioned more than once before. The clause "(﴿Said one who had knowledge from the Scripture﴾)" is also a response within a dialogue.

The meaning of 'ifrit (a powerful, formidable being), as is derived from the various statements of the lexicographers, is a name for one who is strong, who cannot be struck or reached, so he is to be feared for his evil. Originally it is a name for the stubborn among the jinn, and people are described by it figuratively, by way of comparison.

﴿Said one who had knowledge from the Scripture﴾ refers to a man from the people of wisdom, from among Sulayman's attendants.

The "min" in His saying "(min al-kitab, from the Scripture)" is for origin (ibtida'iyyah), meaning: he had knowledge acquired from books, that is, from wisdom. The intended meaning of "al-kitab" is not the Torah. The First Book of Kings, in chapter four, enumerates eleven men of Sulayman's inner circle by name, and the people of tafsir (exegesis, the explanation of the Qur'an) and of narrative (qasas) mentioned that the one "(who had knowledge from the Scripture)" is Asaf ibn Barkhiya, and that he was the minister of Sulayman.

The literal meaning of "irtidad al-tarf (the return of the glance)" is the return of the gaze of the eye from a visible object from which it turned away for an instant. It was expressed by "return" because they describe looking by "sending the glance" and "sending the gaze," so the "return" is a metaphor built upon that.

This debate between the 'ifrit of the jinn and the one who had knowledge from the Scripture signifies that through wisdom and knowledge there is accomplished what cannot be accomplished through strength alone; that wisdom is acquired, by His saying "(who had knowledge from the Scripture)"; and that the strength of the elements is a natural disposition in them, while acquisition through knowledge is a way to employ powers which cannot employ some of themselves through others. Thus this story is mentioned as an example of knowledge prevailing over strength. And since these two men were subjected to Sulayman's service, what they were singled out with of knowledge was a distinction for them which returns to the grace and honour of Sulayman, in that God subjected to him such powers. The station of his prophethood is too exalted for him to undertake the bringing of Bilqis's throne with his own person.

It is apparent that His saying "(before your glance returns to you)" and His saying "(before you rise from your place)" are two examples of speed and of the greater swiftness.

The pronoun attached in "(ra'ahu, when he saw it)" refers to the throne.

Al-istiqrar (being settled) is: being firmly established in the earth, and it is an intensive form of qarar (settledness). This is a particular settledness, different from the general settledness which is synonymous with existence. It is the settledness which is estimated in the reporting of the subject by an adverbial phrase and a prepositional phrase, so that it is connected to them when they occur as predicate or occur as a circumstantial clause, since it is estimated as "(ka'in, existing)" or "(mustaqirr, settled)." That settledness is not something whose mention is required. Ibn 'Atiyya made it, in the verse, one of the manifestations of the omitted element, which is far-fetched.

Since He mentioned the bounty attributed to God in the title of His being his Lord, this shows that His bounty upon him is great, since he is the servant of his Lord. Therefore God's kindness to him is nothing but pure bounty. When the throne was brought to him, Sulayman did not busy himself with rejoicing in his sovereignty or in the capability of his men, but turned instead to thanking God Most High for what He had granted him of bounty and bestowed upon him of hosts subjected to him by knowledge and strength. Thus the merits and virtues of all of them return to His favouring him.

He cited a moral and religious wisdom: ﴿And whoever is grateful, his gratitude is only for himself; and whoever is ungrateful, indeed my Lord is Self-Sufficient, Generous﴾. Every person who draws near to God by a righteous deed must keep in mind that his deed is only for himself, hoping through it for God's reward and pleasure in the Hereafter, and hoping for the continuance of God's favour upon him in this world. So the benefit accrues to him in both abodes, and God does not benefit from any of that.

The lam in His saying "(yashkuru li-nafsihi, gives thanks for his own self)" is the lam of purpose (lam al-ajl), and it is not the lam with which the verb of thanking is made transitive, as in "(wa-shkurū lī, and give thanks to Me)." The intended meaning of "(man kafara, whoever is ungrateful)" is whoever disbelieves God's favour upon him by worshipping other than God. For God is free of need of his gratitude, and He is Generous in His respite and His provision in this world. This was already mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your blessing﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 15].

The shift from the pronoun to the explicit noun in His saying "(﴿indeed my Lord is Self-Sufficient, Generous﴾)" instead of saying "indeed He is Self-Sufficient, Generous," is an emphasis on the acknowledgment of the purity of the bounty derived from His saying "(﴿the bounty of my Lord﴾)."

Or it was when the news reached him that she was approaching the city, so he wished to bring her throne before she entered upon him, in order to show her the capability of the people of his realm.

Her throne may have been carried with her in her baggage; she brought it with her so that she might sit upon it, fearing that Sulayman would not prepare a throne for her, for kings have estimations and suspicions against which they guard, fearing humiliation.

His saying "(I will bring it to you)" may be a verb in the present tense from atā (to come), or an active participle from it; the bā' (with) in both possibilities is for transitivity. When Sulayman knew that she would be present before him, he wished to astonish her by bringing her throne, which she prides herself on and considers the rarest thing in the world. So he addressed his chiefs, that there might become apparent from them the extent of their knowledge and strength. The bā' in "(bi-'arshihā)" is like the bā' in His saying: "(﴿So We will surely bring to them hosts﴾ [An-Naml: 37])," and it admits both possibilities.

The clause "(He said: O chiefs)" is a fresh beginning, resuming a part of the story. The clause "(He said: a powerful one)" stands in the position of a response within a dialogue, so it is separated in the manner of dialogues, as has been mentioned more than once before. The clause "(﴿Said one who had knowledge from the Scripture﴾)" is also a response within a dialogue.

The meaning of 'ifrit (a powerful, formidable being), as is derived from the various statements of the lexicographers, is a name for one who is strong, who cannot be struck or reached, so he is to be feared for his evil. Originally it is a name for the stubborn among the jinn, and people are described by it figuratively, by way of comparison.

﴿Said one who had knowledge from the Scripture﴾ refers to a man from the people of wisdom, from among Sulayman's attendants.

The "min" in His saying "(min al-kitab, from the Scripture)" is for origin (ibtida'iyyah), meaning: he had knowledge acquired from books, that is, from wisdom. The intended meaning of "al-kitab" is not the Torah. The First Book of Kings, in chapter four, enumerates eleven men of Sulayman's inner circle by name, and the people of tafsir (exegesis, the explanation of the Qur'an) and of narrative (qasas) mentioned that the one "(who had knowledge from the Scripture)" is Asaf ibn Barkhiya, and that he was the minister of Sulayman.

The literal meaning of "irtidad al-tarf (the return of the glance)" is the return of the gaze of the eye from a visible object from which it turned away for an instant. It was expressed by "return" because they describe looking by "sending the glance" and "sending the gaze," so the "return" is a metaphor built upon that.

This debate between the 'ifrit of the jinn and the one who had knowledge from the Scripture signifies that through wisdom and knowledge there is accomplished what cannot be accomplished through strength alone; that wisdom is acquired, by His saying "(who had knowledge from the Scripture)"; and that the strength of the elements is a natural disposition in them, while acquisition through knowledge is a way to employ powers which cannot employ some of themselves through others. Thus this story is mentioned as an example of knowledge prevailing over strength. And since these two men were subjected to Sulayman's service, what they were singled out with of knowledge was a distinction for them which returns to the grace and honour of Sulayman, in that God subjected to him such powers. The station of his prophethood is too exalted for him to undertake the bringing of Bilqis's throne with his own person.

It is apparent that His saying "(before your glance returns to you)" and His saying "(before you rise from your place)" are two examples of speed and of the greater swiftness.

The pronoun attached in "(ra'ahu, when he saw it)" refers to the throne.

Al-istiqrar (being settled) is: being firmly established in the earth, and it is an intensive form of qarar (settledness). This is a particular settledness, different from the general settledness which is synonymous with existence. It is the settledness which is estimated in the reporting of the subject by an adverbial phrase and a prepositional phrase, so that it is connected to them when they occur as predicate or occur as a circumstantial clause, since it is estimated as "(ka'in, existing)" or "(mustaqirr, settled)." That settledness is not something whose mention is required. Ibn 'Atiyya made it, in the verse, one of the manifestations of the omitted element, which is far-fetched.

Since He mentioned the bounty attributed to God in the title of His being his Lord, this shows that His bounty upon him is great, since he is the servant of his Lord. Therefore God's kindness to him is nothing but pure bounty. When the throne was brought to him, Sulayman did not busy himself with rejoicing in his sovereignty or in the capability of his men, but turned instead to thanking God Most High for what He had granted him of bounty and bestowed upon him of hosts subjected to him by knowledge and strength. Thus the merits and virtues of all of them return to His favouring him.

He cited a moral and religious wisdom: ﴿And whoever is grateful, his gratitude is only for himself; and whoever is ungrateful, indeed my Lord is Self-Sufficient, Generous﴾. Every person who draws near to God by a righteous deed must keep in mind that his deed is only for himself, hoping through it for God's reward and pleasure in the Hereafter, and hoping for the continuance of God's favour upon him in this world. So the benefit accrues to him in both abodes, and God does not benefit from any of that.

The lam in His saying "(yashkuru li-nafsihi, gives thanks for his own self)" is the lam of purpose (lam al-ajl), and it is not the lam with which the verb of thanking is made transitive, as in "(wa-shkurū lī, and give thanks to Me)." The intended meaning of "(man kafara, whoever is ungrateful)" is whoever disbelieves God's favour upon him by worshipping other than God. For God is free of need of his gratitude, and He is Generous in His respite and His provision in this world. This was already mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your blessing﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 15].

The shift from the pronoun to the explicit noun in His saying "(﴿indeed my Lord is Self-Sufficient, Generous﴾)" instead of saying "indeed He is Self-Sufficient, Generous," is an emphasis on the acknowledgment of the purity of the bounty derived from His saying "(﴿the bounty of my Lord﴾)."

[Page 270]

﴿He said: "O chiefs, which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?"﴾ ﴿A powerful one of the jinn said: "I will bring it to you before you rise from your place. Indeed, I am strong and trustworthy for this."﴾ ﴿Said one who had knowledge from the Scripture: "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you." Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 41:

﴿He said, "Disguise her throne for her; let us see whether she will be guided or whether she will be among those who are not guided."﴾

This is part of the dialogue that took place between Sulayman, peace be upon him, and his council (mala'ihi). For this reason it is not joined with a conjunction (lam yu'taf), because it proceeds in the manner of exchange and conversation.

Al-tankir (disguising) means changing the state of something. Jamil said:

"They said, 'We see her, O Jamil, changed (tanakkarat), and the slanderer has altered her, so I said, "Perhaps she is..."'"

He meant: she had changed in the state of her companionship because of the alteration made by the slanderers, such that some of her attributes had been altered. They (the scholars) said: he intended to surprise her and to test what was presumed about her.

Those commanded with the disguising were those among his council who had the capacity to do so.

And (min alladhina la yahtadun, "among those who are not guided") is more emphatic in negating guidance than "la tahtadi" (you are not guided), as has been mentioned in its parallels more than once.

The verse: ﴿So when she came, it was said, "Is your throne like this?" She said, "It is as if it were it."﴾

When his words (لَمّا جاءَتْ, "when she came") indicate that when the queen learned of the reply Sulayman gave to her envoys, she resolved to come to Sulayman herself, entering under the authority of his kingdom, and that she prepared for the journey to Urshalim (Jerusalem) with what befits someone of her rank.

The account of her departure is omitted, since no significant purpose connected to it lies in the place of lesson. The intended meaning is that she submitted to Sulayman's command and came to him, willing to be associated with him.

The verb (قِيلَ, "it was said") is built in the passive voice, because no purpose depends on identifying the speaker. The apparent meaning is that the one who said this was Sulayman.

[Page 274 begins at "بحيث لا تفهمهم"]

﴿And We were given knowledge before her, and we were Muslims﴾ [An-Naml: 42] ﴿And what she used to worship besides Allah had averted her. Indeed, she was from a disbelieving people﴾.

It is permissible for this to be a conjunction (ʿaṭf) to His saying ﴿This is of the bounty of my Lord﴾ [An-Naml: 40] and what is between them is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ), meaning: this is from the speech of Sulayman.

It is also permissible for it to be a conjunction to His saying "﴿that We may see whether you are guided﴾" [An-Naml: 41] and what is between them is a parenthetical insertion in the same way. It is also permissible for it to be a conjunction to "﴿Is your throne like this?﴾" [An-Naml: 42], with what is between them being a parenthetical insertion that interrupts its answer. The meaning would be: it was said, "We were given knowledge before her," that is, the speaker said, "Is your throne like this?" That is, Sulayman said that in his assembly right after she chose her opinion, giving thanks to Allah for the knowledge he possessed. Or some of Sulayman's chiefs said to one another some of this saying. Perhaps they spoke it in a low voice or in their Hebrew language in such a way that she could not understand them. They said this in boastfulness, that among them were those who had knowledge that the chiefs of the kingdom of Saba' did not have. That is, by what we witness of the glitter of this kingdom, we do not forget that we are in a superior intellectual state. By "knowledge" they meant the knowledge of wisdom (ḥikma) which Allah taught Sulayman and the men of his kingdom. Some of the people of Saba' shared part of it with them, for they were people of knowledge by which they established a civilization that dazzled.

So the meaning of "min qablihā" (before her), if taken literally, is that their people, the Children of Israel, were earlier than the people of Saba' in knowing wisdom and the civilization of kingship. This is because wisdom appeared among the Children of Israel from the time of Musa (Moses), for he laid down the law for them, established for them the order of the community, and taught them the manner of civilization through the planning of the designs of their dwellings and their clothing, and the system of the army, war, seasons and gatherings. Then this continued to rise until it reached a far-reaching height in the time of Sulayman. On this basis, the Children of Israel were earlier to the knowledge of wisdom than the people of Saba'.

If by "min qablihā" is meant the notional priority (al-qablīya al-iʿtibāriyya), which is superiority and excellence in virtues, and this is the most fitting for the meaning, then the meaning is: we are greater and stronger than her in knowledge. As the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "We are the first and the foremost, though they were given the Book before us," meaning: we are the first in the ultimate ends of guidance. As an example of this, he cited the guidance of the people of Islam to Friday, when he said: "This is their day about which they differed, and Allah guided us to it." Thus the more likely meaning of "min qablihā" is that we surpass her in knowledge and attain what she has not attained. They increased in displaying their superiority over her by mentioning the religious aspect, that is, "wa kunnā muslimīn" (and we were Muslims) before her. The mention of the verb of being (kāna) indicates their being firmly established in Islam since antiquity.

As for "wa ṣaddahā" (and it averted her): what she used to worship besides Allah averted her from Islam. That is, what she worshipped besides Allah averted her. The object of the verb "ṣadd" (averting) is omitted, the speech indicating it in His saying "﴿and we were Muslims﴾". What she used to worship was the sun. Attributing the averting to the object of worship is a rational metaphor (majāz ʿaqlī), because it is by means of its averting her from monotheism (tawḥīd), as in His saying, "﴿and they increased them in nothing but ruin﴾" [Hud: 101], and His saying, "﴿their religion has deceived these﴾" [Al-Anfal: 49].

In the mention of the verb of being twice in "﴿what she used to worship﴾" and "﴿indeed, she was from a disbelieving people﴾" there is an indication of her firm establishment in worshipping the sun, and this firm establishment was due to descent from a lineage of polytheists. So polytheism was imprinted in her nature by inheritance. Disbelief had encompassed her through its penetration into her soul, her upbringing upon it, and her being among a disbelieving people. So how could guidance and faith reach her?

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 44:

﴿It was said to her: "Enter the palace." And when she saw it, she thought it was a pool of water, and she bared her shins. He said: "Indeed, it is a palace paved smooth with glass."﴾

The clause ﴿It was said to her: "Enter the palace"﴾ is a fresh, initial resumption (istinaf ibtida'i) introducing a part of the story. The account of her journey to her arrival has been omitted, and it is indicated by her standing before the palace of Solomon, in order to enter with him or to enter upon him while he was inside it.

When Solomon showed her the greatness of his civilization, he moved her to a place where she could see a wondrous work of skilled craftsmanship, namely the palace (al-sarh). Al-sarh is applied to the courtyard of a house and its open space. The apparent view is that the palace (sarh al-qasr) mentioned in the First Book of Kings, chapter 7, is a rough house with two doors, in which Solomon used to sit to judge between people.

The ones who said to her "Enter the palace" were those who were in her company.

The one who said ﴿Indeed, it is a palace paved smooth with glass﴾ was Solomon. He was accompanying her or was awaiting her, and the glass of the palace, with which the palace was paved, lay between them.

Mention of entering implies that the palace is a place having a door. In the First Book of Kings, chapter 10: "When she saw the house that he had built..."

The report that she thought it was a pool when she saw it indicates that this appeared to her at the moment of her entry. This shows that the palace was the first thing that appeared to her from the entrance. It was therefore without doubt a courtyard prepared for recreation, floored with transparent glass, with water flowing beneath it, so that the beholder would take it for a pool of water. This was among the wondrous crafts peculiar to the palaces of Solomon in that era, which were not known in Yemen, given the civilization and grandeur of construction that she had attained.

Qunbul, on the authority of Ibn Kathir, read (ʿan saʾqayha) with a silent hamza after the sin instead of the alif, according to the dialect of those who hamzate the long vowel when it occurs in the middle of a word. From this is the verse of Jarir:

[Page 276]

Lahabba al-mu'qidani ilayya Mu'sa wa Ja'datu idh adaʾahuma al-wuqudu
So he hamzated al-mu'qidani and Mu'sa.

The baring of her shins was because she had gathered up her garments, disliking that they become wet from what she had thought was water. Baring her shins may be by removing her slippers or sandals, or it may be by hitching up her garment. It has been said that she did not wear slippers. Al-mumarrad means smoothed.

Qawarir is the plural of qarura, which is the name of a vessel made of glass that they used for wine, so that the sediment of wine settled at the bottom of the vessel would be visible to the viewer, and the clear quantity would thereby appear. That vessel was named qarura because what settles at its bottom is visible through it. It was pluralized as qawarir. Then this plural was applied to the material from which the qarura is made, which is glass. So qawarir is one of the names of glass. Bashshar said:

Be gentle with ʿAmr when you shake his lineage, for he is an Arab of qawarir (glass)
He means that his lineage among the Arabs is weak; when it is shaken, it breaks. Glass was already mentioned at His words, exalted is He: ﴿The lamp is in a niche (zujaja)﴾ [al-Nur: 35] in Surah al-Nur.

* * *

﴿She said: "My Lord, I have wronged myself, and I have submitted with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾

What she saw of signs overwhelmed her, and from them she knew that Solomon was truthful in what he called her to, and that he was supported by Allah, exalted is He. She knew that her religion and the religion of her people was false, so she acknowledged that she had wronged herself by following misguidance in worshipping the sun. This is a first level in belief, the level of takhliya (emptying), and then she ascended to the level above it, which is the level of tahalli (adorning) with true faith, so she said: ﴿and I have submitted with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. Thus she acknowledged that Allah is the Lord of all existing things, and this is the station of tawhid.

In her words "with Solomon" is an affirmation of the religion that Solomon adhered to, which is the religion of Judaism. She intended by this word to gather the meanings of the religion, so that its detail would be what she received from Solomon of the laws and rulings.

The clause ﴿She said: "My Lord, I have wronged myself"﴾ is an answer to Solomon's words ﴿Indeed, it is a palace paved smooth with glass﴾, and for that reason it is not conjoined by a conjunction.

Islam (al-islam) is submission to Allah, exalted is He. Bilqis's adoption of tawhid was in her own person, because she submitted to Allah with it; it is not established that the people of Saba' had abandoned the worship of idols, as will come in Surah Saba'. As for the entry of Judaism into the lands of Yemen, it will come in Surah al-Buruj. The Qur'an was silent about the rest of her story and her return to her land, and the storytellers have reports that are not authentic. This is the completion of the story.

The point of the lesson in it is taking admonition from the condition of this queen, for her elevated rank and the greatness of her authority did not prevent her, together with the soundness of her nature and the acuteness of her intellect, from looking into the proofs of the truthfulness of the caller to tawhid, becoming certain of the corruption of shirk, and acknowledging the oneness of Allah. So the persistence of the polytheists in their shirk after the guidance of Islam has come to them is only due to the feebleness of their dreams, or to their blindness to the truth, their clinging to falsehood, and their obstinacy in it. There is no basis for what the storytellers and some exegetes mention, that Solomon married Bilqis or that he had a son by her. Rehoboam, his son who succeeded him in the kingship, was from an Ammonite wife.

This is a third example that God set forth concerning the state of the polytheists in relation to the believers, and He made it a consolation for His Messenger ﷺ, that he has a model in the messengers and prophets before him.

The transition from the mention of Solomon's kingdom and the story of the Queen of Sheba to the mention of Thamud and their messenger, without mentioning 'Ad, is due to the proximity of the lands. The dwellings of Thamud lay on the borders of Solomon's kingdom and were on the route of the traveller from Sheba to Palestine.

Do you not see that after mentioning Thamud, He followed with the mention of the people of Lot, who were nearer to the land of Palestine? So the context of these stories was suited to the context of the traveller from the land of Yemen to Palestine. Since what befell the people was more important to mention in this setting, He placed the prepositional phrase (*al-majrur*, the object introduced by a preposition) before the direct object (*al-maf'ul*, the object of the verb), because the prepositional phrase is the locus of the lesson, whereas the direct object is the locus of consolation, and consolation is a secondary purpose.

The oath particle (*lam al-qasam*) emphasizes the sending, taking into account what is connected to it from the rest of the report. Its emphasis may be merely for the sake of attention, or it may be based on treating the addressees as those who doubt what the report contains: the people's denial of him and their scorn for the warning of their Lord delivered through his tongue, and the descent of the punishment upon them on that account. Their failure to take admonition from what happened to those who were like them in their condition made them like one who denies it.

The phrase ﴿that worship Allah﴾ (*an u'budu Allah*) explains what the word "We sent" (*arsalna*) implies of the meaning of saying. The clause ﴿then they became two factions contending with each other﴾ (*fa-idha hum fariqani yakhtasimun*) follows from "We sent to Thamud their brother Salih". The meaning is: We sent to Thamud their brother Salih to rescue them from polytheism, and then, to their surprise, one faction turned away from faith while another believed.

The use of the particle of suddenness (*fa-idha*) is a metonymy indicating that their division was displeasing, as though it was not expected. For this reason, there is no explicit denial that most of them were disbelievers, pointing to the fact that the mere persistence of disbelief among them is sufficient for the ugliness of their conduct. Their condition here is equivalent to the condition of the Quraysh towards the Muhammadan message. The pronoun of "they contend" (*yakhtasimun*) is returned to the dual "two factions" (*fariqani*), taking into account that each of the two factions comprises a large number. Compare the saying of God, Exalted is He: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight one another﴾ (Al-Hujurat: 9), and He did not say "they fought" in the dual feminine.

The two factions are: the faction of those who were arrogant, and the faction of those who were deemed weak, among whom was Salih. The particle *fa-* (then) indicates sequence, and this is a sequence according to what custom requires after hearing the call. The contention occurs with Salih first, and with his followers secondarily.

[Page 279]

When the dispute between the two groups concerned Salih from the start, the reply of Salih was given to address what their dispute contained, namely their attempt to silence him by demanding that the punishment descend. Salih's statement here is not the beginning of his call, for his words ﴿that worship Allah﴾ [al-Naml: 45] came earlier. Rather, it is a reply to what their dispute contained with him. For this reason the clause (﴿O my people﴾) comes separated, following the manner of conversational exchange, since it is the report of a reply to what their dispute contained.

The commentary limits itself to Salih's address to his people regarding their delusion, in that they thought the delay of the punishment was a sign that his threat was false. They said: ﴿Bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful﴾ [al-A'raf: 70], as is reported of them in Surat al-A'raf. This is because the purpose here is to admonish the Quraysh regarding their saying: ﴿Rain down on us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], by means of the situation of Thamud, which is parallel to their situation, so that they may know that the outcome of such conduct is similar to the outcome of Thamud, given the similarity of the two situations. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment, and had there not been an appointed term, the punishment would have come upon them. It will surely come upon them suddenly while they do not perceive﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 53].

The interrogative in His words (﴿Why do you hasten﴾) is a denial of their taking hold of the side of punishment to the exclusion of the side of mercy.

(Al-sayyi'a) is an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning "in a bad condition," and likewise (al-hasana) [means "in a good condition"].

It is permissible that what is meant by (al-sayyi'a) is the bad condition in their treatment of him, through their denial of him. What is meant by al-hasana is the opposite of that, namely their affirmation of what he brought. Thus al-isti'jal means hastening ahead. The bā' is for accompaniment (al-mulabasa). The object of (tasta'jiluna) is omitted, its estimated form being: "you hasten me while clothed in the evil of denial." The meaning is that he denounced them for taking hold of the edge of denial, since they turned away from reflecting on the signs of his truthfulness. That is: if you are hesitant about my matter, then assume my truthfulness and then look. This is a drawing of them down to consideration instead of aversion, and for this reason he combined in his speech the bad and the good.

It is also permissible that what is meant by (al-sayyi'a) is the bad condition they were awaiting, namely what they asked for of the hastening of the punishment reported of them in Surat al-A'raf. By (al-hasana) is meant the opposite of that, namely the condition of their safety from the descent of the punishment. In this case (al-sayyi'a) is the object of (tasta'jiluna), and the bā' is extra, for emphasis of attachment, like His words: ﴿and wipe over your heads﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6].

[Page 280]

The meaning is: a denial of their making the delay of the punishment a sign of the falsity of the threat of it, and that the better course for them would be to make the continuation of safety a sign of Allah's granting them respite, so that they would guard against the descent of the punishment. That is: why do you persist in denial while awaiting the descent of the punishment? It would have been more fitting for you to hasten to affirmation while expecting that the punishment would not descend at all. On both interpretations, Salih's reply to them proceeds according to the wise approach (al-uslub al-hakim, the method of addressing people in a manner suited to their state), by treating their certainty of his falsity as if it were a hesitation between his truthfulness and his falsity.

His words (﴿before the good﴾) are a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to (al-sayyi'a). This is an alert to them regarding their error in thinking that, had Salih been truthful in what he threatened them with, he would have hastened it for them. Its delay is only because it is not a true threat, since the punishment is a great matter, and it is not permissible for minds to enter under its possibility. So the priority in His words (﴿before the good﴾) is a figurative usage (majaz) for choosing to take hold of the side of the possibility of evil and preferring it over taking hold of the side of good, as if they hastened to it and took it before they took the good.

The apparent form of the interrogation is that it asks about the cause of their hastening, but in fact it is an interrogation about the effect, as a metonymy (kinaya) for the absence of what ought to be the cause of hastening the punishment. Thus the denial is directed at the hastening itself, not at its cause.

Then the denial, which calls for their abandonment of this, is followed by an exhortation for them to desist from it through repentance and seeking forgiveness for what has passed from them, and in hope that Allah will have mercy on them so that He does not punish them. Although what proceeded from them necessitates the continuation of Allah's anger against them, Allah, by His mercy, has made the one who repents from sin like the one who has not sinned.

This is from their dialogue with Salih. That is why the two verbs of speech are not joined by a conjunction, and the passage follows the usual pattern for reporting exchanges, as we have explained more than once.

The original of (اطَّيَّرْنا) is تَطَيَّرْنا. The تاء was changed to a طاء because their points of articulation are close. The letter was then made sukun to ease the idgham (assimilation), and a hamzat al-wasl was added because the word begins with a sakin. The باء is for causality (al-sababiyyah).

The meaning of tatayyur (تَطَيُّر, taking omens from bad fortune) is tashA'um (تَشاؤُم, considering something an omen of misfortune). It is so called because most of it arises from inferring from the movements of birds, whether sanih (passing from right to left) or barih (passing from left to right). Tatayyur was among the superstitions of the Arabs, and Thamud were among the Arabs. Their statement reported in this verse is a reported imitation of their own speech. They do not mean the tatayyur that comes from startling a bird (zajr al-tayr), because their words (بِكَ وبِمَن مَعَكَ) in Surat al-A'raf prevent that reading. The meaning of shu'm (شُؤْم, misfortune) was already discussed there.

Salih answered their words by saying that he and those with him are not the cause of misfortune. The true cause of their misfortune and of the harms that befall them is the power of Allah.

The term "bird" (الطائر) is used metaphorically for what befell them, by way of mushakalah (مُشاكَلَة, matching a term to the one used by the other party), in response to their words (﴿اطَّيَّرْنا بِكَ وبِمَن مَعَكَ﴾), and to address them in terms they understand, in order to correct their belief. The context is their own phrase (اطَّيَّرْنا بِكَ).

(عِنْدَ, "with/at") is used for a figurative place, borrowed to mean the realization of an affair of Allah's affairs, by which He decrees good and evil. That is Allah's disposition and His decree. A parallel to this was discussed in Surat al-A'raf.

By (بَلْ) he turned away from the content of their statement (﴿اطَّيَّرْنا بِكَ وبِمَن مَعَكَ﴾), meaning that no misfortune comes from him or from those with him. Rather, those who claimed it are a people whom Satan has tempted with a renewed temptation, by casting into their hearts the belief in its truth.

The report about them, that they are tempted (مَفْتُونُونَ), is phrased by placing the subject before the verbal predicate, to strengthen the judgment. The predicate is expressed as a present-tense verb, to indicate that the temptations are continual and ongoing.

In the word (تُفْتَنُونَ), the second-person address is given precedence over the third-person form, although both are called for by the apparent form. This preference for address is because it is more explicit than the third person.

[Page 281]

[282]
﴿There were nine men in the city who spread corruption in the land and did not reform.﴾ ﴿They said: "Swear to one another by God that we will surely attack him and his family by night, and then we will say to his heir: 'We did not witness the destruction of his family, and we are indeed truthful.'"﴾

He joins one part of the story to another part of it. "Al-madinah" (the city) is Hijr Thamud, with the ḥ vowelled with a kasra and the j silent. Its location is known today in the land of Thamud and the cities of Salih, and it consists of the remains of that city: ruins and houses hewn into the mountains. It lies between Medina and Tabuk, on the route to Syria. The Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims passed by it on their march during the Battle of Tabuk, and they saw wells there. The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade them to drink from them or to perform ablution with them, except for one well, which he commanded them to drink from and to perform ablution with, and he said: "This is the well from which the she-camel of Salih used to drink."

"Al-rahṭ" (a group, gloss: a small band of men, roughly ten) means a number of people around ten, and it is the same as "al-nafar" (a small company of men). The attribution of "tis'ah" (nine) to it is an idafah of a part to the name of the whole, used figuratively. This is a common construction in the Arabic language, like "khams dhawd" (five camels). The grammarians differed over analogy based on it, and the position of Sibawayh and al-Akhfash is that it is transmitted only by usage (sama'iyyah).

These men were among the most obstinate of the people. Their names are disputed in various narrations, which are among the fabrications of the storytellers, and nothing reliable has been established about them. It is well known that the one who hamstrung the she-camel was named (Qudar), with a ḍammah on the m and a light d. Some people have regarded the number nine as ill-omened because of the story of Thamud, and this is the forbidden kind of ill-omen.

"Al-ard" (the land) refers to the land of Thamud, so the definite article is for a known reference.

The conjunction of "wa la yuslihun" (and do not reform) with "yufsidun" (spread corruption) is a precaution, to indicate that they were wholly devoted to corruption and were not among those who mixed corruption with reform.

The clause "qalu" (they said) is either a qualifier (ṣifah, gloss: an adjective describing) of "tis'ah", or a second predicate (khabar) of "kana", or it is itself the predicate of "kana". "Fi al-madinah" is connected to "kana" as an adverbial phrase (ẓarf laghw, gloss: an adverbial complement that is not essential to the meaning). It is not appropriate to make the clause a new sentence (isti'naf, gloss: a resumptive new sentence), because it is the main point of the story. The meaning is: some of them said to others.

"Taqasamu" (swear to one another) is an imperative verb. That is, one of them said: "Swear," that is, some of them began, [283] and said: "Swear." He intended to include himself, since he would not command them to this unless he wanted to share in what was sworn to, as indicated by his words "we will surely attack him." When one of them said this, they agreed to it and repeated it, so all of them were saying it. For this reason the speech is attributed to the nine.

The oath "by God" indicates that they acknowledged God, but they associated gods with Him, as was mentioned earlier in their stories in the surahs that preceded.

"Linubayyitannahu" (we will surely attack him) is the answer to the oath, and the pronoun refers to Salih. "Al-tabyit" and "al-bayat" mean a surprise attack on the enemy by night. Its opposite is "al-tasbih," a raid in the morning. The custom of the Arabs in raids was that they took place in the morning, and for this reason a person warning a people of the arrival of an enemy says: "O morning!" So "al-tabyit" occurs only for the purpose of treachery. The meaning is that they would raid his house at night and kill him and his family treacherously, so that his killer would not be known. Then they would deny that they had killed them or had witnessed their death.

"Al-mahlik" is a noun of place or time from the quadriliteral verb "ahlaka," that is: we witnessed the destruction of those who destroyed them. Their words "and we are indeed truthful" are part of what they prepared to say, so it is coordinated with "what we witnessed of his destruction." That is: and we affirm that we are indeed truthful. They did not say that they would swear that they were truthful.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) recited "linubayyitannahu" with the nun of plurality and a fatḥah on the tā' that precedes the nun of emphasis. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf recited it with the tā' of address at its beginning and a ḍammah on the original tā' before the nun of emphasis. This is based on the assumption that it is the command of some of them to others. Likewise, al-Jumhur recited "linaqulannahu" with the nun of plurality at its beginning and a fatḥah on the lam. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf recited it with the tā' of address and a ḍammah on the lam.

The "walī" (heir, gloss: the nearest relative who takes up the claim for vengeance) of Salih are the nearest of the people when they intend to seek vengeance for him.

This part of the story of Thamud is not mentioned in any surah other than this one. I suppose the reason for its mention is that this surah was revealed at a time when the polytheists were plotting to harm the Prophet (ﷺ), which is the plot that God related in His saying: ﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you, to confine you or kill you or expel you, they plotted, and God plotted, and God is the best of plotters﴾ [al-Anfal: 30]. So God set forth for them an example through the plot of the nine men of the people of Salih against him, and how the outcome of their plot turned out. For this reason you see a resemblance between the two verses, and you see the repetition of the mention of their plot and God's plot against them, and the mention that in their story there is a sign for a people who know.

[Page 285]

Allah called their plotting "makr" (scheming), because it was a plan to harm carried out in secrecy. He emphasized their scheming with the absolute object (al-mafʿul al-mutlaq, a verbal noun used to stress the action), to show its intensity within the category of scheming, and its tanwin (indefinite ending) serves to magnify it.

The scheming attributed to the Name of Majesty (Allah) is figurative (majaz). The word makr is used metaphorically for Allah's act of hastening to destroy them before they could carry out their plan to kill Salih and his family during the night, and for His delaying their destruction. That is, the time when they conspired to kill Salih. The resemblance is between Allah's act and the act of a schemer who postpones an action until the time it is needed, while the one it is done to is unaware.

The divine scheming is emphasized and magnified in the same way their scheming was emphasized and magnified, and in a manner suited to its kind. Allah's punishment cannot be matched by the punishment of people, so its magnitude surpasses anything people can plan.

The scheming attributed to the Name of Majesty refers to what is indicated by the clause (﴿We destroyed them and their people, all of them﴾), and the verse.

In His saying (﴿while they do not perceive﴾) there is a reinforcement of the metaphor of scheming for the planning of their annihilation. There is therefore no tarshih (a metaphor developed by supporting details) or tajrid (abstraction, a metaphor reinforced by mention of its source) in this.

The address in His saying (﴿So look﴾) is to the Prophet ﷺ. Its connection with the particle of consequence (fa) implies that taking lessons from Allah's scheming against them is the purpose of relating the story, by way of allusion that the outcome of his affair with the Quraysh will be that they will be restrained from their plotting and that he will be victorious over them. This is a consolation to him for what he encounters from his people.

The looking (al-nazar) is inward looking (nazar qalbi), and it has been suspended from the two objects by the interrogative (﴿how was the outcome of their scheming﴾).

The majority of readers recited (﴿Indeed, We destroyed them﴾) with a kasra on the hamza, so the clause is a resumed statement (istinaf bayani), answering what the interrogative in His saying (﴿how was the outcome of their scheming﴾) raises, namely a question about this manner. The emphasis is for attention to the report. ʿAsim, al-Kisaʾi, Yaʿqub and Khalaf recited it with a fatha on the hamza, so the verbal noun is a substitute (badal) for (ʿaqibah, outcome). The emphasis is also for attention.

The pronoun of the third person in (dammarnahum, "We destroyed them") refers to the band (of conspirators). (Their people) is conjoined to them because the recompense matches what it is recompense for, since they schemed against Salih and his family, so Allah destroyed them and their people.

Tadmir (destruction) is severe annihilation. It has been mentioned more than once before, including in Surat al-Shuʿara.

The story has already been mentioned, and the rescue of Salih and those who believed with him has also been mentioned: Allah revealed to him that he and those with him should leave for the land of Palestine when he warned his people that they had three days of enjoyment left.

The connection of His saying (﴿So those are their houses, empty﴾) to the clause (dammarnahum) is a connection of consequence in the report. The demonstrative refers to a known thing that is not witnessed, because its certainty takes the place of its presence, since the dwellings of Thamud are known to all the Quraysh, and they pass by them on their journeys to Syria.

(Khawiyah, "empty") is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). Its governing element is the meaning of the verb contained in the demonstrative, as in His saying: ﴿And this is my husband, an old man﴾ [Hud: 72]. This was discussed in Surat Hud.

Khawiyah means "empty," and its verbal noun is khawaʾ, meaning: so the houses, some of them remain in the mountains with no one living in them.

The bāʾ in (bima zalamu, "because they wronged") indicates cause, and (ma, "what") is a verbal (masdariyyah) particle, meaning: their emptiness was because of their wrongdoing. Wrongdoing (zulm) here is shirk (associating partners with Allah) and denying their messenger. This is wrong against Allah, since it is a violation of His right to unity, and wrong against the Messenger by denying him, though he was truthful.

Because Allah specified their action by the description of wrongdoing, among the many states that their disbelief includes, such as corruption, this indicates that wrongdoing has an effect in the ruin of their lands. This is the meaning of what is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, that he said: "I find in the Book of Allah that wrongdoing ruins houses," and he recited: ﴿So those are their houses, empty because they wronged﴾. This is part of the method of taking every meaning of the speech of the Qur'an that it can bear, as we mentioned in the ninth introduction of this tafsir.

We add here something not previously stated in similar contexts: intellectual realities (al-haqaʾiq al-ʿaqliyyah), since the essential constitution of their quiddities (mahiyyat) exists in mental existence, there is a connection and proximity among many of them, so that some are referred back to others according to differences in consideration. Shirk, for example, is a known reality through which it is a rational genus (jins ʿaqli). In terms of what gives rise to it and what results from it, it is connected to other realities, like wrongdoing, meaning aggression against people by taking their rights, since it is one of its causes, and like corruption (fisq), since it is one of its effects. Likewise denial (takdhib) is also one of its effects (﴿Leave Me with the deniers﴾), and so is arrogance, and so is extravagance, since these two are also among its effects. Among the methods of the Qur'an is to express shirk with terms of these realities, to indicate that it combines a number of atrocities, to draw attention to its connection with these genera, and so that believers may know the corruption of these realities in themselves. Here it is expressed as wrongdoing, which is common, so that the listener knows that the category of wrongdoing is ugly and blameworthy, not to mention that shirk is one of its kinds. Similarly is His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor and a liar﴾ [Ghafir: 28], meaning: he is rooted in shirk. Otherwise Allah has guided many transgressors and liars through repentance. And from His saying: ﴿Is there not in Hell a residence for the arrogant?﴾ [Zumar: 60], and similar verses.

The clause ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾ is a parenthetical insertion between the conjoined clauses. The demonstrative refers to what was mentioned of the outcome of their scheming. The sign (ayah) is the proof of Allah's support for His messengers.

The lam in His saying (﴿for a people who know﴾) is the lam of causation, meaning: a sign for their sake, that is, for the sake of their faith. In it there is an allusion that the polytheists, to whom this admonition was addressed, if they do not take heed from it, then they are a people who do not know.

The mention of the word "people" (qawm) implies that whoever takes a lesson from this verse is firmly rooted in intellect, to the point that intellect is part of the characteristic of the people, as was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reason﴾ [Baqarah: 164] in Surat al-Baqarah.

[Page 286]

The clause ﴿And We saved those who believed and used to fear Allah﴾ is placed after the clause ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who know﴾ to reassure the hearts of the believers that Allah will save them from what He threatened the polytheists with, just as He saved those who believed and used to fear Allah from Thamud, namely Salih and those who believed with him. It has been said that those who believed with Salih were four thousand. When Allah wished to destroy Thamud, He revealed to Salih that he and those with him should leave, so they left and settled at the place of al-Rass, and the People of al-Rass were from their descendants. It has also been said they settled on the shore of Yemen and built the city of Hadramawt. In some reports, Salih settled in Palestine. All of these are reports not reliably authenticated.

The addition of the verb of being (kanu) in (wa kanu yattaqun, "and used to fear Allah") serves to indicate that they were firmly established in piety.

[Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah 27, verses 54–55]

﴿And [mention] Lot, when he said to his people, "Do you commit the foul deed while you see [one another]? Do you indeed approach men with desire, instead of women? Rather, you are a people who are ignorant."﴾

Lot (لُوطًا) is coordinated (ʿaṭf, conjunction) with Salih (صالِحًا) in his earlier words: ﴿And We had certainly sent to Thamud their brother Salih﴾ [an-Naml: 45]. The conjunction is not prevented by the fact that the governing verb of the coordinated noun is linked to the phrase ﴿to Thamud﴾ [an-Naml: 45], because the prepositional phrase is not a restriction on its complement; rather, it is like one of the objects, so it has no connection to a noun coordinated with another object. Agreement in case (ʾiʿrāb) distinguishes the noun coordinated with from others. A parallel to this has already occurred in Surah al-Aʿraf. The recipients of the message are not mentioned here as they were mentioned in the story of Thamud, because the resemblance between the people of Lot and the Quraysh is not complete, except in denial and polytheism. It is also permissible for (وَلُوطًا) to be in the accusative by a suppressed verb whose estimate is: "And mention Lot," because the presence of (إذْ) after it brings it close to such constructions as ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30].

The sequence of the story of Thamud followed by the story of the people of Lot follows the usual order of the Qur'an in arranging the stories of these nations, since the people of Lot were later in time than Thamud.

What raises a question here is the restriction to the story of the people of Lot without the stories of ʿĀd and Madyan. I have already explained that this is due to the proximity of the dwellings of the people of Lot to the kingdom of Solomon, and their location between the dwellings of Thamud and Palestine. Their dwellings were the route of the Quraysh to the lands of al-Sham. God said: ﴿And indeed, it is on a road that remains﴾ [al-Hijr: 76], and He said: ﴿And indeed, you pass by them in the morning﴾ [as-Saffat: 137] ﴿and at night. Will you not reason?﴾ [as-Saffat: 138].

The adverbial clause of (إذْ) is connected to (أرْسَلْنا) or to the suppressed (اذْكُرْ), both estimated.

The interrogative in (أتَأْتُونَ) is for denial (inkārī).

The clause (وأنْتُمْ تُبْصِرُونَ) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) adding to the censure, meaning: you do this openly, so that some of you see others. Openly displaying disobedience is itself disobedience, because it indicates approval of it, and that is contempt for the prohibitions.

His saying (أيِنَّكم لَتَأْتُونَ) was mentioned in al-Aʿraf as (إنَّكم لَتَأْتُونَ). Here the interrogative for denial is used, whereas in al-Aʿraf the declarative used for denial is used. It is possible that the difference in reporting is due to the difference in what is reported, such that Lot said both statements to them in two different situations. It is also possible that the difference in reporting is for variety (tafannun) while the meaning is the same. Both styles occur in the Qur'anic stories, because changing the style renews the listener's attentiveness.

Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza, and Abu Bakr on the authority of ʿAsim recited what is in Surah al-Aʿraf with two hamzas, so the two verses are equal in the recitation of these. The aspects of this were mentioned earlier in Surah al-Aʿraf.

In al-Aʿraf occurs ﴿Do you commit the foul deed that no one in the worlds has preceded you in?﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 80], which is not mentioned here, because what happens in the story does not require mentioning all of it. Likewise the statement about not mentioning (وأنْتُمْ تُبْصِرُونَ) in Surah al-Aʿraf, while it is mentioned here.

The rest of the verse is parallel to what came earlier in Surah al-Aʿraf, except that what occurs here is (بَلْ أنْتُمْ قَوْمٌ تَجْهَلُونَ), so He described them with ignorance (jahāla), which is a comprehensive term for the states of corrupt judgment and hardness of heart.

In al-Aʿraf He described them as a people who are ﴿transgressors﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 81], and this is to be understood as a difference of the two statements in two situations.

The insertion of the word (قَوْمٍ) in the two verses has the particularity mentioned earlier in His saying in this surah: ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who know﴾ [an-Naml: 52].

In His saying (تَجْهَلُونَ), the address (khiṭāb) was preferred over the third person (ghayba), so He did not say (يَجْهَلُونَ) with the ya' of the third person, though both fit the apparent meaning, because address is stronger in indication, as is recited in His saying: ﴿Rather, you are a people who are being tested﴾ [an-Naml: 47].
