The sequence of the story of Thamud followed by the story of the people of Lot follows the usual order of the Qur'an in arranging the stories of these nations, since the people of Lot were later in time than Thamud.

What raises a question here is the restriction to the story of the people of Lot without the stories of ʿĀd and Madyan. I have already explained that this is due to the proximity of the dwellings of the people of Lot to the kingdom of Solomon, and their location between the dwellings of Thamud and Palestine. Their dwellings were the route of the Quraysh to the lands of al-Sham. God said: ﴿And indeed, it is on a road that remains﴾ [al-Hijr: 76], and He said: ﴿And indeed, you pass by them in the morning﴾ [as-Saffat: 137] ﴿and at night. Will you not reason?﴾ [as-Saffat: 138].

The adverbial clause of (إذْ) is connected to (أرْسَلْنا) or to the suppressed (اذْكُرْ), both estimated.

The interrogative in (أتَأْتُونَ) is for denial (inkārī).

The clause (وأنْتُمْ تُبْصِرُونَ) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) adding to the censure, meaning: you do this openly, so that some of you see others. Openly displaying disobedience is itself disobedience, because it indicates approval of it, and that is contempt for the prohibitions.

His saying (أيِنَّكم لَتَأْتُونَ) was mentioned in al-Aʿraf as (إنَّكم لَتَأْتُونَ). Here the interrogative for denial is used, whereas in al-Aʿraf the declarative used for denial is used. It is possible that the difference in reporting is due to the difference in what is reported, such that Lot said both statements to them in two different situations. It is also possible that the difference in reporting is for variety (tafannun) while the meaning is the same. Both styles occur in the Qur'anic stories, because changing the style renews the listener's attentiveness.

Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza, and Abu Bakr on the authority of ʿAsim recited what is in Surah al-Aʿraf with two hamzas, so the two verses are equal in the recitation of these. The aspects of this were mentioned earlier in Surah al-Aʿraf.

In al-Aʿraf occurs ﴿Do you commit the foul deed that no one in the worlds has preceded you in?﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 80], which is not mentioned here, because what happens in the story does not require mentioning all of it. Likewise the statement about not mentioning (وأنْتُمْ تُبْصِرُونَ) in Surah al-Aʿraf, while it is mentioned here.

The rest of the verse is parallel to what came earlier in Surah al-Aʿraf, except that what occurs here is (بَلْ أنْتُمْ قَوْمٌ تَجْهَلُونَ), so He described them with ignorance (jahāla), which is a comprehensive term for the states of corrupt judgment and hardness of heart.

In al-Aʿraf He described them as a people who are ﴿transgressors﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 81], and this is to be understood as a difference of the two statements in two situations.

The insertion of the word (قَوْمٍ) in the two verses has the particularity mentioned earlier in His saying in this surah: ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who know﴾ [an-Naml: 52].

In His saying (تَجْهَلُونَ), the address (khiṭāb) was preferred over the third person (ghayba), so He did not say (يَجْهَلُونَ) with the ya' of the third person, though both fit the apparent meaning, because address is stronger in indication, as is recited in His saying: ﴿Rather, you are a people who are being tested﴾ [an-Naml: 47].

Page 5
﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said, "Expel the family of Lot from your township. Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure."﴾ ﴿So We saved him and his family, except his wife; We had decreed her to be among those who remained behind.﴾ ﴿And We rained upon them a rain, and evil was the rain of those who were warned.﴾

The parallel of this verse has occurred in Surat al-A'raf, and this one differs from it in the use of the conjunction "fa" (so) in His saying "fa ma kana jawaba qawmihi" instead of "wa" (and); in His saying "akhrijuu aala Lut" (expel the family of Lot) instead of "akhrijuhum" (expel them); in His saying "qaddarnaha" (We had decreed her) instead of "kanat" (she was); and in His saying "fa saa'a matharu al-mundhirin" (evil was the rain of those who were warned) instead of "fa-nzur kayfa kana 'aqibatu al-mujrimin" (so see how was the end of the criminals).

As for the position of the "fa" here, it is for the sequencing of the sentence joined by "fa" to the one before it, as the sequencing of a part of the story after its beginning. It therefore conveys only the sequencing of the report, and in that respect it is equivalent to "wa". However, the particle of sequencing was preferred in this verse because it follows the pattern in which the story of Thamud was related in His saying, "fa-idha hum fariqani yakhtasimun" (and behold, they were two parties disputing). The difference between this verse and the verse of al-A'raf is therefore a variation in the narration and an observance of the parallel in construction. This is among the styles of the Qur'anic narratives, as I have explained in the seventh introduction to this tafsir.

Likewise His saying "akhrijuu aala Lut" instead of "akhrijuhum": because what is related of the people's speech is their conspiring to expel the family of Lot. So what is here is a narration with the synonymous wording of their speech, while what is in al-A'raf is a narration by meaning, and the purpose is also variation.

Likewise the difference between "qaddarnaha" here and "kanat" in al-A'raf.

Page 6

The intended meaning of "aala Lut" is Lut and the people of his household, because the head of the household is considered in this reasoning, as in His saying, "Admit the family of Pharaoh to the severest punishment," meaning Pharaoh and his household.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr (al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr) on Sūrah 27, verse 59:**

﴿Say: "All praise is for Allah, and peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen."﴾

When the purpose of taking lessons and warning (i‘tibar wa-l-inḏar) had been fully served by mentioning the outcomes of some nations that denied their messengers, nations whose circumstances most resemble those of the deniers of Muḥammad (ﷺ) and of the Book revealed to him, and while, within and alongside that, there was consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) for what he met from his people, Allah turned the address to the Messenger (ﷺ), instructing him what to say after the stories and admonitions that preceded, drawing conclusions and inferences from them and giving thanks to Allah for their purpose.

So the statement is a resumption (isti’nāf), and the connection is as you know. The Messenger was commanded to praise Allah for what the preceding stories contained: the deliverance of the messengers from the punishment that befell their peoples, the victory and elevation of ranks that Allah granted them in return for their patience, and the destruction of the wrongdoing enemies, as in His saying ﴿So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ (6:45). Its parallel is His saying in Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt ﴿Say: "Praise be to Allah." But most of them do not reason.﴾ (29:63), and His saying at the end of this surah ﴿And say: "Praise be to Allah. He will show you His signs, and you will recognize them."﴾ (27:93). So the Messenger (ﷺ) was commanded to praise Allah for that, in view of what the recounting of those stories implied of a promise to the Messenger (ﷺ) of victory over his enemies. Thus His saying ﴿Say: "All praise is for Allah"﴾ is a command to the Messenger (ﷺ) to bring forth the praise of Allah. The form of praise (al-ḥamd) was already discussed at the beginning of al-Fātiḥah.

Coordinated with what he was commanded to say of praise is a command to follow it with peace (salām) upon the messengers who came before him, in proportion to the measure of what they bore in spreading the true religion.

The origin of "salām" is "sallamtu salāman" (I greeted with peace), with the intended meaning being an act of speech (inshā’), so the verb was omitted and its absolute object (maf‘ūl muṭlaq) was put in its place. He moved from the accusative of the absolute object to making it a nominative subject (mubtada’) to indicate permanence and continuance, as was discussed earlier at His saying "al-ḥamdu lillāh" at the beginning of Sūrat al-Fātiḥah.

Salām, in origin, is a noun that one says to the one he meets, with the wording: "Salāmun ‘alayka" or "as-salāmu ‘alayka." Its meaning is safety and firm security for you, without any withdrawal from it, because of the figurative elevation (isti‘lā’) implied by "ʿalā," the intended sense being establishment (tamakkun), as in ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord.﴾ (2:5).

The essential purpose of it is reassurance (ta’mīn) at the time of meeting, since there may be enmity between those who meet, or one of them may be inciting against the other. Thus the phrase "as-salāmu ‘alayka" was like a pledge of safety. Then, when opening with it came to indicate the initiation of honour, gentleness at the meeting, the intention of help and hospitality, the expression "as-salāmu ‘alayka" and the like became common when intending to express gentleness and honour, and its meaning of granting safety and security was forgotten. People began to say it in places where there is no suspicion or fear, and it spread among the Arabs in their quarters and homes, and became like a supplication, which is an expression of wishing well for the one greeted, for his safety in life. Therefore the Exalted said ﴿So when you enter houses, greet one another with a greeting from Allah, blessed and good﴾ (24:61), as was discussed in Sūrat al-Nūr. The saying "as-salām" became equivalent to the saying "ḥayyāka Allāh" (may Allah grant you life), but they reserved the expression "ḥayyāka Allāh" for their kings and great ones, and the expression "as-salāmu ‘alaykum" passed, by this, to another stage of its usage since the era of pre-Islamic ignorance (al-jāhiliyyah). It has been said that it was a greeting for humankind since the time of Ādam.

Then the Qur’ān mentioned peace from Allah, the Exalted, in the sense of it being a dealing from Him, glorified is He, with the honour of praise and good remembrance for those among His servants with whom Allah is pleased in this world, as in His saying, relating from ʿĪsā when He made him speak: ﴿And peace is upon me the day I was born, the day I die, and the day I am raised alive.﴾ (19:33). Likewise in the Hereafter and what is in its meaning of the states of souls after death, as in His saying about ʿĪsā: ﴿And the day I am raised alive﴾ (19:33), and His saying about the people of Paradise: ﴿For them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they call for. Peace, a word from a Lord, Merciful.﴾ (36:57–58).

[p. 8]
The Qur’ān mentioned peace upon five of the prophets in Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt. Also, Allah commanded the community to send peace upon its Messenger, saying ﴿O you who have believed, invoke blessings upon him and greet him with peace (taslīm)﴾ (33:56), that is, say: "Peace be upon you, O Prophet," because the root of the form taf‘īl is sometimes used to indicate a coined utterance in the form taf‘īl. So His saying "sallimū taslīman" means: say the word "salām," like "basmala" when one says "bismillāh," and "kabbara" when one says "Allāhu akbar." In the hadith: «You glorify (Allah), praise Him, and magnify Him after every prayer thirty-three times.»

The meaning of ﴿and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen﴾ is the enactment of a request from Allah that He grant peace upon one of the chosen ones, that is, that He make for them a good remembrance in the exalted assembly (al-malaʾ al-aʿlā).

When someone says "as-salāmu ‘alā fulān" and Fulān is absent or in the status of an absent person, that is an indication that what is intended is supplication for him, that Allah send peace upon him. In that case the meaning of greeting is necessarily removed from it and it becomes specific to supplication. For this reason, «the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade the Muslims, in the tashahhud, to say: "As-salāmu ‘alā Allāh, as-salāmu ‘alā al-nabī, as-salāmu ‘alā fulān wa-fulān." He said to them: "Indeed Allah is al-Salām."» That is, there is no sense in "peace upon Allah" in the context of supplication, because Allah is the One being asked that peace be granted upon whomever is sought for that.

So when the Exalted commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) in this surah to say ﴿peace upon His servants whom He has chosen﴾, He specified this sentence for him to say, asking Allah to honour His servants whom He has chosen with praise in the exalted assembly and good remembrance, since the utmost that the one present can do as a reward to the absent for his good deeds is to supplicate earnestly to Allah that He breathe honour upon him.

The servants whom Allah has chosen are led by the messengers and prophets, and this includes the righteous among His servants, as in the wording of the tashahhud: («Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah»). The discussion of greeting the Prophet (ﷺ) will come in Sūrat al-Aḥzāb.

* * *

﴿Is Allah better, or what they associate?﴾ This is among what the Messenger (upon him be blessings and peace) was commanded to say. So he was commanded to say: "All praise is for Allah, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen," as a preface to His saying "Is Allah better, or what they associate?"

[p. 9]
Because the servants whom Allah has chosen all brought the essential content of this sentence. He was commanded to begin the argument in the hearing of the polytheists, saying this to them, as indicated by His saying "what they associate," with the address form in the reading of the majority (tushrikūna, with the tā’ of address). The question also fits best as directed at those who associated with Allah what does not create, does not provide sustenance, does not bestow blessings, and does not answer supplication. So this is not intended to establish monotheism for the Muslims.

The interrogative is used for compelling and obliging the addressee to acknowledge the truth and alerting him to his error. This is a general (ijmālī) proof, intended as the beginning of reflection (naẓar) in establishing divinity and worship. This is of the kind that al-Bāqillānī, Imām al-Ḥaramayn, and Ibn Fūrak said: that the first of the obligations is the first reflection, or the intention to reflect, and then the detailed proofs come after it. Its generality matches the fact that it is a comprehensive proof for the details that follow, so for this reason the name that gathers the meanings of all the attributes was used in it, which is the name of majesty (ism al-jalālah), Allah. So it was said: "Is Allah better?" And afterwards the relative pronoun was used, for the attributes contained in its relative clauses.

"Khayr" came in the comparative form, intending to go along with their belief that their idols were partners of Allah in divinity, such that they had a generous share of good in their own estimation. So He expressed it with "khayr" to give the impression that the context is to show the superiority of Allah's divinity over their idols, as a way of drawing them on, alerting them to the error, while mocking them, since they preferred the worship of idols over the worship of Allah. A sensible person does not prefer one thing over another except for a motive that calls him to prefer it. So in this question about the better in goodness there is an alert to them of the extreme error and the ruinous ignorance, so that their insight may be opened to the truth, if they intend guidance. The meaning is: "Is Allah the one deserving of divinity, or what you associate with Him?"

The interrogative is in its literal sense, as shown by the presence of "am" (or), which balances the hamzah, since mockery is built upon literal usage.

This statement serves as a preface to all the proofs that come after, based on this general proof, as you will know.

The majority read "tushrikūna" with the tā’ of address. Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim and Yaʿqūb read it with the yā’ of the third person,

[p. 10]
so the statement that the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to say is reported in meaning, and in it the third-person form of the polytheists was observed within the context of the address of the command.

"Mā" is a relative pronoun and the returning pronoun is omitted. The estimated sense is: "what they associate it with," that is, what they associate with Him (of partners), namely your idols.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 60:

﴿Is He not best who created the heavens and the earth and sent down for you water from the sky, and We caused to grow thereby gardens of delight? It was not for you to cause their trees to grow. Is there a god with Allah? Rather, they are a people who ascribe equals (to Him).﴾

"Am" here is disjunctive, meaning "bal" (rather), for a transitional turn (idrab intiqali) from one purpose to another, while preserving the sense or wording of the interrogative after it, because "am" never departs from the meaning of interrogation. By this turn he moved from the real, sarcastic interrogation to the affirmative interrogation (istifham taqriri), and from the general introduction, which is His words "﴿Is Allah better, or what they associate (with Him)?﴾ [al-Naml: 59]", to the intended purpose, which is argumentation. Allah enumerated the good things and benefits as effects of His mercy and of His power. It is therefore an argument mixed with favour, for He reminded them of the creation of the heavens and the earth, which encompasses all the creatures the earth contains, of humans and of animals. It is thus a favour through the blessing of their origination and the origination of what sustains their affairs in life, and through His prior mercy. He enumerated these on them in another place with His words: ﴿Allah is He who created you, then provided for you, then causes you to die, then gives you life. Is there any of your partners who does anything of that? Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate.﴾ [al-Rum: 40].

"Man" is interrogative. It is the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate (khabar) is the clause "khalaqa al-samawat..." etc. It is an affirmative interrogation that Allah is the one God without partner, and there is no omitted element in the sentence. Al-Zamakhshari and all who followed him held that "man" is a relative pronoun (mawsula), that its predicate is omitted, indicated by his words earlier "Is Allah better", and that after "am" there is an omitted interrogative hamza, the full sense being: "Rather, is He who created the heavens etc. better, or what you associate?" This is an interpretation for which there is no need, and it does not fit the meaning of the turn (idrab), because it would then be within the first purpose as he explained it in the Kashshaf, and so the turn of transition would not be appropriate.

So the interrogation is affirmative, as indicated by his words at its end, "Is there a god with Allah?", which is affirmative, to establish that the Creator, the One who causes growth, and the Provider is Allah. It is mixed with rebuke, and therefore he appended it with "Rather, they are a people who ascribe equals," as will come, that is, from the purpose of the general proof to the detailed one.

The address with "lakum" is directed to the polytheists, as a reproach that they did not thank Allah's blessing.

He mentioned the sending down of water because it is among what Allah created, and to cut off the doubt that they might say: the one who causes the tree that is our provision to grow is the water, deceived by the means. So they were promptly reminded that Allah created the means and is the Creator of the effects, by removing the obstacles and hindrances that stand against the influence of the means, by providing the powers present in the means, and by determining the measures suitable for benefiting from the means. For He may send down water in excess, so that it sweeps away the crops and trees or destroys them. For this reason He combined "We sent down" with "so We caused to grow," as an alert to removing the doubt.

The plural nun in "anbatna" is a shift (iltifat) from the third person to the first person. Among its subtleties here is the specification that the intended meaning is ascribing the causing of growth to Him, lest the pronoun of the absent one be taken as referring to the water; for reminding them of the true Causer of growth, who created the means, is more fitting to the context of rebuking them for not heeding His blessings.

"Al-inbat" means the producing of vegetation (takwin al-nabat).

"Al-hada'iq" is the plural of "hadiqa," which is an orchard, a garden containing palm trees and grapevines. It was called "hadiqa" because they used to enclose it with a wall that prevents anyone from entering it, to guard the grapes, since it is not like the palm, whose fruit is hard to pick because its trees are tall. Thus it means "surrounded by (a wall)." The word "hadiqa" is not applied except to this.

"Al-bahja" is the beauty of the sight, because the beholder rejoices in it.

The meaning of "ma kana lakum an tunbitu shajaraha" is: it is not within your possession to cause the trees of those gardens to grow. So the lam in "lakum" indicates ownership, and "an tunbitu" is the subject (ism) of "kana," and "lakum" is its predicate (khabar). He placed the predicate before the subject for emphasis on negating the ownership of that.

The clause "a-ilahun ma'a Allah" is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), which is like the conclusion of the preceding clause, because establishing the creation, provision, and bestowal to Allah, by a proof that leaves them no choice but to acknowledge it, yields that there is no god with Him.

The interrogation is denial (inkari). "Bal" is for turning away from the denying interrogation, and conveys the meaning of "lakin" (but), in view of what the denial contained of the negation that there could be a god with Allah. So the right thing for people was not to associate with Him any other in divinity, and so the contrary was brought by the exceptive turn, because those addressed by His words "and sent down for you" and His words "It was not for you to cause their trees to grow" did not benefit from the proof, though it is a clear and manifest proof. So they are stubborn in turning away from being guided by this proof. They "ya'dilun" (ascribe equals) to Allah others, that is, they make others equal to Him in divinity, though the other is incapable of that; so "ya'dilun" comes from "adala" which is transitive with "bi" (to make equal with), or "ya'dilun 'an al-haqq" (turn away from the truth), from "adala" which is transitive with "'an."

Some Arabs were asked about al-Hajjaj, and he said: "Qasit 'adil" (an unjust one who is also just). They understood it as praise of him, and his saying reached al-Hajjaj, who said: "He meant His words, Exalted is He: ﴿As for the unjust (qasitun), they will be fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Jinn: 15]." That is, this is an indication that the intended meaning of "'adil" is that he deviates from the truth.

Whatever the case, the intent is to rebuke them for associating partners with Allah, despite the clarity of the indication of the creation of the heavens and the earth and of what descends from the sky to the earth of water.

Since that indication is the clearest of the sensible indications pointing to Allah's sole creation, He described those who associate others with Him as, in their association, turning away with stubborn aversion, deviating from the clear truth. Allah says: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "Allah"﴾ [Luqman: 25]. The reporting of them in the present tense indicates that they persist in their polytheism, not enlightened by the proof of reason, nor have they desisted after the reminder of the signs. And in reporting of them that they are "a people" there is an allusion to the deep-rootedness of the attribute of deviating from the truth among them, so much so that it is as if it were one of the constituents of their peoplehood, as has been mentioned more than once before.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 61:

﴿Is He who made the earth a stable abode, and made rivers within it, and made for it firm mountains, and made between the two seas a barrier? Is there a god with Allah? Rather, most of them do not know.﴾ (Am) is for a transitional disengagement (idrab intiqali), like its sister mentioned earlier. This is a transition from argument mixed with favour (imtinan) to pure argument from the signs of His power and knowledge: that He created the great creatures and governs their order, so that none of them overpowers another and the order of all would be disrupted.

Because the purpose of this argument is to establish the greatness of power and the wisdom of workmanship, no address to the polytheists occurs within it, as occurred in His saying in the verse before it, ﴿and sent down for you water from the sky﴾, etc. Although this wondrous workmanship is not free of kindness toward the creatures, which its Creator intended, that is not the primary aim in presenting the proof here.

Al-qarar (translated as "stable abode"): the verbal noun of qarra, meaning to be settled and still. He described the earth with it for emphasis, i.e., it is a place of qarar. The meaning is that He made the earth firm, steady, not agitated. This is a marvellous arrangement, and the full extent of this wondrous workmanship is grasped only by knowing that this earth floats in the air, moving at every instant, yet it appears stable to its inhabitants. This is a more wondrous arrangement, and in it is mercy and blessing. Were it not for its stability, people upon it would be unsteady and agitated, and their affairs would be troubled for them.

Along with making it stable, He cleft rivers through it, making them khilal (within it). The khilal of a thing is the open space between its parts. Rivers cut the earth into trenches, and the earth flows within them.

Al-rawasi: the mountains, plural of rasin, which means firm. The lam in "laha" is the lam of cause, i.e., the mountains are for its sake, that is, for its benefit, for in the formation of mountains is wisdom in averting contact from the earth so that its movement through the atmospheric sphere is moderated, not excessively swift, and thereby its movement endures.

Making the barrier between the two seas is among the marvels of wisdom. It is a non-material barrier resulting from the repulsion of each of the two waters from the other, so that they do not mix, due to the difference in relative weight arising from the differing components of which salt water and sweet water are composed. Thus the barrier is one arising from their very natures, not a separate body dividing them, and this was mentioned in Surat al-Nahl.

This act of making is also a metaphor for creating the two seas, since the separation between them necessitates their creation and the creation of saltiness and sweetness in them.

Then he concluded with the rhetorical question of denial and with a supplementary clause similar to that with which the argument before it was concluded, in the manner of repetition, enumerating the denial and preparing for the rebuke in His saying, "Rather, most of them do not know." The negation of the attribute of knowledge is applied here to most of the polytheists because few of them reflect on the finer details of these created things and their properties; for habitual observation of them from the first beginning of the observer distracts him from what they contain of the signs of wondrous workmanship. Most polytheists are ignorant of this and are not guided by what it contains. As for the believers, the Qur'an has alerted them to this, so they read its verses, in which argument and reflection are repeatedly found.

These proofs are not free of a blessing behind them, as you have learned just now, but they are presented here for the purpose of argument, not for favour.

The argument rose from reminding them of God's lordly control over the essences of created beings to reminding them of His control over the circumstances of people, which no one is free of in some aspects of life. These are the state of need for attaining good, the state of being visited by harm, and the state of exercising dominion over the earth and its benefits. These are thus three kinds of human states: the state of need (ihtiyaj), the state of distress (bu's), and the state of benefit (intifa').

The first is contained in His words: ﴿Is not He who answers the distressed one when he calls upon Him﴾. The mudtarr (the one in dire necessity, ḍarūrah) is the person in a state of necessity that compels him toward things that are hard to obtain. This is the rank of the ḥājiyyāt (the needs, i.e. what is required to avert hardship). A person needs many things by which his livelihood is sustained, which are not inherent in his own essence, such as food, marriage, and necessary clothing. A person seeks these through his existence, through exchanges, and some of them may be difficult, and they become more difficult in proportion to the abundance of their benefits and the rarity of their attainment, so he asks God to give them to him.

Al-iḍṭirār is an iftiʿāl (reflexive form) derived from al-ḍarūrah, not from al-ḍurr. Its meaning is: necessity overtook him and he submitted to it. It has no simple (mujarrad) verb form; rather, one says iḍṭarrahu kadhā ilā kadhā (it compelled him to such-and-such).

The lam in al-mudtarr is for defining the genus, which is called the lam of mental prior reference (al-ʿahd al-dhihnī), meaning: He answers an individual known in the mind as being in the state of necessity.

Page 15
And al-ijābah is giving the thing requested. The meaning is: when the one in necessity calls upon Him to attain what he is compelled toward, none answers him except God, regardless of whether He answers some and delays others.

The state of distress is indicated by His words: ﴿and removes the harm﴾.

Al-kashf (removal) originally means lifting a covering. The harm that befalls the one afflicted is likened to a covering that stands between a person and finding the way to deliverance, a comparison of an intelligible to a sensible thing. The thing likened-to (al-mushabbah bih) is indicated by the kashf, which is among the attributes that accompany the covering. It is also used figuratively for removal, by the indicator of its being transitive to al-sū' (harm). The meaning: who removes the harm. This is the rank of the ḍarūriyyāt (the essentials), for most or all of it is the preservation against harm reaching the important affairs of people, such as the universals (al-kulliyyāt), namely: the preservation of religion, life, intellect, lineage, and honour.

The meaning is: God removes harm from the one who is harmed when he calls upon Him too. So it was omitted from the conjoined clause because of what was mentioned with the preceding clause; that is, He removes harm from the one who is troubled when He is called upon.

The apparent restriction by the temporal adverb ("when he calls") implies a guarantee of answer. In reality, answering is subject to God's will, according to what the state of the supplicant requires and what its opposing principles from other foundations require, and God knows best.

The state of benefit is indicated by His words: ﴿and makes you successors of the earth﴾, that is, He makes you cultivate the earth and gather its benefits. He included in khulafāʾ (successors) the meaning of possessors, so it was attached to the earth with the implied sense: possessors of it. Ownership entails benefiting from what is beneficial in it. The word khulafāʾ implicitly conveys the meaning of inheritance from those who preceded, for every living being is a successor to its predecessor. A nation is a successor to a nation that was before it, generation after generation. This is like His words, quoting Noah: ﴿He produced you from the earth and made you inhabit it﴾ [Hud: 61]. This is the rank of the taḥsīniyyāt (the embellishments).

The verse has gathered an indication of the ranks of the munāsib (what brings benefit or repels harm), which is one of the paths of ʿillah (effective cause) in the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh).

Because succession entails the renewal of children after parents and generation after generation, and what responding and removing harm entail from the multitude of those calling and those troubled, the verb forms of making (al-jaʿl) to which this relates were expressed in the present tense, which indicates renewal, unlike the four verbs of making in the verse before it.

Then, after this argument, a rhetorical interrogative of denial was resumed, repeating what came after the earlier proofs, to add to the enumeration of their error, with His words: ﴿Is there a god with God? Little do you remember.﴾

"Qalīlan" is in the accusative of state (ḥāl) from the pronoun of address in ﴿and makes you successors﴾, that is, He did that for you while you are in a state of little remembrance. Thus the state conveys the sense of wonder at their condition.

Al-tadhakkur is from al-dhikr (with a dammah on the dhāl), which is the opposite of forgetfulness; it is the summoning of what is known, meaning: little is your summoning of your need for God and of the bounty of His favour upon you, so that you would be guided that He is worthy of not associating anything with Him. So the intended sense of remembrance is that which yields a proof. "Mā" is a verbal-masdarising particle (maṣdariyyah), and the verbal noun is the agent of "qalīlan." The "little" here is used as a euphemism for nonexistence, because the intended remembrance is absent from them, and using "little" to mean "nonexistent" is established in their speech. This euphemism is an allusion and an indirect reproach, meaning: if you do remember, your remembrance is little.

The original form of tadhakkarūn was tatadhakkarūn; the tāʾ of the taʿfīl pattern was assimilated into the dhāl because their articulation points are close, for lightness. This is an assimilation known only by transmission (samāʿī).

Al-Jumhur read "tadhakkarūn" with the tāʾ of address. Rawḥ from Abū ʿAmr and Hishām from Ibn ʿĀmir read it with the yāʾ of the third person, as an iltifāt (shift) from address to the third person. In the reading of the majority there is the nuance of directing the address to the polytheists, confronting them; in the reading of Rawḥ and Hishām there is the nuance of turning away from them, because they deserved to be turned away from after having been reminded.

[p. 17]

(*Bal*) is for the transition (*idrab al-intiqal*, a shift to a new line of argument) from the type of evidence drawn from the general dealings of God with people, to the type of evidence drawn from His dealings with travellers among them, on land and at sea. They know these circumstances better, and they are better placed to appreciate what they contain of blessing and favour.

Mention of guidance in the darknesses of night, on land and at sea. The idafa of "darknesses" to "land" and "sea" carries the sense of "in" (*fi*). The guidance in these darknesses is through the movement of the stars, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And it is He who placed the stars for you, that you may be guided by them in the darknesses of land and sea﴾ [al-An'am: 97]. God is therefore the Guide for travel through those darknesses, in that He created the stars in an orderly arrangement suitable for guidance in this, and in that He equipped people with faculties to know them by observing their course, their rising and their setting. He also guided them by the directions of the winds, and enabled them to know their variation by sensing their dryness and moisture, their heat and their cold.

On this occasion, the favour of the winds' benefits is incorporated (*udmija*) into the mention of their stirring up the clouds, which bring the rain, and which is what is meant by God's mercy. His sending the winds is the creation of the causes of their formation.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read (*nushuran*) with two *dammas* and a *nun*. Ibn 'Amir read it with a *damma* and then a *sukun*. Asim read "*bushran*" with a *ba'* and a *sukun* on the *shin*, with *tanwin* (nunation). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a *fatha* on the *nun* and a *sukun* on the *shin*. This has already been discussed in Surat al-Furqan (﴿And it is He who sends the winds as good tidings before His mercy﴾ [al-Furqan: 48]) and in Surat al-A'raf (﴿And it is He who sends the winds as good tidings before His mercy﴾ [al-A'raf: 57]), and the justification for these readings is given there.

This evidence is concluded with the glorification of God, exalted is He, above their associating other gods with Him, because this is the final element (*khatimat*) of the argument against them with what they do not dispute is among God's dealings. Therefore, after it, comes the declaration of His transcendence above all partnership, and this is an explicit statement of what the preceding concluding statements (*tadhyilat*) had alluded to.

[Page 18]

This is a transition to the argument from God's disposal (*tasarruf*) over the first life and the second life, and over His granting of sustenance (*madad*) that sustains the first life for a determined term. It also contains a reminder of the blessing of origination (*ni'mat al-ijad*) and the blessing of provision (*ni'mat al-imdad*). The interrogation is *taqriri* (a question that asserts what the listener must admit), because they do not deny that He originates creation and that He provides for them.

Within the interrogation, His saying ﴿then repeats it﴾ is embedded (*udmija*). This is because accepting that He originates creation compels them to understand the possibility of the re-creation (*i'adat al-khalq*) that they had deemed impossible. Since the re-creation was a matter of dispute, and embedding it serves as an awakening and a reminder, the interrogation is repeated in the clause joined to it by His saying ﴿and who provides for you from the heaven and the earth﴾. Also, because provision is concomitant with the beginning of creation, if it had been conjoined to the re-creation, one might have assumed that He provides for creation after the re-creation, and they would then suppose that their provision in this world is among the blessings of their gods.

Since they denied resurrection (*al-ba'th*), the verse is concluded with a command of challenge (*ta'jiz*) to produce a proof (*burhan*) for the non-occurrence of resurrection.

The *burhan* means the argument or evidence (*al-hujjah*). Its discussion appeared earlier, at His saying ﴿O mankind, there has certainly come to you a proof from your Lord﴾ [4:174], at the end of Surat al-Nisa'.

The attribution of the *burhan* to the pronoun of the addressees, who are the polytheists, indicates that the proof they are challenged to produce is the proof of the non-occurrence of resurrection. That is: "If you are truthful, then produce it." This is because the truthful one is the one whose statement corresponds to reality, and a reality that exists does not lack a proof for it.

The sum of what has preceded in these verses, from His saying ﴿Is Allah better, or what you associate [with Him]?﴾ [27:59], is that they first summarized the argument for the sole entitlement of Allah to divinity, then detailed that with verses from ﴿Who created the heavens and the earth﴾ up to His saying ﴿Say: Produce your proof, if you are truthful.﴾ They began with a near proof, close to the proof of direct observation (*burhan al-mushahadah*), which is the creation of the heavens and the earth and what comes forth from them of good for mankind. Then there is the proof of how the terrestrial sphere was created and what is upon its surface, and this is attached to the observables.

Then it moved to an argument of the kind of established principles (*al-usul al-mawdu'ah*), which is what people agree upon concerning their turning to Allah, exalted is He, when they are in distress.

Then it moved to the argument against them by what He enabled them with of disposal over the earth, when He made mankind vicegerents (*khulafa'*) on the earth and subjected to them the disposal through the various means that assist this vicegerency. These are the establishment of their guidance on land and sea. That comprises the foundations of the dispositions of vicegerency mentioned in travel, trade and military expedition.

All of this was completed with a comprehensive expression that combines the two blessings of origination and provision, and within its folds are the comprehensive elements of the empowerment upon the earth.

I'll translate the passage as instructed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verses 65–66 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah. And they do not perceive when they will be resurrected.﴾ ﴿Rather, their knowledge has caught up regarding the Hereafter. Rather, they are in doubt about it. Rather, they are blind to it.﴾

When the preceding verses nullified the divinity of the idols of the polytheists with converging proofs, and the root of the belief in associationism was cut off, the reins of refutation were turned toward one of the traces of shirk, namely the claim to knowledge of the unseen through soothsaying (kahana) and information from the jinn, as the soothsayers (kuhhan), diviners ('arrafun) and custodians of the idols (sadanat al-asnam) used to claim. The polytheists believe in this. In Ma'alim al-Tanzil and elsewhere it is reported that the verse was revealed concerning the polytheists when they asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the time of the Hour. Their question was only due to their supposition that claiming knowledge of its time is among the matters of prophethood, as a means to deny prophethood if he did not specify for them the time of the Hour. So the verse nullified these allegations with a general nullification, whose criterion is the exception in His saying ﴿except Allah﴾. It is general, but intended to be specific, namely specific to the soothsayers and custodians of the idol houses. He took the path of generality only to nullify whatever might be claimed of that, and because generality is more beneficial and more concise, since that is the condition of the polytheists among those in the heavens and the earth. So the aim here is to discredit the traces of shirk, which are soothsaying and the like. Since created beings are none other than the inhabitants of the heavens or the inhabitants of the earth, because the worlds of existents are confined to that, His saying ﴿None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen﴾ is in effect "No one knows the unseen," but the speech has been elaborated for the purpose of explicitly stating the generalization over all created beings, for the station of the knowledge of creed is a station of exposition to which elaboration is suited.

The exception ﴿except Allah﴾ from it is by interpreting "those in the heavens and the earth" as meaning "anyone," so it is a connected exception according to the verifying scholars, and it occurs in a negated statement. Therefore the excepted term ought to be a substitute (badal) for the term excepted from, in the eloquent language, and so the name of Allah came in the nominative. Had the exception been disconnected, the eloquent language would have put the excepted term in the accusative.

Moreover, the proofs of the transcendence of Allah above indwelling in place and above resemblance to created beings are abundant, and therefore the usage of the Qur'an and the Sunnah proceeds according to the patterns of eloquent usage, knowing that the believer does not imagine what is unfitting to the majesty of Allah the Exalted. Among the exegetes is one who made the exception disconnected, adhering to the apparent sense of the relative clause "those in the heavens and the earth," because Allah is exalted above indwelling in the heavens and the earth.

As for one upon whom Allah bestows favour by making him aware of the unseen, that is included in the knowledge of Allah. He the Exalted said: ﴿the Knower of the unseen, so He does not reveal His unseen to anyone except whom He has approved of from a messenger﴾. So He attributed "unseen" to the pronoun of majesty.

He followed this report with the incidental inclusion that these claimants to knowledge of the unseen do not perceive the time of their resurrection; rather, they denied its occurrence, in order to stir the reminder of the resurrection, given the intense concern of the Qur'an to establish it and its ridicule of those who denied it. This is the position of His saying ﴿and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected﴾, meaning: those who claim knowledge of the unseen do not perceive the time of their resurrection.

"Ayyan" is an interrogative noun of time, and it is the suspending (ta'liq) of the verb "yash'urun" from acting upon its two objects. This is a rebuke and censure of the polytheists, for they do not believe in resurrection, let alone perceive its time.

"Bal" here is for the transitional turning away (idrab intiqali) from the report about them, "they do not perceive when they will be resurrected," to an ascent to something more remarkable and more intense in ascent than rebuking them for not perceiving the time of their resurrection, namely describing their knowledge of the Hereafter, of which resurrection is the first of its conditions and the intermediary between it and this world, as being a knowledge that has "caught up" (mutadarak) or "is attained" (mudrak).

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read ﴿idarak﴾ (the majority reading is "idarak") ... [Note: the Arabic text reads: "وقَرَأ الجُمْهُورُ ادّارَكَ" — the majority reading is ادّارَك.]

By this you know that the expression "those who disbelieve" (alladhina kafaru) here is not an instance of using a full noun in place of a pronoun where a pronoun would have been expected; because "those who disbelieve" is more general in its application than the referent of "whoever is in the heavens and the earth" in His saying, "none in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verses 67–68:

﴿And those who disbelieve say: "When we have become dust, and our fathers, shall we really be brought forth?"﴾ ﴿"We have certainly been promised this, we and our fathers before. This is nothing but the fables of the ancients."﴾

He follows the description of the blindness of those who claim knowledge of the Unseen with the mention of their doubt, which made resurrection appear impossible to occur. For this reason he attributed the statement here to all those who disbelieved, rather than specifically to those who claim knowledge of the Unseen. For this reason the sentence is conjoined (by waw), because it differs from the one before it in being more general.

The expression of them by the relative noun (alladhina kafaru, "those who disbelieved") is because of the allusion within the relative clause to the cause of their saying this statement, namely what the relative clause conveys of their being disbelievers. It is as if it were said: "They said, in their disbelief: 'When we have become dust...' to its end," in the form of an interrogation meaning denial.

They expressed the denial in the form of a question in order to show the ignorance of the one who holds this belief and to render him incapable of an answer in their own view. The emphasis by "inna" (verily) is to match the speech of the one being refuted with denial. And the emphasis is mocking.

Page 25
Nafi' and Abu Ja'far read (﴿idha kunna turaban﴾) with a single hamza, which is the hamza of (idha), on the assumption of an elided interrogative hamza for lightening, to avoid the meeting of two hamzas; or by making (idha) an adverbial complement placed before its governing verb, while the thing being questioned about is (inna lamukhrajun, "that we shall indeed be brought forth").
Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Hamza read with two hamzas in "a-idha" and "a-innana," on the basis that the interrogative hamza is repeated in the second for emphasis of the first. However, Abu 'Amr lightened the second of the two hamzas in both places, while 'Asim and Hamza made them clear (full). All of these omitted the first-person nun after the nun of (inna). Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read (a-idha) with two hamzas and (innana) with a single hamza and two nuns, relying on the first hamza as the interrogative; all of these are eloquent usages.

This same statement, reported of those who disbelieved, has already been mentioned in Surah al-Mu'minun, except that the first demonstrative came after "nahnu" in Surah al-Mu'minun and came before it here. Its placement before or after is equivalent in the basic meaning, since it is the second object of "wu'idna" and occurs after the deputy of the subject in both verses. The question that properly arises is about its placement before the emphatic pronoun which stands as deputy for the subject. In the Kashshaf, al-Zamakhshari answered that placement indicates that the thing placed first is the purpose intended by the mention and for the sake of which the speech is driven. Al-Sakkaki clarified in al-Miftah that what occurred in Surah al-Mu'minun was the normal order, with the object placed after the subject, which is its proper position. As for what is in Surah al-Naml, the object was placed before the subject because it is more important there. This is shown by the fact that what precedes it here is "﴿idha kunna turaban wa-aba'una﴾" and what precedes the verse in Surah al-Mu'minun is "﴿a-idha mittna wa-kunna turaban wa-'izaman﴾" (23:82). So the aspect considered there in Surah al-Mu'minun is that they themselves became dust and bones, while the aspect considered here in Surah al-Naml is that they themselves and their fathers became dust, with no part of their structure remaining in its form (bunyah, plural of binyah) — that is, remaining in the form they had while alive. There is no doubt that this is more forceful for them in making resurrection seem remote, so it required greater attention to mention it, and this incidental feature made it more important. End.

The sum of the matter is that each verse relates a style of their speech; indeed they said the same as the earlier ones said: "When we have died? We and our fathers were already promised this."

After this, there has arisen, between the wording of the two verses, a variety of expression, as was mentioned in the Seventh Introduction.

Al-asatir (the fables) is the plural of ustura, which means a story or narrative. This subject was discussed earlier at the words of God Most High, ﴿When it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?" they say, "Fables of the ancients"﴾ (16:24), in Surah al-Nahl. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verses 67–68:

﴿And those who disbelieve say: "When we have become dust, and our fathers, shall we really be brought forth?"﴾ ﴿"We have certainly been promised this, we and our fathers before. This is nothing but the fables of the ancients."﴾

He follows the description of the blindness of those who claim knowledge of the Unseen with the mention of their doubt, which made resurrection appear impossible to occur. For this reason he attributed the statement here to all those who disbelieved, rather than specifically to those who claim knowledge of the Unseen. For this reason the sentence is conjoined (by waw), because it differs from the one before it in being more general.

The expression of them by the relative noun (alladhina kafaru, "those who disbelieved") is because of the allusion within the relative clause to the cause of their saying this statement, namely what the relative clause conveys of their being disbelievers. It is as if it were said: "They said, in their disbelief: 'When we have become dust...' to its end," in the form of an interrogation meaning denial.

They expressed the denial in the form of a question in order to show the ignorance of the one who holds this belief and to render him incapable of an answer in their own view. The emphasis by "inna" (verily) is to match the speech of the one being refuted with denial. And the emphasis is mocking.

Nafi' and Abu Ja'far read (﴿idha kunna turaban﴾) with a single hamza, which is the hamza of (idha), on the assumption of an elided interrogative hamza for lightening, to avoid the meeting of two hamzas; or by making (idha) an adverbial complement placed before its governing verb, while the thing being questioned about is (inna lamukhrajun, "that we shall indeed be brought forth").
Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Hamza read with two hamzas in "a-idha" and "a-innana," on the basis that the interrogative hamza is repeated in the second for emphasis of the first. However, Abu 'Amr lightened the second of the two hamzas in both places, while 'Asim and Hamza made them clear (full). All of these omitted the first-person nun after the nun of (inna). Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read (a-idha) with two hamzas and (innana) with a single hamza and two nuns, relying on the first hamza as the interrogative; all of these are eloquent usages.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 69:

﴿Say: "Travel through the earth and observe how was the end of the criminals."﴾

The Messenger (ﷺ) was commanded to say this word to them, and for that reason the verb "qul" (say) was separated (by a full stop from what precedes it, i.e., it was given independent, unconnected phrasing). Its counterpart has already occurred in Surat al-An'am. The point of relevance in both places is admonition through the condition of those who denied, because their denial of the Resurrection is a denial of the Messenger and an act of criminality. The threat that there would befall them what befell those before them is the same in both, except that there the phrase was conjoined with "thumma" (then) in "thumma unzuru" (then observe), while here it is conjoined with the particle "fa" (so) in "fa-unzuru" (so observe). The two are interchangeable in meaning. There he mentioned "the end of the deniers," and here he mentioned "the end of the criminals," since the deniers are criminals. The variation between the two narrations is for stylistic variety, as we indicated in the Seventh Introduction.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 70:

﴿And do not grieve over them, nor be in distress because of their plotting.﴾ Mercy was predominant in the Prophet (ﷺ), and compassion for the community flowed from his very nature. When the deniers were warned with this threat, compassion stirred in the soul of the Messenger, peace be upon him, so God steadied his heart with this encouragement, that he should not grieve over them if what they had been warned of befell them. It was also part of his mercy (ﷺ) to be eager for them to desist from their denial of him and their plotting against him, so God put into his heart composure (ribatat jash) through His saying: ﴿And do not be in distress because of their plotting﴾.

Al-dayq (ضيق, distress): it is read with a fatha and with a kasra on the dad; the majority (al-Jumhur) read it with a fatha, and Ibn Kathir with a kasra. Its literal meaning is the insufficiency of a place or container for what is meant to be placed within it. Here it is a metaphor for the constricted state that comes over the soul when it dislikes something, so that a person senses within the passages of his breath a tightness like the one that has overtaken it. It is in reality a contraction in the nerves of the chest. This was already discussed at His saying ﴿and do not be in distress because of what they plot﴾ at the end of Surah al-Nahl.

The particle of place (al-zarfiyyah) is figurative, meaning: do not be encompassed or surrounded by any distress because of their plotting.

Al-makr (plotting) was discussed at His saying ﴿and they plotted, and God plotted﴾ in Surah Al 'Imran. The "ma" here is verbal (masdariyyah), meaning: because of their plotting.

﴿Those who disbelieve say, "When will this promise be fulfilled, if you are truthful?"﴾ ﴿Say, "Perhaps some of what you are hastening will have drawn close to you."﴾

It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "﴿And those who disbelieve say, 'When we have become dust...'﴾ [an-Naml: 67]." The use of the present tense here indicates the continual recurrence of that statement from them, meaning they never ceased saying it.

By "the promise" is meant what they were warned of, namely the punishment. The question concerns its time, and it is a mocking question from them, as shown by His saying "if you are truthful."

God commanded His Prophet to answer their statement, because this is among the knowledge of the unseen, which none knows except God and whomever of His chosen servants He informs of some of it.

The answer follows the wise approach (al-uslūb al-ḥakīm), by taking an interrogative in its literal sense of asking, as an alert that it is incumbent upon them to ask about the time of the festival (al-ʿīd) so that they might anticipate it through faith. ʿAsā ("perhaps") expresses hope, and it is used here to convey proximity together with certainty.

Radifa means "to follow closely." It is construed here with the preposition lām, although it can take a direct object without it, either because it is implicitly construed with the meaning of "to draw near" (iqtaraba), or because the lām is for emphasis, as in shakara lahu. The meaning is: in hope that this will be near in time. This refers to what would befall them on the day of Badr.

The object of tastaʿjilūn is omitted, meaning: "you hasten for it."
