Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 73:

﴿And indeed, your Lord is full of bounty toward mankind, but most of them do not give thanks.﴾

The placement of this verse is that of an exception (istidrak) to His saying, ﴿Perhaps some of what you seek to hasten has drawn near to you﴾; that is, the delay of the punishment for them is among the bounties of Allah upon them. This is a statement specific to the Prophet ﷺ, as an alert that the postponement of the threat is one of the effects of Allah's mercy, because the times of delay are times of respite (imhal), during which they are in a blessing; for Allah is full of bounty toward all people. We had already discussed the question of whether the disbeliever's blessing is a true blessing or not, and the disagreement on that is between al-Ash'ari and al-Maturidi.

The expression ﴿dhu fadl﴾ ("full of bounty") indicates that bounty is among His attributes. The indefiniteness of ﴿fadl﴾ ("bounty") is for magnification. The emphasis by ﴿inna﴾ ("indeed") and the lam is considered with regard to the state of people, not the state of the Prophet ﷺ; so the emphasis stands in the position of a contrast with them, by the indication of His saying ﴿but most of them do not give thanks﴾. And ﴿lakinna﴾ ("but") is an exception arising from the generality of the bounty from Him, the Exalted; for its generality and its recurrence deserve that people should know it and thank Him, but most people do not give thanks, like those who said ﴿When is this promise?﴾, for they seek to hasten the punishment mockingly and as a challenge in their claim, not being capable of appreciating the value of the blessing of being left alone.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 74:

﴿And indeed, your Lord knows what their breasts conceal and what they disclose.﴾

The placement of this statement is that of an explanatory resumption (al-isti'naf al-bayani), because His saying, ﴿Indeed, your Lord is full of bounty toward mankind﴾, raises a question in the minds of the believers: they might say, "These deniers have concealed their scheming and openly displayed their mockery, so does their condition not call for delaying them?" The answer is given: the One who has granted them respite is aware of what is in their breasts and of what they have openly displayed, and He has granted them respite despite His knowledge of them, for a wisdom that He knows.

In it there is an indication that they conceal things both against the Prophet (ﷺ) and against the believers. Among them: they wait for calamities to befall them, and thoughts of expelling him and the believers occur to their minds. Since this resumption carries an aspect of the meaning of describing God with the comprehensiveness of knowledge, it was conjoined to the sentence describing God with bounty, so by the conjunction a second important purpose was achieved, and the meaning of explanatory resumption was derived from the content of the sentence.

As for the emphasis with "inna" (indeed), it is of the same kind as the emphasis of the sentence before it. You may also take it as treating the questioner as one who is hesitant, and that is an allusion to reproach.

"Tukinnu" means "conceals," and it derives from (akanna), when one makes a thing be kann, i.e., situated in a kinn (a covering). Al-kinn: the dwelling place. Attributing "tukinnu" to the breasts is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), based on the consideration that the breasts are its place. And al-i'lan: the disclosing.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 75:

﴿And there is not a thing unseen in the heaven and the earth but that it is in a Clear Record.﴾

It is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause "And indeed your Lord knows what their breasts conceal and what they disclose," and it is in the sense of a tadhyil (a concluding generalization appended to a preceding clause) for the clause mentioned, since the knowledge of God regarding their inner thoughts was mentioned in it, so this was concluded with the statement that God knows every unseen thing in the heavens and the earth.

It came conjoined because it is worthy of standing by itself, insofar as it is a teaching about the attribute of God's knowledge, and an admonition to them from their heedlessness regarding the comprehensiveness of God's knowledge of what their breasts conceal and what they disclose. Al-ghaʾibah (the unseen thing) is a noun for the thing that is absent, and the ta' in it is for transferring the word from being an adjective to being a noun, like the ta' in al-ʿafiyah, al-ʿaqibah, and al-fatihah. It is a noun derived from al-ghayb, which is the opposite of presence, and what is meant is the thing hidden from the knowledge of people. He used al-ghayb to mean concealment, as a metonymy (majaz mursal).

The Book (al-kitab) is used to express the knowledge of God; the Book is borrowed for it because of what it contains of certainty and of not accepting change. It is permissible that it is a created, unseen entity in which whatever is going to happen is recorded.

Al-mubin means the detailed, because a thing that is detailed is clear and evident. The meaning is that the reality of nothing that is hidden from the worlds escapes God's knowledge. This entails that everything the messengers receive from God, the Exalted, is true and does not admit that the matter could be otherwise. Among this is what the discussion concerned regarding the matter of resurrection, which they denied and whose reports they rejected.

**[Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur, *al-Taḥrīr wa'l-Tanwīr*, on Surah 27, verse 76]**

﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel most of that about which they differ.﴾ This is a refutation of the saying of those who disbelieve: ﴿This is nothing but the myths of the former peoples.﴾ It has a connection with His saying: ﴿And there is not a thing unseen in the heaven or earth but that it is in a Clear Record.﴾ [an-Naml: 75]. The Qur'an is a revelation from God to His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ). Everything in it is therefore one of the effects of God's knowledge. When God wills to teach the Muslims something that the Qur'an contains, it is the true knowledge once understanding reaches the grasp of its intended meaning, according to the levels of indication (*marātib al-dalālah*), whose foundations lie in the science of the Arabic language (*ʿilm al-ʿarabiyyah*, the science of Arabic grammar and lexicon) and in the science of the foundations of jurisprudence (*ʿilm uṣūl al-fiqh*, the principles of Islamic law).

Among this is what the Qur'an contains of verifying matters of the earlier laws and the past nations, concerning which the books of the Children of Israel became confused, owing to what befell their books of dispersal, decay, and poor transmission from one language to another in the ages of the decline of the Israelite nation. Also [included is] what the Qur'an contains of clear principles concerning divine matters (*al-ilāhiyyāt*, theology), which exposes the Children of Israel's misinterpretation of the words of their Book concerning the ambiguous passages on anthropomorphism (*al-tajsīm*) and the like. For you will not find in the Torah anything equal to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [ash-Shura: 11].

So the meaning is: a denial that it is the myths of the former peoples, by establishing that it is an instruction for the believers and an instruction for the People of the Book. He related to them most of what they differed over, namely that part of the truth in it which benefits the Muslims, and He turned away from what is beneath that. Thus the placement of this verse is to complete the aspects of the Qur'an's guidance for the nations. The surah began by saying that it is a guidance and good news for the believers, and that the polytheists who do not believe in the Hereafter wander blindly in their error and therefore did not benefit from its guidance. So this verse completes what came with regard to the guidance concerning the Children of Israel, as to what is of concern among what they differed about.

The emphasis by *inna* is like what preceded in its counterparts. The majority of what they differ about is what came in the Qur'an refuting their statements in matters where guidance towards the truth requires that it be made clear to them, and what is less than the majority is what has no benefit in clarifying it for them.

Among the connections of the alert that the Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel most of what they differ over: what it related of the events that took place between the Queen of Sheba and Solomon contained elements that contradict what is in the First Book of Kings and the Second Book of Chronicles. In those two books, the Queen of Sheba undertook the journey and came to Jerusalem of her own accord, out of love to learn about the greatness of Solomon's kingdom and his wisdom which had reached her ears, and that after she was hosted by Solomon she returned to her kingdom. But it is not consistent, by the judgment of reason and the evidence of history in those ages, that a great queen like the Queen of Sheba would deliberately leave her land and enter the land of another king without fear, unless she was compelled to do so by the policy of choosing the lesser of two harms, since Solomon had obliged her to enter within the sphere of his authority. Her presence before him was therefore an act of submission and an acknowledgment of his sovereignty, after she had tried to evade that by sending the gift, and after she saw Solomon's determination to carry out his command.

And it is strange that the Jewish Book neglects Solomon's call of Bilqis to the doctrine of monotheism. Could it be supposed of a prophet that he would allow polytheism to its adherents?

[Page 31]

This refers back to his saying at the opening of the surah, ﴿a guidance and good tidings for the believers﴾ [al-Naml: 2]. It is mentioned here to encompass the aspects of the Qur'an's guidance. As for its being guidance for the believers, it is evident. As for its being mercy for them, it is because when they were guided by it, they attained success in this world through the rectification of their souls, the uprightness of their deeds, and the unity of their word, and in the Hereafter through attaining Paradise. The Muhammadan message, although it is a mercy to all the worlds, as has preceded in His saying, ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya: 107] in Surah Hud, its mercy to the believers is more specific.

The emphasis by "inna" (indeed) is considered in relation to the context (al-ma'rid, the setting of the discourse), as has preceded in His saying, ﴿Indeed, your Lord is full of bounty toward mankind﴾ [al-Naml: 73].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 78:

[p. 32]
﴿Indeed, your Lord will judge between them by His judgment, and He is the Almighty, the All-Knowing.﴾ When the mention of the polytheists was preceded by their slander of the Qur'an and their denial of its warning, and the mention of the Children of Israel was accompanied by what implies their slander of it, namely that it contradicts what is in their books, and the mention of the believers was accompanied by the fact that they were guided by it and it was a mercy for them, since they are certain of what it contains, the discourse yielded a conclusion: that people are divided over the Qur'an into two groups, a group that slanders it and a group that is certain of it. Therefore, this necessarily brought about a clash between the two groups. This raises in the souls of the believers a question about the extent of this clash and the disagreement between the two groups, and when the truth will be revealed. So His saying ﴿Indeed, your Lord will judge between them by His judgment﴾ came as an explanatory resumptive discourse (istiʾnaf bayani), from which it is understood that judgment requires parties who differ. And the word "between" (bayna) requires more than one party. Thus it conveys that Allah judges between the believers and those who slander it, a judgment that makes clear the one who is right from the one who is wrong. This is a consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to the believers for their impatience for victory, since the Prophet is the first of the believers, and the believers only adopted what he was informed of. So judgment in favour of the believers is judgment in favour of him first and foremost.

In it there is the directing of the address to the presence of the Messenger (ﷺ), and the attribution of judgment to Allah in his regard, under the title that He is his Lord, which carries an allusion (iyma') that the judgment will be pleasing to him and to the believers. Thus the Messenger in this discourse is placed in the position of one who conveys, and the judgment between his community, believer and disbeliever, is made, and it hastens the joy of the Messenger through this allusion.

Since judgment has been attributed to Allah and a ruling has been connected to Him, being an addition to His pronoun, it is necessarily determined that what is meant by the object of the connection is other than the thing connected to it. This necessitates one of two things. Either: an interpretation (taʾwil) of the meaning of the addition of "judgment" that differs from the meaning of the attribution of "judgment," if the two expressions are regarded as synonymous both in wording and in meaning. Then what the addition indicates, namely the exclusivity of the annexed thing to the annexing thing, is intended to mean what the annexed thing is known for in relation to the annexing thing. This is because everyone knows that the judgment of Allah is justice, and because the one to whom it is annexed is the Just Judge. So the meaning according to this is that your Lord will judge between them by His well-known, established judgment, which befits the comprehensiveness of His knowledge and the consistency of His justice. Or: "judgment" is interpreted as "wisdom" (hikmah), which is a common usage. He, exalted is He, said ﴿And to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾ [al-Anbiya': 79], and He said ﴿And We gave him judgment while still a child﴾ [Maryam: 12]. Yahya was not a judge; rather he was a wise prophet. So the meaning according to this is: Indeed your Lord will judge between them by His wisdom, that is, by what wisdom requires, namely the granting of victory to the one who is right over the one who is wrong.

[p. 33]
The outcome of the two interpretations is one and the same meaning.

By this there becomes apparent the excellence of the placement of the two sublime names in its concluding appendage (tadhyil), in His saying ﴿and He is the Almighty, the All-Knowing﴾. For the Almighty does not flatter or yield, and the All-Knowing does not miss the truth. And there becomes apparent the excellence of the placement of the consequential linkage (tafri') in His saying

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 79:

﴿So put your trust in Allah. Indeed, you are upon the manifest truth.﴾ The fa' (fa, "so") is connected to the report that the Lord of the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, judges between those who differ concerning the matter of the Qur'an. It is a command to the Messenger to be at ease in heart and to place his trust in his Lord regarding what He decides, for He will decide in his favour with his right, and against his opponent with what he deserves. Thus the command to trust (al-tawakkul) is used both in its implicature (kinayah) and its literal sense, for it entails that he has conveyed the message of his Lord, and that the turning away of those who turn away from the command of Allah is not a shortcoming on the part of the Messenger ﷺ. This meaning is repeated in the Qur'an, such as His saying ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 3] and His saying ﴿And do not grieve over them﴾ [al-Naml: 70].

Al-tawakkul (trust, reliance): it is of the form tafa''ul from wakkala ilayhi al-amr, meaning when one entrusts to him the management and undertaking of a matter; so the tafa'ul form is for emphasis (intensification). It has been discussed previously at His saying ﴿And when you have resolved, then rely upon Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159] in Al 'Imran, His saying ﴿And upon Allah rely, if you are believers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 23] in al-Ma'idah, and His saying ﴿And let the believers rely upon Allah﴾ [Ibrahim: 11] in Surat Ibrahim.

The clause ﴿Indeed, you are upon the manifest truth﴾ occupies a position in which Allah the Exalted has not addressed any of His messengers with its like. This was therefore a testimony to His Messenger of complete greatness, free of every deficiency, owing to what the particle "upon" (ʿala) indicates of firm establishment, what the word "truth" (al-haqq) indicates of a meaning comprehensive of the realities of things, and what the descriptor "manifest" (mubin) indicates of clarity and prominence.

The clause ﴿Indeed, you are upon the manifest truth﴾ comes as a justification for the command to trust in Allah, signalling that he is upon the truth, so one does not expect from his trust in the just Judge anything but that His judgment be in his support and benefit. When "inna" (indeed) comes in a context of causal justification, its function is that of the fa' (so/therefore), so it does not indicate emphasis, but rather it is for attentiveness (al-ihtimam).

The divine name was used in the act of trust, with the designation of the Name of Majesty (ism al-jalalah), because that name includes all the meanings of perfection, and among the highest of them is justice in judgment and the victory of the one who is in the right. This comes after the pleasing allusion had hastened ahead to indicate that the judgment is on the side of the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, by attributing the judgment to the designation of the Lord (al-Rabb) added to the pronoun of the Messenger, as has been mentioned just above.

The fronting of the predicate (musnad ilayhi) before the verbal predicate (khabar fi'li) was required by the presence of the factor calling for the particle of emphasis, to convey causal justification; so the fronting does not convey restriction (takhsis) nor reinforcement (taqwiyah).

Al-Mubin: the clear one, about which there should be no doubt, nor any flattery of the one in whose favour the judgment is made.

In the verse there is an indication that one who knows that the truth is on his side is worthy of trusting that Allah will manifest his right, even if after a while.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 80:

﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn away, retreating.﴾ This is a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani), answering a question that comes to the listener's mind after His words ﴿Indeed, you are upon the manifest truth﴾ [al-Naml: 79], namely, why the people of polytheism turn away from what the Messenger possesses of manifest truth. It is also another justification for the command to rely upon Allah, when considered in terms of its implied meaning (madlul kinai). Thus the placement of the emphatic particle in it is like its placement in the justification by the clause preceding it. This is an excuse for the Messenger ﷺ and a consolation to him. Because it provides a justification for one aspect of the construction, namely the implicit (kinai) aspect, which differs from the one justified by the clause ﴿Indeed, you are upon the manifest truth﴾ [al-Naml: 79], this clause was not conjoined to the one before it, to draw attention to its independence in providing justification.

Al-isma' (causing to hear) means conveying speech to the ears.

"Al-mawta" (the dead) and "al-summ" (the deaf) are metaphors (musta'aran) for the people who do not accept the true word and who obstinately oppose the one who speaks it to them. They are likened to the dead by way of metaphor (isti'ara) in the absence of their understanding the meanings of the Qur'an,

[p. 35]
and they are likened to the deaf likewise in the absence of the effect of the eloquence of its wording upon their souls.
The Qur'an has two effects. One is what it contains of meanings acceptable to people of sound intellect, which are the meanings that whoever it reaches perceives and accepts, even through translation, such that Arab and non-Arab alike equally grasp them. This is an intellectual effect.

The second effect is the indication of its composition and eloquence that it is beyond the capacity of the eloquent Arabs. This is a verbal effect, and it is the proof of inimitability (i'jaz). It is specific to the Arabs directly, and it is attained by others among those who reflect and contemplate, when they consider the inability of the eloquent people of the tongue in which the Qur'an came. Such people become certain that the inability of the eloquent people of that tongue to oppose it indicates that it is beyond their capacity. Thus the polytheists were likened to the dead with regard to the first effect, and likened to the deaf with regard to the second effect, so two metaphors arose. The negation of making them hear, in both cases, is a supporting complement (tarshih) for the two metaphors, and both are used metaphorically for the absence of any attempt to get the message through to them.

Because both effects are taken into account, on which the two comparisons are based, the two supporting complements were mentioned again, so ﴿and you cannot make the deaf hear﴾ is conjoined to ﴿you cannot make the dead hear﴾. It was not sufficient to say: "Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear, nor the deaf."

The restriction of the deaf to the time of their turning away, retreating, is because that state is more extreme in the negation of their hearing. A deaf person who faces the speaker may hear some of the speech through shouting and derive the rest by the movement of the lips, but that is further from hearing for him.

'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, used this verse to reject the apparent meaning of the hadith of Ibn 'Umar: that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood at the well of Badr, in which were the corpses of the polytheists, and called them by their names and said: "Have you found what your Lord promised you to be true?" Ibn 'Umar said: It was said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, do you call out to the dead?" He said: "Indeed, they now hear what I say to them." 'A'isha said: The Prophet ﷺ only said: "Indeed, they now know that what I used to tell them is the truth." Then she recited ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ until she recited the verse.

[p. 36]
This is among the cases of deriving proof from the apparent indication of the Qur'an, even by a weak possibility, as we explained in the ninth introduction (al-muqaddima al-tasi'a). Otherwise, "the dead" here is a metaphor and not a literal meaning.

The two pronouns in ﴿when they turn away, retreating﴾ refer back to the deaf. This is a completion of the comparison (tatmim lil-tashbih), since they are likened, in the failure of words to reach their minds, to deaf people who turn away, retreating. The one who retreats moves away from the place of the one speaking to him, so he is further from listening, as was mentioned just before.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 81:

﴿And you cannot guide the blind away from their error.﴾ He repeated the comparison of the polytheists in their turning away from the truth by likening them, in this respect, to the blind, after they had been likened to the dead and to the deaf, by way of metaphor (isti'ara), as an elaboration (itnab) in denouncing their described condition, in accordance with what is well known among the eloquent (bulaghā') regarding the repetition of a comparison, as already explained at the words of the Exalted ﴿Or like a rainstorm from the sky﴾ [al-Baqara: 19] in Surat al-Baqara.

What made this repetition good here is the differences between the two comparisons alongside the unity of the aim. For they were likened to the dead in the absence of perceiving meanings, which intelligent people enjoy; and to the deaf in the absence of perceiving the eloquence of speech, which the eloquent of the Arabs master. Thirdly, they were likened to the blind in the absence of distinguishing between the path of guidance and the path of error, inasmuch as they did not follow the guidance of the religion of Islam. The aim is one, namely the absence of their following Islam. So in likening them to the blind there is an explicit metaphor (isti'ara musarraha), and the negation of their being rescued from their error is a supporting element (tarshih) of the metaphor, because the blind man does not reach knowledge of the path by the description of one who describes it.

Guidance (al-huda) is indicating the path to the traveler by describing it to him, such as saying, for example: "When you reach the valley, take the right-hand road."

The one who leads caravans along the courses of the road is called a guide (hadi).

Reaching knowledge of the road is called being guided (ihtida'). This supporting element is also a metaphor for the clarification of truth and rectitude to people. The blind is not receptive to guidance in either of two states: the state of description, which is evident, and the state of being led, for the Arabs did not take the blind with them on their journeys, because they would obstruct the caravan's progress.

Page 37
His saying ﴿from their error﴾ contains a hidden metaphor (isti'ara makniyya) whose indication is contextual (qarina haliyya). He likened the true religion to the clear road, and attributing error to its travelers is a supporting element (tarshih) for it and an imaginative representation (takhyil). Error (al-dalala) is also used metaphorically for the failure to perceive the truth, following the hidden metaphor, and here it is applied to the failure to be guided to the road. The pronoun in "their error" refers to the blind. To achieve this graceful metaphor, the expression was shifted from attaching to guidance what ought to be attached to it, and instead was attached to it what the negation of guidance entails of turning away and distancing. Thus it is said ﴿from their error﴾ by implying in "guide" (hadi) the meaning of "one who turns away" (sarif). So it becomes: "You are not one who guides them," meaning: "You are not one who turns them away from their error," just as it is said: "He gave him to drink to turn him away from al-'ayma," i.e. he gave him drink diverting him from al-'ayma, which is the craving for milk.

In the sentence, the two preceding negations in His saying ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call﴾ [al-Naml: 80], which were applied to verbal predicates, were shifted here to a negation applied to a nominal sentence, to indicate the permanence of the negation. This permanence is further emphasized by the superfluous "bi" (ba' zā'ida), to emphasize the negation.

The reason for selecting this sentence with these two confirmations is that, when the discourse arrived at the negation of their being guided, and their being guided was the utmost aspiration of the Messenger (ﷺ), the context indicated a remnant of his hope for their guidance, out of concern for them. So what would dispel that hope was emphasized for him. This is like His saying ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ [al-Qasas: 56], and His saying ﴿And you are not over them a compeller﴾ [Qaf: 45]. In the explanation of the parallel of this verse in Surat al-Rum there will come an explanation of enumerating the three comparisons beyond what is here, so consult it.

Hamza alone read (wa-ma anta tahdi) with a second-person feminine... [Note: the Arabic reads "bi-mutharrāh fawqiyya fī mawḍi' al-muwaḥḥada" — a ta' (taa) in place of the ba' — and without an alif after the ha'.]

﴿You will only make hear those who believe in Our signs, so they are Muslims.﴾
An explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) answering the listener's anticipation of knowing who is guided by the Qur'an.

Making hear is used in its figurative sense, as already explained.

Page 38
The present tense was chosen in His saying "who believes" (man yu'minu) so that it includes those who had believed before, and the present tense indicates the continuity of their faith and of those who will believe.

It has become apparent from the division arising from His saying ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ [al-Naml: 80] up to here, that people are of two kinds: among them are those on whose hearts God has set a seal and whom He knows will not believe until destruction overtakes them; and among them are those for whom God has written happiness, so they believe, quickly or slowly, before death.

Upon this is built ﴿so they are Muslims﴾, which indicates permanence and stability; for when they believe, Islam has become firmly established in them and securely settled within them, and likewise faith, once its radiance mingles with the hearts.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 82:

﴿When the word is fulfilled against them, We will bring forth for them a creature from the earth that will speak to them, [saying] that mankind did not believe with certainty in Our signs.﴾ This is a transition to the reminder of the Resurrection and of the threat of punishment stored up for them. This sentence is conjoined to the sentences before it by the conjunction of one narrative to another. The reason for mentioning it is what preceded in His words ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ [al-Naml: 80] up to His words ﴿from their misguidance﴾ [al-Naml: 81]. The pronoun refers to the dead, the deaf, and the blind, who are the polytheists.

By "the word" (al-qawl) is meant the reports of the threat, which they denied, mocking and asking about its delay with their words ﴿When will this promise be, if you are truthful?﴾ [al-Naml: 71]. The definite article in it is for a known referent (al-ʿahd), which the context explains.

"Fulfilment" (al-wuqūʿ) is used metaphorically for the arrival of its time, which is from the time the world prepares for annihilation until the people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of the Fire enter the Fire.

The verse points to some of the portents (ashrāt, signs preceding events) of the arrival of the threat they were warned of, namely the greatest threat, the threat of resurrection. It thus points to some of the portents of the Hour, which are among the extraordinary events that break customary patterns (khawāriq al-ʿādāt). The expression of its occurrence in the past tense is to bring the time of the present closer to the past, meaning that its occurrence has drawn near, and the past verb after ʾidhā turns to the future.

"Dābba" (creature) is a name for a living being other than a human, derived from "dabīb," which is walking on the earth, and walking is one of the characteristics of living things. The discussion of the word "dābba" has already passed in surah al-Anʿām. Reports about the description of this creature, the time of its emergence, and its place have been transmitted, which are confused and weak in their chains of transmission. Consult them in the tafsir (exegesis) of al-Qurṭubī and others, since there is no benefit in collecting and criticising them.

The emergence of the creature from the earth is to show them how God brings the dead to life, since they had denied resurrection. There is no doubt that its speech to them is an address to them about the arrival of the gathering. God created speech for them through the tongue of a creature in order to belittle them and to reproach them for their refusal to accept the most eloquent and most effective speech from the noblest and most eloquent of humans. This is so that it becomes a disgrace for them at the end of time, by which they are reproached at the place of gathering. It will be said: these are the ones who turned away from the speech of a noble messenger, so they were addressed through the speech of a dumb animal. This is in the manner of what has been said: a receiver's benefit from the source depends on the correspondence between them.

The clause ﴿Indeed, mankind did not believe with certainty in Our signs﴾ is a justification for the manifestation of this extraordinary event, since the polytheists did not have certainty in the signs of the Qur'an. So God made that a compulsion for them at a time when it will not benefit them.

The majority of reciters read ʾinna (indeed) with a kasra on the hamza of "ʾinna" in this manner, and the position of "ʾinna" in such a case is causal. ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī read ﴿ʾanna al-nāsa﴾ with a fatḥa on the hamza. It is also for causation, because the fatḥa on the hamza of "ʾanna" indicates an implied preposition, namely the prepositional bāʾ of causation, meaning: it speaks to them by the outcome of this, which is the verbal noun. The meaning is that it records against the people, meaning the polytheists, their not affirming the signs of God. This is a recording of reproach and blame, because at that time the word has been fulfilled against them: ﴿Faith will not benefit a soul if it did not believe before﴾ [al-Anʿām: 158]. To take this sentence as a report of what the creature says to them is far-fetched.

[Page 40]

"Yawma" (the day) is in the accusative. It is either an object governed by an implied "udhkur" (remember), or a time adverbial (ẓarf) governing "qāla a-kadhdhabtum", placed before it for emphasis.

This is a specific gathering, following the gathering of all creation mentioned in His words after this: ﴿And the day the Horn is blown, whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be seized with terror﴾ [al-Naml: 87]. It has the same sense as His words: ﴿And separate yourselves today, O criminals﴾ [Yā-Sīn: 59]. So from every nation will be gathered those who denied its messenger.

"Fawj" means a company of people. The "min" attached to "kulli ummah" (every nation) is partitive (tab'īḍiyya). The "min" attached to "man yukadhdhibu" (those who deny) may be explanatory (bayāniyya), so that the "fawj" is the entire company of each nation. This company consists of the leaders and imams of the deniers, who will be at the front of the column going to the punishment.

This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, when he said: "Like Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and Shayba ibn Rabi'a, they will be driven before the people of Mecca. Likewise, the leaders of each group will be driven at the head of it." The explanation of ﴿so they will be driven back﴾ was given earlier, in the story of Sulayman in this surah.

The meaning here is that they will be driven back harshly, as prisoners are treated.

The discussion of ﴿until, when they came﴾ is like the discussion of ﴿until, when they came upon the valley of the ants﴾ [al-Naml: 18]. The place they came to is not mentioned because it is evident, and it is the place of punishment, that is, Hell, as He said in the verse ﴿until, when they come to it﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 20] in the surah Fuṣṣilat.

"Ḥattā" in ﴿ḥattā idhā jā'ū﴾ is initial (ibtidā'iyya). "Idhā" which follows "ḥattā" is a time adverb, and the meaning is: "until the time when they came."

The verb in ﴿qāla: a-kadhdhabtum bi-āyātī﴾ (He said: "Did you deny My signs?") is, in the underlying structure, the head of the sentence, and what precedes it is placed before it for emphasis. The underlying sense is: "He said, 'Did you deny My signs?' on the day We gather from every nation a company, and when they came." In "qāla" there is a shift (iltifāt) from the first person to the third person.

The statement ﴿a-kadhdhabtum bi-āyātī﴾ is a statement issued by God Most High, which they hear, or which the angels convey to them.

The interrogative may be a rebuke (tawbīkh), used for its implication, which is compelling them to admit that the matter questioned about did occur from them, as a means of confounding them. For this reason He joined to it the words ﴿am māḏā kuntum ta'malūn﴾ (or what were you doing?). The particle "am" in it has the meaning of "bal" (rather), for transition. The counterpart of the implied interrogative hamza is omitted, and it is indicated by His words ﴿what were you doing?﴾. The underlying sense is: "Did you deny My signs, or did you not deny them? Then what were you doing, if you did not deny them? You did not believe, so what were you doing during the period when your call to Islam was repeated?" From here came the compulsion to admit that they had denied.

Among the subtleties of eloquence is that the first counterpart was stated explicitly, because it was the established fact concerning them, so He said ﴿Did you deny My signs?﴾, and He omitted its other counterpart, to draw attention to its being negated, as if it were said: "Is it the denial that was known from you, or has some other event occurred?" Thus this counterpart is presented as uncertain, and the speech passes to an interrogative. This is a rebuke to them.

Al-Zamakhsharī said in al-Kashshāf: "An example of this is that you say to your shepherd, when you know that he is a bad shepherd: 'Are you eating my camels, or what are you doing with them?' You make the thing you began with, and made the foundation of your speech, to be that which you are certain of, namely his eating and corruption, and you cast in your words, 'or what are you doing with them?', although you know that he does nothing with them except eating, in order to confound him. It is also permissible for the interrogative to be a confirmation (taqrīr), and 'am' is then connected (muttaṣila), and what follows it is the counterpart of the interrogative in meaning, as if it were said: 'Did you deny, or did you not deny? Then what were you doing, if you did not deny? You did not follow My signs.'"

The clause ﴿while you did not encompass them with knowledge﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), that is: "You denied without encompassing them with knowledge, by the indication of the signs." "Ilman" (with knowledge) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz) of the relation of "tuḥīṭū" (you encompass), that is: "Your knowledge did not encompass them." He turned from attributing the encompassing to knowledge, to attributing it to the persons addressed, so that the emphasis of the statement falls first on the general attribution and then on the detail through the specification.

The encompassing of knowledge concerning the signs is used to mean that knowledge has taken firm hold, as if it were a container enclosing them. This is an expression directed at them, and a rebuke that they denied the signs before reflecting upon them.

"Māḏā" is an interrogative and also a demonstrative, and it has the meaning of a relative pronoun when it follows "mā". The referent is the content of the clause after it, in His words "kuntum ta'malūn". Because the referent in such a case is a clause, the demonstrative after the interrogative takes the force of a relative pronoun, as if it were said: "What is it that you were doing?" This is the meaning of the grammarians' statement that "dhā" after the two interrogatives "mā" and "man" has the meaning of the relative "mā". It is an explanation of meaning, not an explanation of the original lexical form.

﴿And the Word will come true against them because of what they did wrong, so they will not be able to speak.﴾ The waw may be a circumstantial (ḥāl) conjunction, and the meaning is: it will be said to them, "Did you deny My signs while the Word had already come true against them?" This Word is the same Word mentioned in the verse ﴿And when the Word comes true against them﴾ [An-Naml: 82], since that Word encompasses many events, so whenever any of them is realized, the Word has come true. The past tense in His saying "came true" (waqa'a) here is literal, and it is repeated to magnify its terror. It is also possible that the waw is conjunctive (ʿāṭifa), with "the Word" referring to the first Word, and the clause is joined to the similar clause before it in order to establish upon it the cause of the Word's coming true, namely that it is because of their wrongdoing (ẓulm), and in order to make His saying ﴿so they will not be able to speak﴾ a consequence of it. The use of the past tense in this way is because the event is certain to occur in the future, so it is treated as though it has already occurred and passed.

"What they did wrong" (mā ẓalamū) is in the sense of a verbal noun (maṣdar), and the bāʾ is causal, meaning "because of their wrongdoing." Here, wrongdoing (ẓulm) means polytheism (shirk) and what follows from it of transgression against the rights of God and the rights of the believers. Thus their wrongdoing was the cause for the threat befalling them. In a hadith (a report from the Prophet ﷺ) it is said: "Injustice is darknesses on the Day of Resurrection." So everyone who does wrong will be struck by the Word promised to the wrongdoers, because wrongdoing is connected to polytheism, and this connection is as was explained earlier, at His saying ﴿So those are their houses, empty because of what they did wrong﴾ [An-Naml: 52] in this surah.

The clause ﴿so they will not be able to speak﴾ is a consequence of ﴿the Word came true﴾ [An-Naml: 82], meaning that it came true upon them in a way that prevents them from speaking, that is, from speech of excuse or denial. That is, they will be struck dumb at the occurrence of what they were promised. God, Exalted, says: ﴿This is a Day on which they will not speak﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 35], and ﴿nor will they be permitted to give excuses﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 36].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 86:

﴿Have they not seen that We made the night for them to rest therein, and the day giving sight? Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾ This discourse is connected to His saying ﴿And the word will fall upon them because they wronged﴾ [An-Naml: 85], i.e., because they associated (others with Allah).

صفحة ٤٣
So He reminded them of the proofs of Divine Oneness by mentioning the most evident signs, the most frequently repeated before their senses, and the most fitting to be persuasive in turning them back from their polytheism. It is a sign that accompanies them throughout their lives, occurring to their minds at least twice every day. This is the sign of the alternation of night and day, which indicates that He, the Exalted, alone exercises control over this world; their idols are subject to His action, so that they (the idols) darken their own essences at night and shine during the day. In it there is also a reminder through the likeness of death and life after it, by the stillness of night and the breaking forth of day after it.

The sentence is interposed between the sentence ﴿And the word will fall upon them﴾ [An-Naml: 85] and the sentence ﴿The Day when the Trumpet is blown﴾ [An-Naml: 87], so that the threat is interspersed with argument; thus the call to the truth is by intimidation at one time and by inviting reflection at another.

The interrogative is used figuratively to express wonder at their condition, because its strangeness necessitates the question of one who asks why they do not see. This is the relation, or the justification, for using the interrogative to express wonder, and it is a hidden relation, which al-Sa'd al-Din (in al-Mutawwal) indicated as not being apparent, while al-Sayyid al-Sharif undertook to clarify it to the utmost clarity and traced it back to metonymy (al-majaz al-mursal). So reflect upon it.

The verb "to see" (al-ru'yah) may be mental (qalbiyyah), and the clause "that We made" (anna ja'alna) occupies the place of the two objects, i.e., "How did they not know that We made the night for them to rest therein and the day giving sight, although that is clearly indicative of this making?" The verb of seeing was chosen from among the verbs of knowledge because this knowledge resembles perceived objects.

It may also be that the seeing is visual (basariyyah), and the verbal noun (al-masdar) formed from the clause is the object of seeing.

The meaning: How did they not perceive the making of the night for rest and the day for sight, although that is before their eyes? "Making" is intended in terms of its effect, which is the compulsion of people to rest at night and to disperse during the day. Thus the seeing of the effect of the making is placed in the position of seeing that making itself. This is widespread in Arabic, that the effect may be placed in the position of the agent, and the indicator in the position of the indicated. Al-Nabighah said:

And I have feared, until my fear increases not
Over a wild goat on the mountain of al-Mutarah, a sensible one.
I.e., over the fear of a wild goat.

"Giving sight" (al-mubsir) is the active participle of abṣara in the sense of ra'a. The description of the day as giving sight is of the type of metaphor in the intellect (al-majaz al-'aqli), because the light of day is the cause of sight. It may also be that the hamzah is for transitivity, from abṣarahu, if he made it seeing.

The sentence ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾ is a reason for the wonder at their condition, since they did not draw evidence from the alternation of night and day for Divine Oneness nor for the Resurrection.

The reason the signs in that are many, as the plural requires, is that in the order of the night there are signs of the sole agency in creating the sun, creating its light which breaks through darkness, creating the earth, and creating the system of its daily rotation facing the rays of the sun, which is the rotation that produces night and day; and in the creation of human nature, by which one seeks stillness in darkness because of the lassitude that besets the nerves, unlike some animals that become active at night, such as insects and bats. In that there is also evidence of the succession of death and life. So these are signs, and in each sign there are subtleties and great orders which, if the discussion of them were expanded, would fill volumes of knowledge.

In making the day giving sight there are many signs of Divine Oneness and the precision of craftsmanship, corresponding to what preceded in the signs of making the night a dwelling. In it there is evidence that there is no impossibility nor improbability in the Resurrection after death, and that it is like the awakening after sleep. In the great and subtle of those signs there are many signs, so this is the reason that it is described as "signs" and not as "two signs."

The meaning of ﴿for a people who believe﴾ is: for people whose disposition is belief and acknowledgment of proof. For this reason belief was made an attributive quality applied to "a people," for what we have stated more than once: that attaching the judgment to the word "qawm" (people) indicates that the judgment is firmly established among them, to the point that it is as if it were among the constituents of their peoplehood. From this is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And they swear by Allah that they are surely of you, but they are not of you; rather they are a people who are fearful﴾ [At-Tawbah: 56], i.e., fearfulness is among the constituents of their peoplehood, so how could they be of you while you are not fearful? That is, in that are signs for those whose motto is reflection and attribution, i.e., these are not in that position.

Because belief is intended as something hoped for from them, it is expressed with the present tense (al-mudari'), since the intent is not that in that are signs for those who already believe, because that is obtained by implication and by priority. The meaning becomes: Indeed in that are signs for the believers and for those from whom belief is hoped upon examining the proofs. Close to this meaning is His saying ﴿It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds﴾ [At-Takwir: 27] for whoever among you wills to be upright.

صفحة ٤٥
This is why there is a difference between what is here and what is in Surah Yunus, where He said ﴿It is He who made the night for you to rest therein and the day giving sight. Indeed in that are signs for a people who hear﴾ [Yunus: 67]; because the verse of Yunus is directed toward argument and enumeration of favours, so it addressed all people, believer and disbeliever, and therefore came in the form of address, and its indication was made for everyone who hears the proofs of the Qur'an, among whom are the guided and the astray. For this reason the verb "they hear" was used there, indicating compliance and attentiveness to seeking guidance.

As for this verse, it is directed toward wonder and reproach, so what is in it was made signs for those among whom belief is a characteristic, to convey by its implication that no evidence arises from it for one who is not characterized by fairness and acknowledgment. For this reason the verb "they believe" was preferred in it.

What is peculiar to the night is expressed by the form of causation with the lam in His saying ﴿to rest therein﴾, and what is in the day by the form of the object of making in His saying "giving sight," for variety, and because of the intensification that "mubsiran" conveys. The meaning on the causal reading and on the object reading is one in its ultimate result. With this al-Zamakhshari said (the antithesis is observed in meaning, and this is the arrangement of natural, uncontrived speech). That is, in the verse there is ihtiba' (a rhetorical figure of omission), since the meaning is: We made the night dark so that they might rest therein, and the day giving sight so that they might disperse therein.

Know that what has been established here applies to the verse of Surah Yunus apart from what belongs to the aspects of rhetorical differences; so refer to it there.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 87:

﴿And [remember] the Day when the Trumpet is blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified, except whom Allah wills. And all will come to Him in humility.﴾ It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿And [remember] the Day when We gather from every nation a company﴾ [al-Naml: 83]. The context returns to exhortation and warning, for when they were reminded of the Day of Gathering to the Fire, they were also reminded of what precedes it, which is the Day of the blowing of the Trumpet, as a record against them by establishing the occurrence of resurrection and a warning of what follows it, as indicated by His saying ﴿all will come to Him in humility﴾ and His saying ﴿whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified, except whom Allah wills﴾.

Page 46

The blowing of the Trumpet has already been mentioned in His saying ﴿And to Him belongs the dominion on the Day the Trumpet is blown﴾ [al-An'am: 73] in Surah al-An'am, and it is an approximation of the manner in which the creative command for the revival of the dead is issued. It is the second blast mentioned in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Then it will be blown again, and at once they will be standing, looking on﴾ [al-Zumar: 68], and that is the Day of Reckoning. As for the first blast, it is a blast by which revival is meant, that is, the breathing of souls into their bodies, and it is the moment the worldly life ends, so they swoon (yuṣʿaqūn). For this reason, His saying ﴿so whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified﴾ is made consequent upon it, meaning that terror occurs after it, which is fear of the outcome of the Reckoning and witnessing the preparations for punishment. So everyone fears that he will be punished. The terror thus occurs after the blast and is not terror from the blast itself, because people at the time of the blast are dead.

The exception (istithnaʾ) is general (mujmal), and it is clarified by His saying, exalted is He, afterward: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have better than it, and they will be safe from the terror of that Day﴾ [al-Naml: 89], and His saying ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward has preceded from Us﴾ [al-Anbiya': 101] up to His saying ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾ [al-Anbiya': 103]. This occurs by the angels hastening to them with glad tidings. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿The angels will receive them: "This is your Day which you were promised"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 103], and He said: ﴿For them are good tidings in the worldly life and in the Hereafter﴾ [Yunus: 64].

The past tense is used in His saying "fa-faziʿa" (so terrified), although the blowing is in the future, to indicate the certainty of the terror and that it is bound to occur, like His saying ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ [al-Nahl: 1], because the past tense entails certainty; the past form is thus a metonymy (kināya) for certainty. The indication of the future is evident from the present tense in His saying "yunfakhu" (is blown).

Al-dākhirūn: those who are abased (al-ṣāghirūn), meaning the humiliated (al-adhillāʾ). It is said: dakhara, on the pattern of manaʿa and fariḥa, and the verbal noun is al-dakhar (with a vowel on the second letter) and al-dukhūr.

The apparent pronoun of absence in "ātūhu" refers to the Name of Majesty (Allah), and "coming to Allah" means being brought forward to the place of His judgment. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to "the Day the Trumpet is blown," with the estimate "ātūna fīhi" (they will come in it), and the object of "kull," whose tanwin is replaced by it, is understood as: "whoever is terrified among those in the heavens and the earth, they will all come to Him in humility." As for whom Allah excepted, by His willing that they not be terrified, they will not have dust or humiliation covering their faces.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (ātūhu) in the form of the active participle from atā. Hamza and Hafs read

ātawhu in the form of the past verb, and it is like His saying "fa-faziʿa."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (*al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*) on Surah 27, verse 88:

﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them fixed, while they pass by as the clouds pass. It is the handiwork of God, who perfected everything. Indeed, He is Aware of what you do.﴾

What the majority of the exegetes (*mufassirun*) have said is that the verse narrates an event that will occur on the Day when the Trumpet is blown. They took His saying, ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them fixed﴾, as a conjunction (*'atf*) upon ﴿the Trumpet is blown﴾ (27:87). That is, "and on the day you see the mountains, thinking them fixed, etc." They took the seeing to be visual. They took ﴿pass by as the clouds pass﴾ as a simile for their movement by the speed of the passing clouds. They took the choice of the simile of the passing clouds as intended to incorporate (*idmaj*) a comparison between the state of the mountains at that passing and the state of the clouds in the loosening of their parts and their scattering. This would be included in the meaning of His saying, ﴿And the mountains will be like carded wool﴾ (101:5). They took the address in His saying "you see" as addressed to an unspecified person, so that it includes everyone who sees. And they took the meaning of this verse to be the meaning of His saying, ﴿And the Day We set the mountains in motion﴾ (18:47).

It became problematic, however, that these conditions would occur before the Day of Gathering, because the verses in which the crumbling and scattering of the mountains are mentioned indicate that this happens at the end of the world, at the Striking Calamity (*al-qari'a*), which is the first blast or just before it. They answered that the mountains will then be crumbled and afterwards set in motion on the Day of Gathering, based on His saying, ﴿Say: My Lord will scatter them as dust﴾ (20:105), up to His saying, ﴿On that Day they will follow the caller, with no deviation﴾ (20:108). The caller is Israfil. But in this there is the point that "following" has many states, and "the caller" also has several meanings.

Some exegetes said: this occurs at the first blast, and likewise all the verses in which the scattering, crumbling and pulverizing of the mountains are mentioned. It seems they did not make the conjunction of ﴿And you see the mountains﴾ upon ﴿the Trumpet is blown﴾ so that the operation of the word "day" (*yawm*) would govern it. Rather, they made it a conjunction of one sentence upon another. The *waw* does not require the order of the conjoined with the conjoined-to. So it is a conjunction of one lesson upon another, even if the one mentioned first occurs second.

**[Page 48]**

Both groups made His saying ﴿the handiwork of God﴾ and what follows it intended to magnify the power of God, the Exalted, and to show that the blowing of the Trumpet and the moving of the mountains are among the wonders of His power. They thus interpreted *sun'* (handiwork) in the sense of the general act, without binding it to what the root *ṣ-n-'* carries of the meaning of composition and bringing into being, since *al-itqan* (perfection) is excellence, and demolition does not require perfection.

Al-Mawardi said: it has been said that this is a parable (*mathal*) which God set forth, that is, it is not a report. Concerning what the parable is about there are three views. The first: it is a parable for the world (*dunya*), whose beholder thinks it is firm like the mountains, while it is taking its share of passing away like the clouds. This was said by Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah al-Tustari. The second: it is a parable for faith (*iman*), which you think is firm in the heart, while its deed rises up to heaven. The third: it is a parable for the soul (*nafs*) at the departure of the spirit (*ruh*), and the spirit travels to the Throne. It seems they meant by "parable" a simile and a metaphor.

No one with a discerning critical eye can fail to see the remoteness of these three interpretations. For if "the mountains" is the thing compared, then this state is not one that is fixed for them, so that it would be the point of comparison. And if the word "the mountains" is used metaphorically for something, and the passing of the clouds is likewise, then what is metaphorically meant (*al-musta'ar lahu*) is neither explicitly stated nor implicit.

There is nothing in the words of the exegetes that cures the question of why this verse is specific to the fact that the beholder thinks the mountains fixed, nor the explanation of the aspect of the likeness of their motion to the motion of the clouds, nor the connection of the concluding phrase (*tadhyil*) with His saying, ﴿the handiwork of God, who perfected everything﴾. Therefore this verse has a subtle placement and a meaning worthy of reflection. Its placement is that it occupies the position of an intervening sentence between the general statement and its explanation, from His saying, ﴿So whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth is terrified﴾ (27:87), to His saying, ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have better than it, and they will be safe from the terror of that Day﴾ (27:89). It is an insertion of a proof of the subtle handiwork of God in the course of warning and threat, a combination of calling people to reflect with admonitions and warnings, as was done in the sentence ﴿Have they not seen that We made the night for them to rest therein?﴾ (27:86), and so on. Alternatively, it is conjoined to the sentence ﴿Have they not seen that We made the night for them to rest therein?﴾ (27:86), and the sentence ﴿And the Day the Trumpet is blown﴾ (27:87) is an intervening clause between them, for the affinity of what the conjoined sentence contains, namely an allusion to the representation of life after death. But this is a call to the people of knowledge and wisdom, so that their attention is directed to the subtle wisdom in the universe and the marvelous craftsmanship.

This is from the knowledge deposited in the Qur'an so that it may be a miracle from the scientific side, which the people of knowledge perceive, just as it was a miracle to the eloquent from its compositional side, as we have mentioned in the second aspect of the tenth introduction.

People used to think that the sun revolves around the earth, so that from its revolution arises the system of night and day, and they regarded the earth as stationary. Some of the Greek scholars came to the view that the earth is what revolves around the sun, in each day and night a single revolution, from which the darkness of approximately half the terrestrial globe and the light of the other half are formed, and this is what is expressed as night and day. But this was a theory that was regarded critically, and what indicated it was only the principle that the smaller body is more fitting to move around the larger body to which it is bound in its course. This is a persuasive reason, since motion has different orbits, so there is no obstacle to the smaller moving around the larger in the view of the eye and the measurement of calculation. This theory was not confirmed until the seventeenth century through the Italian mathematician Galileo. The Qur'an incorporates within its many proofs, following the proof of the formation of light and darkness, a proof that it alluded to by a symbol, so the exegetes did not address it, and you do not hear from them a sound.

It connected the indication of the earth's motion to the motion of the mountains upon it, because the mountains are the protruding parts of the terrestrial globe. The appearance of the motion of their shadows, decreasing before noon until they reach the limit of their decrease, and then increasing after noon, and the observation of the motion of those shadows, a motion that resembles the crawling of ants, is clearer to the observer. Likewise, the appearance of the motion of their peaks in front of the disc of the sun in the morning and evening is more manifest, even though the sun is fixed in its place according to the observations of the constellations and the lights.

It is for this consideration that the method of argument changed from the one in His saying, ﴿Have they not seen that We made the night for them to rest therein?﴾ (27:86). Here it was made in the form of address: ﴿And you see the mountains﴾. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), as an instruction to him concerning a meaning whose reality he perceives. For this reason the address was restricted to him and was not generalized as the saying ﴿Have they not seen that We made the night for them to rest therein?﴾ (27:86) was generalized in that address. It was also a reserving of it for the scholars of his community who would come at the time when this subtle truth becomes manifest. The Prophet (ﷺ) was informed by God of this marvelous secret in the order of the earth, just as God informed Abraham (peace be upon him) of how the dead are brought to life. God singled out His Messenger (ﷺ) with knowledge of this at his time and entrusted him with knowledge of this marvelous secret in His Book, and He did not command him to convey it, since the knowledge of it had no benefit for people at that time,

**[Page 50]**

until, when knowledge uncovered it from its veil, the people of the Qur'an found this to be true in His Book, and they drew the sword of proof with it, and it was in its sheath.

This interpretation of the verse is the one supported by His saying ﴿And you see the mountains﴾, which implies that the beholder sees them in the appearance of stillness, and by His saying ﴿thinking them fixed﴾. For this interpretation, in the sense of "fixed," is the one that suits the state of the mountains, since mountains are not molten.

His saying ﴿while they pass by﴾, which means movement, ﴿as the clouds pass﴾, means a clear passing, yet it is not evident at first glance. And His saying after all this, ﴿the handiwork of God, who perfected everything﴾, implies that it is a consideration of the state of their familiar order, not of the state of the order's breakdown, because the disruption of the order does not suit the description of it as a perfected handiwork. Rather, it is described as a great matter or something similar, among the states of the Hereafter, which do not fall within the grasp of imagination.

﴿as the clouds pass﴾ is a verbal noun (*masdar*) specifying the kind of passing of the mountains, that is, a passing by which they move from one direction to another, while the beholder supposes them fixed in their place, just as the observer of the clouds, which cover the horizon, supposes them stationary while they move from one quarter and rain on one place to another, so the observer does not perceive them until they have gone out of his sight. By this you know that *marr* (passing) is other than the *sayr* (travel) in His saying, ﴿And the Day We set the mountains in motion, and you see the earth laid bare﴾ (18:47), for that is at a time when the order of the terrestrial world is disrupted.

His saying ﴿the handiwork of God﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun, emphasizing the content of the clause ﴿they pass by as the clouds pass﴾, with the implied meaning: God made that handiwork. This is a glorification of this marvelous order, for great bodies move over vast distances while people suppose them stable and at rest, while they carry them along without their noticing.

*Al-jamida* means the stationary; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. In *al-Kashshaf* (of al-Zamakhshari): *al-jamida* derives from *jamada* in its place, when it does not move. He means that its stillness is figurative, and this figurative usage became so common that it equaled the literal meaning.

*Al-sun'* (handiwork): al-Raghib said: it is the excellent performance of an act. Every *sun'* is an act, but not every act is a *sun'*. God said, ﴿and he builds the ship﴾ (11:38), and ﴿and We taught him the craft of armor for you﴾ (21:80). It is said of a skilled, accomplished man: *sani'*, and of a skilled, accomplished woman: *sanna'*. End of quotation. Al-Jawhari, the author of *Lisan* (Ibn Manzur), and the author of *al-Qamus* (al-Firuzabadi), and its supplement in *Taj al-'Arus* (al-Zabidi), fell short in explaining *sun'*. I say: as for His saying, "*bi'sa ma sana'ta*" (What an evil thing you have done), it is meant as a rebuke to someone who thought he had done a good act and did not notice its ugliness. So *sun'*, when used absolutely, is directed to good and beneficial work, and when another sense is intended, it must be restricted, either because it is rare, or sarcastic, or by way of mutual correspondence (*mushakala*).

Know that *sun'* is used of skilled work, whether good or evil. God said, ﴿What they have fashioned will only be the trick of a magician﴾ (20:69). His description of God as ﴿who perfected everything﴾ is a generalization intended to make the matter easy, that is: this marvelous handiwork is nothing but like its counterparts among the divine crafts, which are finely made. This implies that the moving of the mountains is a perfected order, and that it belongs to the kind of creation, bringing into being, and the sustaining of order, not to disruption and dismantling.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, He is Aware of what you do﴾ is a concluding phrase (*tadhyil*) or an intervening statement at the end of the speech, for admonition, exhortation and warning, following His saying ﴿who perfected everything﴾. For the perfection of craft is one of the effects of the breadth of knowledge. The One who by His knowledge perfected everything is Aware of what creatures do, so let them beware of disobeying His command.

Then, to detail this, came His saying ﴿Whoever brings a good deed﴾ (27:89), up to the end of the verse. Thus it was a transition (*takhallus*) and a return to what occurs on the Day the Trumpet is blown. And those who made the matter of the mountains one of the events of the Day of Gathering made the sentence ﴿Indeed, He is Aware of what you do﴾ an explanatory resumptive sentence (*istinaf bayani*), answering an unstated question: "What will come after the blast, the terror, the presence before God, and the moving of the mountains?" It was answered in a general way, that God is Knowing of people's deeds. Then it was detailed by His saying ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have better than it﴾ (27:89), up to the end of the verse.

The majority read *bi-ma taf'alun* (what you do) with the second-person *ta'* (addressing you). Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read *yaf'aluna* with the third-person *ya'* (they do), its pronoun referring to ﴿whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth﴾ (27:87).

**[Page 52]**

Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr (*al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr*) on Surah 27, verse 89:

﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have better than it, and they will be safe from the terror of that Day.﴾ ﴿And whoever brings an evil deed, their faces will be overturned into the Fire.﴾ [al-Naml: 90] This sentence is an explanation arising from His words ﴿So whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified, except whom Allah wills﴾ [al-Naml: 87], because terror necessitates being gathered and presented for reckoning. The *man* (whoever) in both sentences is conditional (*sharṭiyya*, a conditional particle).

The verb *jāʾa* (came, brings) is used in its literal sense (*ḥaqīqa*, its primary meaning). The *bāʾ* in *bi-l-ḥasanati* and *bi-l-sayyiʾati* is the *bāʾ* of accompaniment (*lil-muṣāḥaba*) in its figurative sense (*majāziyya*), and its meaning is: he who possesses the good deed or he who possesses the evil deed. This is not like His words ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like, and whoever brings an evil deed will be recompensed only with its like﴾ [al-Anʿām: 160] at the end of al-Anʿām. The meaning here is: whoever comes on that Day while being among the doers of good deeds, and whoever comes while being among the people of evil deeds. Thus *al-majīʾ* (the coming) relates to His words ﴿and all of them will come to Him humbled﴾. The words *ḥasana* (good deed) and *sayyiʾa* (evil deed) here are generic, and the generic is taken to mean its most complete instances in the rhetorical context (*al-maqām al-khiṭābī*), i.e., whoever's state is purely of good deeds or whose good deeds are the predominant part of his condition, as His words ﴿and they will be safe from the terror of that Day﴾ require. Likewise, whoever's state is purely of evil deeds or predominantly so, as His words ﴿their faces will be overturned into the Fire﴾ [al-Naml: 90] imply.

The phrase ﴿*khayrun minhā*﴾ (better than it) is an elative noun (*ismu tafḍīl*, comparative form) to which the comparative *min* (*min al-tafḍīliyya*) is attached. That is: he will have a recompense better than a single good deed, in accordance with His words in the other verse ﴿then he will have ten times its like﴾ [al-Anʿām: 160]; or it means better than it in honour, because the good deed is the servant's act while the reward for it is Allah's bounty.

His words ﴿and they will be safe from the terror of that Day﴾ are an elaboration of His earlier words ﴿except whom Allah wills﴾ [al-Naml: 87]. These are the ones who were the people of good deeds, i.e., they were purely devoted to them, or their good deeds overwhelmed their evil deeds to a great degree, such that their evil deeds were of the type forgiven by good deeds or cancelled by repentance and the restoration of wrongs. Likewise His words ﴿And whoever brings an evil deed, their faces will be overturned into the Fire﴾ [al-Naml: 90], i.e., their evil deeds overwhelmed them and covered their good deeds, or they were purely devoted to evil deeds, by being disbelievers, or by being among the believers who were people of crimes and wretchedness. Between the people of these two states there are many categories, in degrees of reward and degrees of punishment. The sum of the matter is that a good deed has its effect on that Day, either immediately or in the hereafter, and that an evil deed has its evil effect in proportion to its magnitude and to what accompanies it of its like and what counterbalances it of good deeds, its opposites ﴿So no soul will be wronged in the least﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 47].

The majority of reciters read ﴿*min fazaʿi yawmaʾidhin*﴾ (from the terror of that Day) with the word *fazaʿ* (terror) in the genitive, being annexed (*iḍāfa*) to *yawm* (day) from *yawmaʾidhin*, and *yawm* annexed to *idh* (when). The vowel of *yawm* is then a fixed vowel (*fatḥat bināʾ*, a vowel of indeclinability), because it is a noun of time annexed to a non-declinable noun. So *fazaʿ* is definite by annexation to *yawm*, *yawm* is definite by annexation to *idh*, and *idh* is annexed to its sentence, for which the compensatory *tanwīn* (*tanwīn al-ʿiwaḍ*, the nunation serving as compensation) stands in as substitute. The implied meaning is: from the terror of the Day when they come to their Lord.

ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read *fazaʿin* with *tanwīn* (nunation), and *yawmaʾidhin* in the accusative as an adverb of time (*mafʿūl fīhi*), dependent on *āminūn* (safe). The meaning is the same in both readings, since what is intended is the terror mentioned in His words ﴿So whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified﴾ [al-Naml: 87]. Since it is specific, its definiteness and indefiniteness are equivalent. Thus the two readings agree in meaning, because the annexation of a verbal noun and its indefinite form are equal in not conveying generality, so it is determined that it is one single terror.

*Al-Kabb* means turning the outer surface of a thing toward the ground. In this verse *al-kabb* is attached to the faces (*wujūh*) rather than to the rest of the body, although the overturning applies to the whole body, because the faces are the first part to be turned toward the ground when one is overturned, as in the words of Imruʾ al-Qays:

*yakubbu ʿalā l-adhqāni dawḥa l-kanahbali*
(He falls upon his chins among the great trunks of the kanahbal tree.)

This belongs to the same category as His words ﴿they bewitched the eyes of the people﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 116], and His words ﴿and when they were struck with remorse [lit. when it fell into their hands]﴾, and the words of al-Aʿshā:

*wa-uqdimu idhā mā aʿyunu l-nāsi tafraqu*
(And I advance when the eyes of the people are terrified.)

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 27, verse 90:**

﴿Are you recompensed except for what you used to do?﴾

This is a *tadhyil* (a concluding clause that restates the general point after what has preceded). It serves as a conclusion to the preceding warnings. The address is to the polytheists who hear the Qur'an, in the manner of *iltifat* (a shift from the third person, using apparent nouns, which are of the category of the absent) to direct address. The pronouns referring to them begin from His words, "Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear" and the verses that follow up to this point. The apparent requirement would have been to say, "Are you recompensed except for what you used to do?" This sentence therefore summarizes what came before: that the recompense is according to their beliefs and deeds, and belief is nothing but an act of the heart. For this reason the address was directed to them face to face.

It is also permissible that this be a quoted statement, following an omitted verb of saying addressed to the people on that Day. That is, it is said to every group: "﴿Are you recompensed except for what you used to do?﴾"

Page 54

The interrogative form here carries the sense of negation, as indicated by the exception (*istithna'*). Ibn Hisham, in *Mughni al-Labib*, counted the use of *hal* to mean negation as a ninth usage. He said: that the interrogative with it is intended as negation, and for this reason the exception *illa* ("except") follows the predicate after it, as in "﴿Is the recompense of goodness anything but goodness?﴾ [al-Rahman: 60]." The *ba'* in his saying:

*"Is there not one who enjoys a pleasant life that is lasting?"*

He said at the end of his discussion: among the meanings of denial that the interrogative is used for is the denial of the occurrence of a thing, and this is the meaning of negation. This is something that *hal* alone has, unlike the *hamza*. Al-Damamini said in *al-Hawashi al-Hindiyya*, regarding his statement, "the interrogative with *hal* is intended as negation": this indicates that there is an interrogative here, but it is figurative, not literal, and so on.

I say: this usage is common, and from it is the saying of Labid:

*"Am I not but of Rabi'a or Mudar?"*

and the saying of al-Nabigha:

*"Is there any shame upon me in that I fear you?"*

Here he used *min* ("any"), which enters upon an indefinite noun in a negative context to make the generality explicit, and its examples are numerous. Perhaps the origin of this is that it is an interrogative about the negation, for the purpose of affirming the negation. The estimated sense is: "Are you not recompensed except for what you used to do?" Then, because the exception accompanied it regularly, and because the superfluous particle of negation appears in some contexts, they omitted the negative particle and imbued the interrogative particle with the meaning of negation, relying on the context. Thus the import of the utterance became negation, and *hal* was stripped of the interrogative sense and came to express negation. I have already pointed to this verse when discussing His words, "﴿Are they recompensed except for what they used to do?﴾ [al-A'raf: 147]," in *al-A'raf*.
