Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 27, verses 91–92:

﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, who has made it sacred, and to Whom all things belong. And I have been commanded to be among those who submit (to Him). And to recite the Qur'an. Whoever is guided, is guided only for his own soul. And whoever goes astray, say: I am only one of the warners.﴾

This surah addresses many of the objections of the polytheists against the Qur'an and against what it brought of the fundamentals of Islam: monotheism (tawhid), resurrection (ba'th), and warning (wa'id). It does so through various forms of explicit statement, implication, and allusion, and through reference to the situation of the earlier deniers. This is detailed at length, beginning with His saying: “﴿These are the verses of the Qur'an and a clear Book﴾ (al-Naml: 1) ﴿a guidance and good tidings for the believers﴾ (al-Naml: 2)” up to this point. When, in the course of that, they persistently pressed the Messenger (ﷺ) to bring them what he had promised them, or to specify the time of it, and said: ﴿When will this promise be fulfilled, if you are truthful?﴾ (al-Naml: 71).

It also refuted their objections, their excuses, and their evasions with various kinds of proofs, by analogy and by example. God strengthened His Messenger with various kinds of reassurance, beginning with His saying ﴿When Moses said to his family: I have perceived a fire﴾ (al-Naml: 7) and His saying ﴿So put your trust in God; you are indeed upon the manifest truth﴾ (al-Naml: 79), together with what accompanied that of mention of what the earlier messengers encountered.

After all of that, the discourse was resumed in a manner that serves as a summation (fadhlaka) of the reckoning and a conclusion for the surah, and a decisive word (fasl al-khitab). By it, He undermined the arrogance of the polytheists, who imagined that they had silenced the Messenger (ﷺ) with what they had thrown at him, and whose vain pride (ghurur) soars with the sophistry they had composed and the confusion they had brought. It also strengthens the Messenger and reassures him that he has pleased his Lord by discharging the trust of conveying the message. This is because the Messenger (peace be upon him) was commanded to say to them: ﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, who has made it sacred﴾. This is an instruction (talqin) to the Messenger (ﷺ). The sentence is the object of an omitted verb of speech, indicated by what is conjoined to it twice in this verse, namely: ﴿So say: I am only one of the warners﴾ and ﴿Say: Praise be to God﴾ (al-Naml: 93). The first is a consequence of it and thus connected to it, while the second is conjoined to the beginning of the discourse.

The opening of the speech with the particle of restriction (hasr) is to convey a relative restriction (hasr idafi), in view of what their previous exchanges contained of demanding the hastening of the threat, and of their disputing with it the denial of the gathering (hashr).

The meaning is: I have not been commanded with anything of what you seek, neither specifying the term of the threat, nor uprooting the denial of resurrection from your souls, nor anything other than this: except that I remain steadfast in worshipping one Lord, that I be one who submits, and that I recite the Qur'an to you. In it are the shining proofs and the decisive evidences. ﴿Whoever is guided﴾ then does not confer a favour upon me by his guidance; he benefits only his own self. ﴿And whoever goes astray﴾, I am not capable of guiding him, but I warn him, just as the messengers warned their peoples, and they did not possess guidance for them until God destroyed the misguided. This is in the sense of His saying: ﴿If they argue with you, say: I have submitted my face to God, and so have those who follow me﴾ (Al 'Imran: 20).

Within this there has been woven an acknowledgment of the status of Mecca, and an allusion to them regarding their disbelief in the One who settled them there and made it sacred, so that they benefited from its sanctity. It also informed them that they do not own that city. God thus laid bare to them what their breasts conceal of thoughts of expelling the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers from Mecca. This is among what His saying required: ﴿Indeed your Lord knows what their breasts conceal and what they reveal﴾ (al-Naml: 74).

For these subtleties, He attributed the relative clause "who has made it sacred" (harrama tilka al-balda) to God, rather than making the relative pronoun refer to the city. Therefore He did not say "which God has made sacred", because the relative clause contains a reminder of the favour upon them, and an allusion to their misguidance in worshipping idols which own nothing of the city and have not conferred upon it any virtue or distinction. This is like His saying: ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House﴾ (Quraysh: 3).

The demonstrative reference is to the city in which they are, because it is present before them by the presence of what is manifest of it to the eyes. The demonstrative pointing to places in this sense is common. God said: ﴿And they were followed in this world by a curse﴾ (Hud: 60), and He said: ﴿Indeed We will destroy the people of this town﴾ (al-'Ankabut: 31).

The shift from mentioning Mecca by its proper name to the form of demonstrative reference is for the veneration that the demonstrative implies.

The specification of the demonstrative by "the city" (al-balda) is because al-balda, with the feminine ending, is a name for a particular, definite, known, and bounded tract of land. It therefore includes Mecca and what surrounds it up to the limits of the sanctuary (haram). The meaning of "harramaha" is "made it forbidden (haram)". Haram means "prohibited", and tahrim means "prohibition". The object of the prohibition is known from the context, through what suits the prohibited thing. So what is meant by the prohibition of the city is the prohibition of anything entering it that opposes its welfare and the welfare of what is in it of inhabitants, animals, and trees. This includes forbidding raiding its people, aggression against them, oppressing them, terrifying them, hunting its game, and cutting its trees within known boundaries. This prohibition is among what God revealed to Abraham (peace be upon him) when He commanded him to build a House for His unity, and by answering Abraham's supplication when he said: ﴿My Lord, make this a secure city﴾ (al-Baqarah: 126).

Prohibition may be a perfection for what is prohibited, and it may be a deficiency, depending on the consideration of the cause and the nature of the prohibition. The prohibition of a place or a time is a distinction and an elevation. The prohibition of indecencies, carrion, blood, and wine is a debasement of them. And the prohibitions regarding lineage, nursing, and marriage by affinity are an increase in the sanctity (hurma).

The prohibition of a place is the forbidding of what harms the one who dwells in it. The prohibition of a time, such as the prohibition of the sacred months, is the forbidding of what harms those who are present in it.

The following of this with the sentence ﴿and to Whom all things belong﴾ is a precaution (ihtiras), lest one imagine from the attribution of His lordship to the city that His dominion is restricted to it. This makes known that this attribution is for the honouring of the one to whom it is attributed, not for defining the one attributed by specifying a manifestation of His dominion.

The repetition of "I have been commanded" (umirtu) in His saying ﴿And I have been commanded to be among those who submit﴾ is to indicate the difference between the two commands. The first is a command he carries out for his own self, and it is a command of inspiration (ilham), since God preserved him from worshipping idols before prophethood. The second is a command that requires prophethood, and it encompasses calling creation to monotheism. For this subtlety, "I have been commanded" is not repeated in His saying ﴿and to recite the Qur'an﴾, because both submission and recitation are among the affairs of prophethood.

In His saying ﴿to be among those who submit﴾ there is an honouring of this community, since God made His Messenger one of its individuals. This is a subtle point about the departure from saying "to be one who submits" (musliman).

Recitation (tilawa) is the reading of a specific speech to people. It has been discussed earlier in His saying ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recite it as it should be recited﴾ (al-Baqarah: 121), and His saying ﴿and they followed what the devils recited over the kingdom of Solomon﴾ (al-Baqarah: 102), in Surah al-Baqarah.

The object of recitation is omitted because it is evident, that is: to recite the Qur'an to the people.

What is derived from recitation is what requires the division of people into one who is guided and one who is astray, that is, one who benefits from the recitation of the Qur'an upon him, and one who does not benefit. It makes clear that whoever is guided, his guidance is for the benefit of his own self. This is an added encouragement to the listeners to be guided by the guidance of the Qur'an, since in it lies their benefit, as the lam (of benefit) indicates.

The explicit mention of the verb of saying here is to emphasise that the share of the Prophet (ﷺ) in calling those who turn away and are astray is to convey the warning to them. So they should not hope that his being turned away from will lead him to press them insistently to accept his call. What is meant by "the warners" is the messengers, that is: I am only one of the messengers; I have not been a novelty among the messengers, and my way is the way of those sent before me, which is conveyance (tabligh): ﴿Upon the messengers is nothing but clear conveyance﴾ (al-Nahl: 35).

﴿Say: "Praise be to God. He will show you His signs, and you will recognize them. Your Lord is not unaware of what you do."﴾

What the Messenger ﷺ was commanded to say to the obstinate opponents included the affirmation that God had guided him to the true religion, which consists of monotheism and the laws of Islam, and that God had guided people through him by means of what God revealed to him of the Qur'an that is recited, and that He had placed him among the warning messengers. This was among the greatest of blessings bestowed upon him in this world, and the most glad-tidings of the highest rank in the Hereafter. For this reason he was commanded to praise God with the very words by which God praised Himself, namely the phrase "Praise be to God" (al-Hamd lillah), which comprises many meanings of praise, whose explanation has already been given at the beginning of Surat al-Fatihah. The discussion of His saying, ﴿Say: "Praise be to God, and peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen"﴾ [al-Naml: 59], in this surah, has also already passed.

Then He continued with a precaution against what the obstinate opponents might suppose when they hear the verses disavowing knowledge of the unseen, and restricting the station of messengership to calling to the truth. Lest there be in that a contradiction of the threat of punishment, He concluded the speech by affirming that the threat is near and unavoidable, and that God does not break His promise, so that the proofs of God's truthfulness in His promise will become manifest to them. For this reason He described the threat as "signs," indicating that what the Messenger ﷺ had told them would indeed befall them, and that they would then be certain that what he had been saying to them was true. Thus the meaning of "you will recognize them" (fa-ta'rifunaha) is: you will recognize their indication of what the Messenger conveyed to you of warning, because when recognition was linked to them under the title that they are "signs of God," the object of recognition was what the notion of indication and sign contained in the title of "signs."

The particle sin (in sa-yurikum, "He will show you") indicates that the showing is near. The signs therefore occur in this world, such as the smoke, the splitting of the moon, and the destruction of their leaders on the day of Badr. Their recognition of them occurs immediately after they happen, even at the time of the death-throes and the rattle of death. Abu Sufyan said on the night of the Conquest: "I have indeed known that had there been with God another god besides Him, it would have availed me nothing." And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth﴾ [Fussilat: 53]. Among the signs within themselves is the striking of the swords of the believers, whom they had been belittling, upon the necks of their masters and great men on the day of Badr. Abu Jahl, with his spirit at his throat on the day of Badr, said: "Have I been made to suffer by a man whom his own people have killed?" meaning himself, and this was something that had never occurred to his mind.

[Page 59]

As for His saying, ﴿Your Lord is not unaware of what you do﴾, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hafs, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read "ta'malun" ("you do") with the ta' of address (tā' al-khitāb). In that case this is part of what the Messenger, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him, was commanded to say to the polytheists, and it contains an added warning that their deeds merit what they will see of the signs. What is intended is what they do in the matter of receiving the call of His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ and his Qur'an, because the negation of heedlessness regarding God is used in an allusive sense to mean that He is lying in wait for them and leaves none of their deeds unaccounted for.

The rest read "ya'malun" ("they do") with the ya' of the third person (yā' al-ghayba). In that case it is coordinated with "Say" (qul), and the intended purpose is to console the Messenger, peace be upon him, after he was commanded to say what he said, namely that God has counted their deeds and will recompense them for them, so that he should not despair of God's help.

This verse has come as a concluding statement that is comprehensive and reaches the utmost limit of the eloquence of a fine conclusion.

In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful.

Surat al-Qasas

It is called Surat al-Qasas, and no other name for it is known. The reason for this name is the occurrence of the word "al-qasas" (the narrative) in it, in His saying: ﴿And when he came to him and related to him the narrative﴾ [al-Qasas: 25].

The "narrative" to which the surah is attributed is the narrative of Musa (Moses), which he related to Shu'ayb, peace be upon them both, concerning what he encountered in Egypt before leaving it. When what Musa related was reported in the surah, this surah became one containing narrative for the purpose of recounting a narrative, so the narrative pervades it. The word "qasas" also occurs in Surat Yusuf, but Surat Yusuf was revealed after this surah.

It is Meccan according to the opinion of the majority of the Successors (tabi'un, the generation after the Companions). It contains the verse: ﴿Indeed, He who has ordained the Qur'an upon you will surely bring you back to a place of return﴾ [al-Qasas: 85]. It was said that it was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ at al-Juhfah, on his way to Madinah for the Hijrah, as consolation to him for leaving his homeland. This does not conflict with its being Meccan, because what is meant by "Meccan" (makki) is what was revealed before the Prophet ﷺ settled in Madinah, just as what is meant by "Medinan" (madani) is what was revealed after that, even if its revelation took place in Makkah.

It is reported from Muqatil and Ibn 'Abbas that His saying: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book before it, they believe in it﴾ [al-Qasas: 52], up to His saying: ﴿Peace be upon you; we do not seek the ignorant﴾ [al-Qasas: 55], was revealed at Madinah.

It is the forty-ninth surah in the order of the revelation of the surahs of the Qur'an. It was revealed after Surat al-Naml and before Surat al-Isra'. These three Ta-Sin surahs were thus revealed consecutively, as they are arranged in the Mushaf. They are alike in that all three begin with mention of Musa, peace be upon him. Perhaps this is what led the compilers of the Mushaf to place them together in sequence.

It has eighty-eight verses by the agreement of those who count the verses.

* * *

[Page 62]

Its Objectives

This surah contains the exalting of the matter of the Qur'an, and an allusion that the eloquent among the polytheists are unable to produce a surah like it. It also contains a detailed explanation of what was summarized in Surat al-Shu'ara' regarding the words of Pharaoh to Musa: ﴿Did we not raise you among us as a child?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 18], up to His saying: ﴿and you were of the disbelievers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 19]. Surat al-Qasas thus explains how Musa was raised in the household of Pharaoh.

It also explains the cause of the end of Pharaoh's kingdom.

It contains a detailed explanation of what was summarized in Surat al-Naml regarding His saying: ﴿When Musa said to his family: "Indeed, I have perceived a fire"﴾ [al-Naml: 7]. Surat al-Qasas explains how Musa travelled with his family, where he perceived the fire, and describes the place where he was addressed with revelation, until it mentions Musa's call to Pharaoh. This surah is therefore the most comprehensive account of the circumstances of Musa's upbringing up to the time he conveyed the call. Then it summarized what followed, because its detailed account is in Surat al-A'raf and Surat al-Shu'ara'. The purpose of the detail is what it contains of added admonitions and lessons.

Since the recounting of that narrative is solely for lesson and admonition, so that the polytheists may know God's way in sending messengers and His dealing with the nations that denied their messengers,

and since He challenged the polytheists with the knowledge of the Prophet ﷺ of that, though he was unlettered, who neither read nor wrote, nor had he mixed with the People of the Book, God appended to that a warning to the polytheists about it and a caution about the evil outcome of polytheism, and warned them with an eloquent warning.

He refuted their saying: ﴿Why was he not given the like of what was given to Musa?﴾ [al-Qasas: 48], by referring to the miraculous signs such as the turning of the staff into a serpent, and then exposed their inconsistency in their saying when they had denied Musa too.

He challenged them with the inimitability of the Qur'an and its guidance alongside the guidance of the Torah.

He nullified their excuses, then warned them with what befell the nations that denied God's messengers.

He presented them with proofs of the Oneness of God, all of which are blessings upon them, and reminded them of what would befall them on the Day of Recompense.

[Page 63]

He also rebuked them for their arrogance over the Muslims in their strength, their blessings, and their wealth, showing that this is the enjoyment of the worldly life, and that what is stored up for the Muslims with God is better and more lasting.

He followed this by setting forth for them the example of Qarun among the people of Musa. He then passed from this to remind them that the likes of those will not enjoy the bliss of the Hereafter, and that the final outcome belongs to the God-fearing.

Interwoven with all this is an allusion to the approaching migration of the Muslims to Madinah, and an allusion that God will grant them victory over the polytheists, by His saying: ﴿And We wish to bestow favour upon those who were oppressed in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 5], and so on.

He concluded the speech with consoling the Messenger ﷺ, strengthening him, and promising him that He will place his city under his control and empower him over the foreheads of the misguided.

It seems closest to me that the Muslims wished that the story of Musa's mission be explained in detail to them, so the purpose was that they benefit from what is in its details of useful knowledge, as a parallel to their own situation and that of their enemies. Therefore the primary intended audience is the Muslims, and for this reason He, exalted is He, said at its beginning: ﴿We recite to you from the news of Musa and Pharaoh in truth for a people who believe﴾ [al-Qasas: 3], meaning, for the believers.
